US officials want Section 702 renewed before damaging court ruling goes public

Ars Technica October 27, 2026

Senators say officials hid a ruling on warrantless searches past its release deadline.

Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, Senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay.

Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers.

Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version.

This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.”

While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.”

According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI Director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.”

Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.”

Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.”

The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March.

Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it.

Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Employees in the US, Canada, India, and the UK may receive offers to leave MS today.

On Monday, Microsoft said it is offering voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees, or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout.

Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company’s employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels. fyi, levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected “based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.”

The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. In July, the Xbox division laid off 3,200 employees, or about 20 percent of its entire gaming division. As reported by CNBC, about 30 percent of eligible employees accepted the retirement offer, lessening the impact of the planned layoffs, according to Coleman. While the offer in April went out to long-tenured employees who might be nearing the end of their career, the VEO expands the effort to a much larger potential pool.

In comments to GeekWire in July, Coleman said Microsoft was looking into making voluntary exits part of workforce management more regularly. She described the current VEO as something that “builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.”

While layoffs remain the most common way to reduce headcounts in the tech world, Microsoft may be following Google’s playbook. As Business Insider reported, Alphabet offered employees voluntary exit packages in June and October 2025, and again in February 2026. Now, eligible Microsoft employees may have to decide whether to take a deal now or keep their jobs and face the uncertainty of future company-wide layoffs.

According to Microsoft’s blog, employees eligible for the VEO were to be contacted via email today. Microsoft will announce its latest earnings after market close later this week.

Worms mate in man’s eyes, get plucked out right before larvae burst out

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Case study gives a whole new meaning to “bedroom eyes.”

After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man’s peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes.

The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths’ hanky-panky.

According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm.

Examining the worms under a microscope, the doctors identified them as Thelazia callipaeda nematodes, which are widespread across Asia and have also established in parts of Europe. These parasites primarily infest the eyes of cats and dogs but can sometimes make their way into human eyes inadvertently.

The worms’ life cycle depends on flies that feed from the animals’ eyes, slurping up tears and secretions. When they feed from an infested eye, the flies can pick off the worms’ first-stage larvae, which use the insect as both an incubator and an air taxi. Inside the fly, the larvae molt twice, becoming third-stage larvae, which then migrate to the fly’s mouthparts and await the next stop at a suitable watery eyeball. The larvae disembark their flying nannies and take up a permanent peeper residence, where they develop into adults after one more molt. Adult worms then live and mate directly on a victim’s eyes.

Unlike other worms, female T. callipaeda are ovoviviparous, meaning that embryos develop within eggs inside the female worm’s body. Females release large broods of densely coiled first-stage larvae, which await being lapped up by a thirsty fly.

Some of the female worms pulled from the man’s eyes were plump with embryonated eggs. Doctors noted that coiled larvae began bursting out of some of them after they were pulled from the man’s eyes. The male worms, meanwhile, were identified by their copulatory spicules, needle-like structures used to facilitate mating.

Luckily for the man, having all of the adult worms plucked from his orbs meant the infection was over—no antiparasitic medication required, even if some of the larvae had been left behind. At a follow-up appointment two months later, doctors noted that all his eye symptoms had resolved and there were no more worms.

Meet the real-life Scottish surgeon who inspired Sherlock Holmes

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Lindsey Fitzharris chats with Ars about her new book, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes.

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland’s University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes, by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris.

A noted science communicator with a fondness for the medically macabre, Fitzharris published a biography of Scottish surgical pioneer Joseph Lister, The Butchering Art, in 2017—a great, if occasionally grisly, read. She followed up with 2022’s The Facemaker: A Visionary Surgeon’s Battle to Mend the Disfigured Soldiers of World War I, about a WWI surgeon named Harold Gillies who rebuilt the faces of injured soldiers.

In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of…, exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. And last year she and her husband, caricaturist Adrian Teal, collaborated on an illustrated children’s book, Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failures that Sparked Medical Marvels.

With Sleuth-Hound, Fitzharris returns to the Edinburgh of The Butchering Art, of body snatchers and surgeons’ discovery of ether, which was also the Edinburgh of Arthur Conan Doyle and Joseph Bell. Bell was notorious for his peculiar method of diagnosis: he was able to infer a patient’s occupation and personal habits, as well as any ailments, just by looking at them. For instance, Bell once figured out the route a patient had taken walking to the infirmary by identifying the type of clay on the patient’s boots—an incident Doyle used in The Sign of the Four. Bell was also something of a medical detective, working with a local police surgeon on some of the most famous murder cases of his day.

Ars caught up with Fitzharris to learn more.

Ars Technica: What drew you to writing an entire book about Joseph Bell?

Lindsey Fitzharris: I’ve known about Bell because I’m a medical historian and I knew that he was an inspiration for this character, but nobody had written a big commercial book on him. There was a book in 1982 by a guy named Ely Liebow. So people in the Sherlockian world, they know a bit about Bell through him, but I really wanted to bring a medical history lens to it.

When I sold the Sleuth-Hound proposal, I had never read the original Sherlock Holmes tales. I decided to put off reading them initially because I knew enough about Bell to know that it became an irritating comparison; he found it rather reductive at the end of his life. I really wanted to bring the real man behind the myth to life in Sleuth-Hound, not just as the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes, not just as this parlor trick, but as this complex character. I’ve been talking to a lot of Sherlockians who have been really surprised at how much Bell is Sherlock, but also how much he isn’t Sherlock. That’s an interesting discussion as well: why Conan Doyle focused on this one aspect of him.

Ars Technica: What are some of the ways Bell is and isn’t Sherlock?

Lindsey Fitzharris: He had this Sherlockian way about him where he could tell everything about a person before they ever spoke a word: a callous, a stain, a limp, all were clues to Bell if you only knew how to see it. But in a lot of ways he wasn’t Holmes. For instance, he was a deeply empathetic character. He was very feeling for his patients. And he also was a family man. His wife dies when he’s in his 30s, and he doesn’t remarry his entire life. He holds the torch for her. She dies in childbirth, and he raises his three children alone.

My husband is a caricaturist, and we have this discussion about how he can only caricature people he doesn’t know well. That’s because caricature is about those first impressions. I think Conan Doyle knew Bell in his capacity as a student, but he didn’t know Bell the man. So he took the most recognizable flashy trait of Bell and transposed that onto Sherlock Holmes. The question I pose at the end of the book is, would Holmes exist if Conan Doyle had known Bell better, or would he exist in the same format?

Ars Technica: Did Conan Doyle’s contemporaries recognize the similarities?

Lindsey Fitzharris: Those who knew Bell recognized it immediately. Robert Louis Stevenson reads Sherlock Holmes. He writes to Conan Doyle and he says at the end of the letter, “One thing bothers me, could this be our old friend Joe Bell?”

But Bell was a lot more complex, and I really wanted to bring that medical history lens, because this isn’t just a story about his relationship with Conan Doyle and the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes. It’s about the development of forensic medicine. It’s about the moment that medicine enters the courtroom for the first time. Bell wasn’t just the inspiration for Holmes; he was actually doing what Holmes was doing in practice. He was working officially with a police surgeon named Henry Duncan Littlejohn, who was fascinating in and of himself. He was a pioneer of fingerprinting and courtroom photography. They end up partnering and working on some of the biggest high-profile cases in Scotland in the 19th century.

Ars Technica: I was frankly shocked about the baby farming case; I had no idea that was a common practice.

Lindsey Fitzharris: It’s such a crazy story. The thing that I want people to contextualize here is that there was no birth control. So there were a lot of women having a lot of children, and they were deeply impoverished, and they didn’t have enough money to feed these children. So they turned to the baby farmer. In theory, the baby farmer took the child and then took a fee from you, the mother, with the promise that they would farm out the child to somebody who could take care of the child. That was how it was supposed to work. There were no legal routes for adoption in the 19th century, so they turned to the baby farmer.

The case in Sleuth-Hound, the baby farmer, Jessie King, ends up taking the fee and then just killing the infants. This was a horrific case. The chapter opens with these boys finding this bundle of rags and using it as a football and kicking it around. And then they open it, and it’s the decomposing remains of a child. Littlejohn and Bell work on the case. They perform the postmortems; they testify in the trial.

One of the dark themes of this book is that a lot of early forensics was built on the brutalized bodies of women in particular. Jessie King was killing infants, but this is a crime that is particular to women—women trying to get their children into families that could afford to feed them. A lot of the crimes are committed on women who never receive any justice, but the science outlives what their bodies taught these early forensic investigators like Bell and Littlejohn.

Ars Technica: Case in point: the infamous Chantrelle murder case and how it coincides with the rise of toxicology.

Lindsey Fitzharris: The Chantrelle case is so fascinating to me. Eugene Chantrelle was this respectable gentleman who lived in Edinburgh. He was a French tutor, and his wife Lizzie is seemingly poisoned by a gas leak, a broken pipe in the flat, and she’s removed from the property and later dies. But it turns out that Chantrelle was abusing her the entire marriage.

We think Littlejohn brought Bell onto the case. Bell and Littlejohn discover that it was opium poisoning, and they test the vomit on her nightgown, and they’re able to tie him to this crime. Bear in mind, Bell worked like Sherlock Holmes. He worked in the shadows. So in these earlier cases, it was very difficult to know if Bell really did work on them.

But there’s a really intriguing clue at the end of this story. Littlejohn investigates, [Eugene Chantrelle] is convicted, and he is hanged for this murder. On the scaffold, he allegedly looked around at the audience, locked eyes with Littlejohn, and shouted, “Give my regards to Joe Bell. He did a good job putting the noose around my neck.” This was such a Sherlockian moment. How did Chantrelle know that Bell had worked on this case? We don’t have any records that actually confirm this except that he allegedly said this on the scaffold.

The other extraordinary aspect of this story is that Chantrelle was drinking buddies with Robert Louis Stevenson, so he becomes one of the inspirations for Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde: this respectable person on the outside and very sinister and evil on the inside. The prosecutor told Stevenson that this was not Chantrelle’s first victim and that he had killed four or five other people with his opium and cheese parties.

Ars Technica: Your book launch should feature an opium and cheese party.

Lindsey Fitzharris: (laughs) And ether drinks. You’re invited. The Victorian period was wild because there were a lot of poisons that you could just get over the counter from your pharmacist. Chantrelle had trained as a doctor at one point and had bought a huge amount of opium just before the murder. Even the chemist thought that this was strange, but he assumed that Chantrelle was a doctor. So poison was a big problem in the Victorian period. Some of it was legal, it was hard to detect. Forensic medicine was just developing. I call it the golden era of murdering because you probably had more of a chance in the 19th century of getting away with it.

Ars Technica: Sleuth-Hound is written in a deceptively novelistic style, but you’ve clearly done very extensive research on this. What sources did you find most helpful?

Lindsey Fitzharris: One of the things that happened was that Bell’s diary became available, that had been locked away for over a century by the Bell family. Perhaps they were waiting for enough time to pass. I almost called the book Sleuth-Hounds because I do also think Littlejohn taught Conan Doyle as well. Bell gave Conan Doyle the method, and Littlejohn gave him the world of forensics. He was a professor of forensics in Edinburgh at the time. We can flesh out what Bell was doing because we know that they worked together often on these cases.

You do get dialogue through the murder trials, because there’s so many documents and court records that go along with these trials. There are a lot of letters, diaries. Nothing’s made up, but sometimes I had to take educated guesses. For instance, Conan Doyle is a terrible narrator of his own life. He constantly is contradicting himself, even in his own memoirs. It was difficult figuring out when he came into contact with Bell for the first time. I believe it’s in the winter of 1878, and I provide a lot of context for that in the back notes of the book.

I’m a historian. It’s got to be armed to the teeth with sources. But I want people to be able to pick up the book, not know anything about Sherlock Holmes, not know anything about medical history or forensics, and just be able to enjoy it. Medical history is the most universal way into the past. I make the past relatable. I tell you what that was like a hundred years ago.

My superpower in 2026 is that I’m one of the few people who can make you feel good about living today. Progress is not a straight line necessarily, but if you had that medical crisis a hundred years ago, it would’ve been a lot worse. I’ve been through cancer myself. Today is the best day to be alive and to get that diagnosis and tomorrow will be a little bit better, because I’m an optimist when it comes to medicine. I’m hoping that chemotherapy or radiation treatments will become obsolete. They’re brutal. And there’s a cancer vaccine on the horizon.

Ars Technica: In the US, sadly, we’re going backwards on vaccines for preventable diseases like measles.

Lindsey Fitzharris: I know. We have short memories. We don’t remember. It’s weird to me as a medical historian because I remember it all. I remember the times when parents lost their children to preventable diseases. It’s coming back, and it’s sad to see that repeat. If I could just show people the diaries and the letters of brokenhearted parents who lost child after child to measles or polio and all of these diseases we can now treat and prevent. I put up pictures of smallpox on social media, and people think it’s AI. They can’t believe that something like that existed. It’s the only human virus we’ve ever eradicated. It should be celebrated. So I’m always out there banging the drum. I hope that we steady the ship a bit and people learn from the past again.

Apple releases iOS and macOS 27.2 with new Siri AI features, new Music logo

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Included is the ability to limit which applications Siri can directly access.

Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.

Let’s start with iOS 27.2. This update is heavily focused on Siri AI. It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you. It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.

On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).

Other additions include context-aware suggestions within Messages (like turning a message inviting you to something into a calendar entry), SynthID watermarking support in Photos, and support for user profiles in the Apple TV app. There’s also the new Apple Music branding, plus the arrival of previously promised Apple Pencil support on the iPhone Duo foldable.

The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes. The same goes for the Apple Watch—again, mostly the same Siri-related updates. visionOS 27.2 includes the new languages and updated Music icon, as well.

Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.

Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

Apple reveals updated iPad mini with a bigger OLED screen for $700

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Apple claims this is the most significant update ever for the iPad mini line.

The iPhone Duo may be a bit of a risk right now, but there’s a new mid-size Apple touchscreen device that might do the job. Starting at $699, the 8th-gen iPad mini price has gone up, but there are some big changes. Apple says the refreshed 8th-gen iPad mini marks the most significant update ever for its petite tablet, featuring an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip that we first saw in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The device is almost a full millimeter thinner than the last iPad, coming in at just 5.4 mm. The chassis is also IP67 rated for water and dust protection. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn’t have any official IP rating.

The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we’ve come to expect from Apple’s Pro-level devices.

The 2-nanometer A20 Pro chip was a noticeable upgrade in the iPhone 18 Pro, and it will be even more significant in this tablet. The previous model had a 3-nanometer A17 Pro chip, which was already a year old when it appeared in the iPad mini. In the iPhone 18 Pro, we found the A20 Pro significantly improved graphics performance thanks in part to a 50 percent increase in memory bandwidth.

Higher memory speed also helps with on-device AI applications, but the Neural Engine is the primary factor. Unfortunately, not all versions of the new iPad mini will be equally capable. Apple notes the 512GB configuration will have the dual 16-core Neural Engine we saw in the iPhone 18 Pro, but the 128GB and 256GB versions will have a single 16-core NPU. These versions will also have a slightly different CPU configuration, with five cores instead of six.

Apple has retained the 12 MP cameras for the front and back of the tablet, but the front-facing one has changed location. Rather than being on the short edge for portrait-orientation video calls, it’s now on the long edge. That might take a little getting used to for those who frequently use their tablets for FaceTime.

The $699 base price gets you 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s $100 more for 256GB and $300 more for 512GB. The nano-texture display is also a $100 upsell, but it’s only available for the 256GB and 512GB versions. The step up to cellular will cost $849 for the 128GB model.

Pricing is, sadly, not eye-popping for 2026, but it marks yet another price increase for Apple. The 7th-gen iPad mini launched for $499 in 2024, but it has since risen to $599. The new model adds $100, but it does have some nice upgrades. Preorders for the new iPad mini begin at 10:10 am PT on October 28 (Wednesday), and devices will arrive on doorsteps and in stores on November 6.

ICE plan to buy robot dogs spurs protest from hundreds of Boston Dynamics employees

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

US robotics company stands by ICE deal as more than 300 employees warn of risk.

Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized.

On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station.

“Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.”

The petition described the signatories as employees who normally “love showing off what we do to our friends, family and the world” and who “love challenging ourselves to innovate and change the perception of what robots can do.” The 300 signatures come out of a total Boston Dynamics workforce of approximately 1,400 people.

The ICE contract covers the purchase of four Boston Dynamics Spot robots that were modified by Radeco to be marketed as a robot platform named Cerberus. The contract describes these Cerberus robots as being intended to “detect radiation, toxic gas leaks and explosive threats in urban environments or disaster zones,” along with enabling other remote observation and inspection missions.

A centerpiece of the upgraded robot is an oxygen sensor that is intended to “ensure the air quality is breathable when personnel are placed in confined spaces such as tunnels.” The Cerberus robot dog also has a camera equipped with 30-times zoom capability, 360-degree cameras, and infrared thermal imaging.

The Cerberus robot dog would come with an optional Spot robotic arm that enables it to manipulate objects and open doors, along with providing additional camera views when extended. The ICE contract describes the robot as being generally capable of navigating complex industrial environments on its own and executing “repeatable autonomous missions with minimal human intervention.”

Such a purchase was justified in the ICE contract as supporting the Homeland Security Task Forces’ mission to carry out “counter-illicit cross-border tunnel operations” and dismantling “cross-border human smuggling and trafficking networks” being conducted by “criminal cartels, foreign gangs and transnational criminal organizations throughout the United States.”

“Spot robots are tools that help keep people out of harm’s way,” a Boston Dynamics spokesperson told Ars in a statement. “Regardless of any political implications or personal feelings about the organizations involved, if our robot can help keep people safe, we believe it should.”

Boston Dynamics has also emphasized that the robots would primarily be used by ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations unit that is focused on combating transnational criminal organizations, according to WBUR.

However, the Brennan Center for Justice has documented the Homeland Security Investigations unit as frequently being involved in deporting undocumented workers and conducting workplace raids during the first administration of President Donald Trump. These operations occurred between 2018 and 2021, before being halted by US Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas early in the term of President Joe Biden.

During Trump’s second term that began in January 2025, the Homeland Security Investigations unit once again diverted thousands of agents to immigration enforcement and deportations after one of Trump’s executive orders redefined the unit’s primary mission, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project.

The Boston Dynamics employee petition specifically referenced an ICE and Homeland Security Investigations workplace raid that detained 475 primarily South Korean workers at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America facility in Georgia on September 4, 2025. Hyundai Motor Group became the parent company of Boston Dynamics after acquiring the US robotics company in June 2021.

“We cannot be proud of working at Boston Dynamics when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues at Hyundai,” according to the employee petition. “All elements of the ICE organization, not just Enforcement & Removal Operations, have worked to sow fear among all people living in this country.”

That single largest immigration enforcement operation of its kind sparked public outrage in South Korea and led to South Korean leaders questioning the country’s business investments in the United States. However, Hyundai has maintained its operations at the US electric vehicle production at the Metaplant America factory and still plans to deploy thousands of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots starting at its US facilities.

The Boston Dynamics leadership team has stood by the ICE contract with Radeco, which would mainly involve Boston Dynamics providing technical support for the modified robots, according to The Boston Globe.

The company also responded to the employee petition via an email from Amanda McMaster, former interim CEO for Boston Dynamics. That email was obtained and quoted in part by both The Boston Globe and WBUR.

“We believe this decision is in line with our purpose of ethically advancing intelligent machines in service of humanity,” McMaster wrote in her email. She urged workers to “respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it.”

McMaster also pointed to the company’s terms and conditions for sale of the Spot robots that prohibit “intentional use of the Product to harm or intimidate any person or animal, as a weapon, or to enable any weapon.” The company previously signed an open letter opposing the weaponization of “advanced-mobility general-purpose robots.”

The Boston Dynamics spokesperson told Ars that the company has “worked productively” with the Department of Homeland Security and Homeland Security Investigations unit for years, and said the latter have abided by the company’s terms and conditions of sale.

The robotics company said it would also “take immediate action” if any customer misused Spot, although it said “there have been no cases of a customer violating those terms and conditions” while working with the Department of Homeland Security and other “public safety agencies.”

“That would include specific steps like voiding the warranty, refusing all future software updates, terminating their license, taking any appropriate legal action available to us, and likely never selling to that customer again,” said the Boston Dynamics spokesperson.

The Boston Dynamics employee backlash to the ICE contract comes as the company is developing a new advanced robotics and AI facility in Waltham, Massachusetts, near its headquarters. The $100 million project includes creating 1,250 new jobs by 2033, according to a company press release.

The ICE contract represents “a complicated and emotionally charged topic for many people, including some of our own employees,” said the Boston Dynamics spokesperson. “As our company continues to grow at a rapid pace, we will continue welcoming a highly diverse group of employees with views on every side of the social and political spectrum.”

But as Boston Dynamics ramps up its production capabilities and deployment of robots such as Spot and Atlas, the employees who signed the petition expressed concerns that the company’s association with the ICE contract will threaten both workforce hiring and retention.

“We fear we will lose teammates over this decision, and worry about the risk it creates to achieve our shared company goals,” according to the petition. “This decision makes Boston Dynamics a less attractive employer—it will make it more challenging to build the team we need as we scale.”

Musk accuses Ukraine of violating Starlink terms with deadly drone strikes

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Ukraine says Starshield back to normal, denies misuse of Starlink commercial service.

Elon Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink terms of service by using it for lethal drone strikes.

Musk said Ukraine used the Starlink commercial service for offensive drone strikes. Musk’s comment on Saturday came after SpaceX imposed a restriction preventing Ukraine from using the satellite technology on drones flying above certain speeds.

One current and one former Ukraine official denied Musk’s accusation and said previous limits imposed by SpaceX already prevented Ukraine’s military from using Starlink in the way Musk described. Ukraine officials have accused Musk of throttling their use of Starshield, the military variant of Starlink that Ukraine has access to through a deal with the US government.

Meanwhile, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said over the weekend that the new satellite restrictions have been lifted, possibly ending a controversy that began almost two weeks ago.

Musk wrote on Saturday that “using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be. Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”

Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, denied the allegation in a Telegram post on Sunday. Beskrestnov wrote that all Starlink terminals located over Ukrainian territory, including territories occupied by Russia, were already subject to a movement speed limit of 70 to 90 kilometers per hour. He added that Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.

“Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations,” Beskrestnov wrote. He called it “very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine.”

Musk wrote on Sunday that Zelenskyy himself “posted about using Starlink for offensive drone strikes, which has always been against Starlink’s terms of service.” Musk cited a Zelenskyy post in which he said, “We also use Starlink for mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories.”

The Starlink and Starshield names are often used interchangeably by government officials discussing military use, making it difficult to determine whether certain statements refer to the civilian or military version of the technology. Zelenskyy and other Ukraine officials this month referred to both Starlink and Starshield when they complained that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour).

Ukraine officials say the restriction imposed earlier this month has been lifted. “Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again,” according to The Kyiv Independent.

Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday, “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds we had before the restrictions. The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered ‘shaheds.’”

Serhii Sternenko, who served as an advisor for the Ukraine Ministry of Defense earlier this year and now runs an organization that supplies drones to the Ukraine military, wrote that “Ukraine did not violate the terms of use.”

“Elon Musk claims that Ukraine allegedly violated Starlink’s terms of use and used the system on combat drones. As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko wrote. “In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians. But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work. In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”

Musk initially responded to the controversy by stating that, unlike the Starlink commercial service, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Musk added that “Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action,” but did not at first accuse Ukraine of violating that restriction.

President Trump denied making the decision to limit Ukraine’s satellite connectivity and reportedly called Musk to ask him to lift the restrictions.

SpaceX confirmed in 2023 that it had blocked Ukraine from using Starlink with military drones, saying its contract with Ukraine did not allow offensive uses. In May 2026, Musk said that US military suicide drones set up by a contractor incorrectly used Starlink instead of Starshield.

On Saturday, Musk wrote that “Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.”

Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Investigators explain how highway thieves stole $100M in data center equipment.

Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment.

NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.”

Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring.

Equipment commonly targeted includes “servers, fiber-optic cables, computer memory chips, copper wires, and bitcoin mining machines,” NBC News reported.

Some trailers hit seem to be carrying only data center equipment, like two stolen freights found in Illinois. The Cook County Sheriff’s Office estimated those contained $300,000 worth of copper wire spools and about $1 million in “custom-made data center modular power solutions equipment,” NBC News reported. Other trucks impacted were carrying additional freight, like a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department case where “data center cooling equipment” bound for Deepcool AI was recovered among nicotine pouches, televisions, shoes, printers, speakers, and skin care cosmetics. Experts worry that means Americans may be broadly harmed by the thefts, not just the AI industry.

While some stolen goods have been recovered, in two of the largest thefts that NBC News found, none of the equipment was found, and off-duty cops hired to escort the shipments were targeted in hit-and-runs.

A trailer carrying “several hundred pounds” of “computer server equipment” worth $13 million was destined to land in Fayetteville, Georgia, “home to one of the largest data center developments in the country.” Two off-duty cops hired as escorts lost sight of the trailer after an unmarked sedan struck their car and forced the cops to stop as the trailer drove on. Gerardo Pachuca, a private investigator and former LASD cop investigating cargo theft, told NBC News that “the accident was not an accident. The bad guys wanted that load, so they intentionally took out the escorts.”

The same thing happened with another shipment out of California, headed to Texas, NBC News reported. Carrying “server rack components estimated to be worth around $10 million,” that trailer also sped off after the security escorts’ vehicle was struck by an SUV. And troublingly, in that case, it didn’t matter that the “cargo was also being monitored by an application tracking its location,” because “the tracking coordinates had apparently been spoofed.”

In that second case, the spoofing shows one of many ways that highway thieves have begun leveraging digital tactics to target data center shipments more precisely, experts warned.

Broadly, cargo thieves are infiltrating email accounts to find lucrative shipments, misdirecting shipments, disrupting GPS tracking, and using AI to create fake driver’s licenses to get accomplices hired as delivery drivers. LASD’s Sgt. David Pantoja told NBC News “that’s how most of it is being done,” which is a big shift from the past when highway thefts were largely opportunistic.

As NBC News explained, these extreme examples where escorts were violently attacked are isolated events, but they’re part of a growing trend in high-end technology cargo thefts. Since 2025, there have been “nearly two dozen cargo theft incidents” in “states including California, Texas, and Utah,” and the “issue is only expected to grow” as AI firms continue to invest billions into data center infrastructure. Keith Lewis—head of operations at risk-assessment firm Verisk CargoNet, which tracks cargo thefts—told NBC News that “it’s like stealing pure gold bars,” and “it’s so much easier to steal this than to rob a bank.”

Unlike other kinds of cargo theft, data center equipment doesn’t often get sold in online marketplaces, experts told NBC News. Instead, stolen shipments can be broken down into parts and sold on gray markets to tech firms that rely on questionably sourced equipment to keep costs low. In many cases, an overseas buyer is already lined up before the theft occurs, investigators said, particularly in regions where access to high-end technology from the US may be restricted, like China.

For the AI industry and their freight industry partners, strengthening security is a critical step, and to do it right, they seemingly can’t rely too much on AI. In the past, vetting drivers and knowing clients was a key part of protecting shipments and ensuring they weren’t intercepted by bad actors bent on messing with the logistics.

Scott Cornell is chair of the Transported Asset Protection Association, Americas, or TAPA Americas, which is “the largest global nonprofit organization dedicated to supply chain security standards.” He told NBC News that although overseas crime rings currently tapping highway thieves are “playing chess in the supply chain,” there seems to be an easy path to checkmate if freight companies would slow down to run background checks on drivers.

“The only way this works is if the drivers are not properly vetted,” Cornell said.

Lawmakers are pushing to find solutions, too, including talking to people in industries hardest hit and proposing paths to strengthen federal response to overseas thefts. In the meantime, states coping with large thefts have formed specialized task forces to trace stolen shipments, and companies continue to look to escorts to solve the problem, despite the instances of violence.

Mike Duffy is the co-founder and CEO of Solutions Group International, which NBC News noted is “a security escort company based in Southern California, where much of the high-value goods are being manufactured.” He confirmed that “we’re escorting hundreds of loads per month” and “much of it” is “associated with data centers.”

F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend

Ars Technica October 26, 2026

Ars spends the weekend with the Audi Revolut F1 team at the Circuit of the Americas.

AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it’s the one the real fans mostly attend.

Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes.

It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle, and that’s just in the real world. Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts, how Pirelli designs its tires, and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes. And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September.

It’s changed a lot since I attended the first USGP back in 2012. There’s more landscaping. The grassy banks that surround the track are now covered in hospitality structures, including one connected to the paddock building by cable car, complete with not one but two swimming pools. Along its fringes, the skyline is now studded with rollercoasters and amusement rides, part of COTA’s diversification strategy that combines theme park, concert venue, and, of course, a place to race.

The basic track layout hasn’t changed in those 14 years, but the track surface has. Between the earthworks required to create the elevation changes and the extremes of central Texas’ weather, it gets bumpier each year.

I asked Allan McNish if one of America’s newest F1 venues might be turning into a modern equivalent of Sebring, one of its oldest US F1 venues. Located in central Florida, Sebring’s bumpy concrete was poured during WWII when it was a B-17 training facility; these days, it’s one of the toughest sports car races on earth thanks to the torture it puts a car through. McNish would know: He’s racing director of Audi’s F1 team, but he was one of its star drivers during the marque’s glory days in endurance racing, with three Le Mans and five Sebring wins.

“It’s funny. Sebring is bumpy as hell. It hasn’t changed since Stirling Moss drove there in the ’50s,” McNish told me. “It’s the same piece of tarmac into [turn] 1 and 17 and everything else. But the characteristics of what you need for a 12 hours of Sebring—or for us as we used it for [testing for] Le Mans—was basically it just shook everything.”

“It wasn’t the damping side of it and the aero and the impact… but in reality, if it survived that beating, then it was going to have a good chance to survive in Le Mans,” he said. “Here it’s different because we’re shorter in terms of timing. It’s really bumps only in three places.”

Unfortunately for the drivers, those are three very important spots on the track: “the braking zones, which is because of the amount of energy that’s going in through the brakes, into the tire and then into the tarmac. It’s like if you slide on a carpet and put your feet down, then the carpet bunches up,” McNish said.

“It might cause some problems, might cause downshift issues or whatever because a car’s moving around—it’s inconsistent because of that. But that’s what it is. Circuit’s the same for everybody, get on with it,” he said, with a chuckle, adding that’s easy to say now as he sits behind the pit wall and not behind a steering wheel.

As a former driver himself, McNish has insight into what his two drivers need from the team. “From my point of view, I do live inside the cockpit with them virtually when I’m watching what they’re doing, see what the car’s doing,” he said. “I understand when the car’s dancing around a little bit, what the reaction is and what they need from it and try and correlate the support in behind that with the engineering as well. So… I suppose my style is living it from the cockpit.”

2026 is Audi’s first year as an official F1 constructor, having completed its purchase of Sauber in 2024. The company wouldn’t be in the sport if it didn’t want to win races and championships, but it also recognizes that’s not the work of a minute. It has hardly embarrassed itself this year, though, considering it has no prior experience in the sport.

“We’re consistently fighting in and around Q3 [qualifying for the 10 fastest cars], which is now the point where you can get points,” McNish said. “So the momentum for us is the fact that we’re coming off best result for the weekend that we’ve had all year and career [in Singapore]. It’s the first time we’ve had a car in both the points in the sprint and in quali and the race. And at the same time, I think it was a really good one because we were so close in the two previous races and lost the point in the last lap, and that was hurting, really hurting.”

The team brought some aerodynamic upgrades to COTA, which it A/B tested during the first free practice session on Friday. “We brought one to Baku, which was a few races ago, and then this was the second part,” McNish said. “And that should give us a little bit more performance in the first sector. So basically through the fast esses, but also in the lower speed. And that’s maybe an area where we’ve—not so much lately—but struggled a little bit more earlier in the season.”

That work is forward-looking. “That’s for next year so that we can be more confident as we go forward with our tools. We can’t control the opposition. We don’t know them. What we can control is what our roadmap is, where we are going and how we are going to get there,” McNish said.

“And our roadmap really looks toward 2030, not just ’27. So we’re looking in terms of all of our preparation toward that bigger goal with different things on the way,” he said. “I think what you will find next year is that the top four teams will be the top four teams. I don’t think that’ll change because it doesn’t change overnight in these situations. And we’ve got to improve in all of the areas.”

Right now, the Audi is good in medium- and high-speed corners but less effective out of the slow ones and in terms of straight-line speed. That is partly due to the decision to use a larger turbocharger. “There’s [a] downside of that, and downside of the fact that one of the important things in the first season was to have a robust solid power unit and to make sure we had reliability from that, which is a really important part. You can see how difficult it is with the reliability issues that everybody had,” McNish said.

The unreliability of the new power units was probably to be expected; as McNish noted, there were also a lot of breakdowns in 2014, the first year of the last engine regulations. But this year’s hybrid systems have also come under fire for being too complicated and unpredictable. There’s a reason it’s all automated, though, even if earlier reports this season about the use of AI/ML were overstated.

“You’ve got your internal combustion and you’ve got your electric energy, and it’s how you recuperate, how you boost, how you work those profiles,” McNish explained. “Now, I go back to my last race here in 2013. We were doing the same thing. Actually, here we learned a lot in the race because suddenly we learned that actually high-speed recuperation was the most efficient gain of energy.”

“And it was literally coming down off the back straight,” he said. “Now those profiles are, I would say, predetermined. We’ve got simulation simulator, actively run on the simulator… working on energy management profiles and things like that. And then you have to adapt to what is right on the day, especially coming to a new circuit.”

Even though Audi took over the Sauber team, the fact that Sauber used a Ferrari power unit until last year means Ferrari has all that data, not Audi.

“Every single circuit for us is new,” McNish said. “So we’ve got our pre-profiles and our understanding of ‘yep, this is where we think we are.’ Every race, we are honing that and getting close in the same way as we are doing with aerodynamics and the same way with our simulation to get to the point where we can predict better. But prediction’s one thing. The reality of what you’re fighting against in a race situation can be something different.”

But like this year’s F1 machinery, McNish’s hybrid Le Mans winners were also highly automated. “So in 2014, when they brought in the new regulation for an energy per lap, with that first year, it was very manual, and it was just impossible for the drivers, to the point where I was sitting on the pit wall happy I wasn’t driving because of the brain overload,” McNish said.

Quickly, the power unit control was automated to give the drivers mental bandwidth to manage all the other tasks required during a race stint. “What strategy of tire feedback, the information, maximizing different things on differential… whatever it may be that he’s getting spoken to about. But at the same time, he’s racing. And so the more you can take away from the driver, the better it is,” McNish said.

“However, ultimately, the driver has got to maximize. So there’s a lot of communication with the driver and there’s a lot of adaption as the race goes on. As fuel load comes down, as tires degrade, a circuit grip comes up, as maybe the track cools off as it should do here on Sunday afternoon. So it is definitely adaptive,” McNish told me.

The race itself was not one of the season’s more exciting contests. Antonelli scored pole on Saturday and disappeared into the distance on Sunday to win comfortably, extending his lead. George Russell needs to score 23 points more than Antonelli in Mexico City to remain in title contention; Lewis Hamilton must score 24 points more than Antonelli to remain with a mathematical chance. Neither is likely to happen, and we’ll almost certainly see Antonelli seal the deal next time out.

“We’re very close, but we’ll try to finish on a high, and hopefully we can clinch it very soon,” he said after the race.

It was a less successful day for Audi. The team’s fast rookie was handicapped by a 20-place grid penalty for changing power unit components in the lead-up to qualifying, and his teammate Nico Hulkenberg made a poor start and lost five places at the beginning of the race. In the garage, engineers analyzed telemetry screens and even images snapped mere seconds earlier by trackside photographers. Mechanics clad in black waited patiently for the team’s first pit stops. Even though it was the mildest weather I’ve experienced at COTA, it was still stifling in the garage; I was sweating in short sleeves, never mind layers of fire-retardant Nomex.

“Both drivers delivered strong recovery drives today, although unfortunately we came away just outside the points,” said McNish after the race. “For Gabi, starting from the back row following the penalties for the changes we had to make, P13 was realistically the best result available. He drove a clean, very calculated race and made good progress through the field.”

“Nico’s race was compromised at the start when the anti-stall kicked in, dropping him to P15,” he said. “To recover to P11 and to close in on P10 was a superb effort. Ultimately, the result didn’t reflect the performance he delivered or what could have been possible with a clean start. We head to Mexico next week determined to turn that performance into points, and we’ll be back on the attack.”

A new report from Europe raises serious alarms about orbital collisions

Ars Technica Long form September 23, 2026

“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits.”

The 2013 sci-fi blockbuster film Gravity, starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, popularized the notion of the Kessler syndrome. In the movie, Russia shoots down a defunct satellite and creates a cloud of debris, leading to serious tension in orbit.

The movie is fantastic, a true thriller, and while some liberties were taken with the depiction of outer space, the basic premise of a cascading series of collisions rendering orbits too cluttered with debris to be usable is valid. The idea was first proposed by NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais nearly half a century ago.

Still, the movie was science fiction, right?

Well, a lot has changed since Gravity‘s release. At the time that theatergoers were sitting on the edges of their seats and watching Bullock dodge debris, there were only about 1,000 active satellites in orbit. Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak.

The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, which now has approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit, with many thousands more on the way. And SpaceX is not alone in the race to provide Internet from space. Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites, with thousands more to follow. Multiple Chinese Internet constellations are likewise in progress.

Then there are the orbital data centers, which may produce hundreds of thousands of satellites.

We’ve written a lot about these constellations, and they have generated a bunch of questions. Most prominent among them: Just how sustainable is all of this? Will we see the Kessler syndrome play out in real time? Here are some answers.

It depends on who you ask, so let’s start with the glass-half-empty and glass-half-full outlooks.

Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago, one of the world’s experts in orbital debris, University of Texas at Austin professor Moriba Jah, told Ars that he worries a lot about the consequences of satellites and debris in low-Earth orbit.

“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits because the carrying capacity is going to get saturated by objects and junk,” Jah said. ” I also predict that we will see a loss of human life by (1) school bus-sized objects reentering and surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or (2) people riding on this wave of civil and commercial astronauts basically having their vehicle getting scwhacked by an unpredicted piece of junk. I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.”

At the other end of the spectrum is the person almost solely responsible for the remarkable growth in satellites over the last decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk. His attitude has largely been that space is big, and things will probably be just fine. For example, during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer at the company’s Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas, Musk said, “Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.”

So in one way of thinking, very, very bad things are coming. In another, everything’s fine. Where does the truth actually lie?

One of the most credible sources for this kind of information is the European Space Agency, which has long studied space debris and its impacts on various orbits.

Fortunately, it just released its annual Space Environment Report a week ago. The European agency has produced such a report over the last decade to provide a transparent overview of global space activities and assess the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight.

There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations.

“The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario,” the report states. “In particular, the growing influence of large constellations highlights the limitations of traditional mitigation approaches when applied to future traffic at unprecedented scales. At the same time, the results are affected by the limited availability of detailed and verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies of these systems.”

More satellites mean an increasing probability of collisions, which helps to push us toward a Kessler-like scenario.

As part of the report, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered.

“The extrapolation of our current behavior, which assumes the continuation of explosion in orbits at current rates, adherence by constellations to at least the minimum desirable post-mission disposal success rates, and continuation of the currently estimated post-mission disposal success rates for all other objects, leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially,” the report states.

In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Such a scenario, with a dramatic growth in constellations using best practices for satellite disposal, looks like this in terms of collisions in orbit.

It does indeed start to look pretty dicey by mid-century.

Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers, as they exclude projects “still being prepared” for launch. It remains unclear whether these mega-megaconstellations of data centers in space will prove to be economically viable, but if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability.

The European Space Agency talks a lot about the need for responsible behavior, and in managing its massive Starlink constellation, SpaceX has been responsible. The company has been effective at deorbiting satellites that lose functionality and at managing a constellation of thousands of satellites. It’s an unprecedented task that the company has learned, on the fly, to carry out at a scale no government or company has attempted before.

We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission that SpaceX is frequently moving satellites around in orbit, making small but precise maneuvers to avoid collisions. Five years ago, its (much smaller) constellation made about 500 such maneuvers a month. During the most recent reporting period, through May 2026, that number had jumped to nearly 35,000 per month. That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.

It is important to characterize these properly. Each maneuver is not a “near miss.” Rather, SpaceX has significantly lowered the probability threshold to trigger a collision avoidance maneuver. The NASA standard for maneuver is 1-in-10,000. At the outset of Starlink, though, SpaceX used a 1-in-100,000 threshold and has since become even more conservative, with a threshold of 3-in-10 million, according to a 2025 letter to the FCC.

So it’s clear that SpaceX is not operating its Starlink constellation in a cavalier manner. But it’s also clear that the company’s constellation, and those like it, are cause for significant concern going forward.

No credible experts are saying that the Kessler syndrome could happen imminently—a single collision won’t set off a Gravity-style cascade.

But space is getting more crowded, particularly orbits from 520 km to 1,000 km above Earth. A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler (yes, that Kessler) found that some orbital bands in this region have already reached what is known as a “collisional-runaway threshold,” which is to say that any serious collisions there may create new debris faster over time than debris would be naturally removed by the pull of gravity, down into Earth’s atmosphere.

Another concern comes from spent “rocket bodies,” upper stages from rockets that were not properly disposed of after launch. This was more common in decades past, but some launches today still do not reserve enough propellant to properly deorbit a second or third stage. These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, said LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight. They are winging around uncontrolled, of course. And the higher the altitude, the longer the debris hangs around, from decades to centuries.

Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit, it would be relatively easy for bad actors to start shooting missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could potentially wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage. The probability of Kessler syndrome becomes much higher if humans start deliberately blowing things up in space. Did we mention that Iran recently became the ninth country to put a domestically built satellite into orbit?

In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable. But it will likely become more and more expensive to operate there when considering avoidance technology, people to manage all of this, and propellant for maneuvers. And finding launch windows that avoid known debris will become more difficult.

Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer, a Kessler-syndrome type outcome may start to become increasingly plausible.
