Vaccines could be about to revolutionise acne treatments

New Scientist October 27, 2026

It’s a cruel twist. Just as we become more concerned about our appearance, our faces start to erupt in great red spots. Pimples cause anguish for many teenagers and can persist into adulthood too. But now two companies are developing vaccines that they hope will revolutionise the treatment of acne. Is an end to the misery at hand?

The main idea behind this new approach is that acne is caused by the immune system overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Triggering the body to produce antibodies against these proteins should block this process and prevent – or at least reduce – acne. Pharma giant Sanofi is preparing for trials in the US and Canada of an mRNA vaccine targeting at least one bacterial protein, while US start-up Armora Biosciences is focusing on a different protein.

Better treatments for acne are certainly needed. “Acne causes a significant emotional burden,” says Tomasz Zastawny at Armora. “It can lead to the development of depression, social isolation and other psychological outcomes as well.”

Advertisement

Antibiotic-resistant acne could be treated by phage therapy

It has been known for decades that acne is linked to the presence of a bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes, which thrives deep in hair follicles where there is little oxygen. But C. acnes is the most common skin bacterium, present on just about everybody – including those that don’t have acne – so there’s a lot more to it.

One factor is the surge in hormones during puberty, which increases the production of fatty substances in the skin, affecting bacterial growth. But not everyone gets pimply during adolescence, so there seem to be genetic factors involved as well.

“Acne is very complicated. It’s not an infection,” says Richard Gallo at the University of California, San Diego. “It’s an immune problem.”

In other words, while the presence of C. acne doesn’t usually cause problems, sometimes it may trigger a strong immune response inside a follicle. During this response, some cells in the skin actually turn into fat cells and start releasing alarm signals and antimicrobial substances – a process known as reactive adipogenesis. “This is a normal way to fight an infection, but in this case, it’s an inappropriate response,” says Gallo.

What triggers that response? C. acnes can secrete a toxin known as Christie-Atkins-Munch-Petersen factor, or CAMP. The bacteria may ramp up production of CAMP in certain circumstances.

So, Gallo’s team tried vaccinating mice against CAMP, to make the animals produce antibodies that neutralise the toxin. A number of studies by his team suggest this could help prevent or treat acne.

Sanofi has now developed an mRNA vaccine that targets CAMP, possibly along with some other C. acnes proteins – the company hasn’t revealed exactly what’s in the vaccine and, after much back and forth, declined to talk to me about it.

While there have been reports that the Sanofi trial is already underway, it is labelled as “not yet recruiting” as per the latest update on 18 September. This means it may be some time before we know if it works. That said, while these initial trials are primarily intended to establish safety, it should be clear to volunteers within weeks if it is making a difference to their acne – this isn’t like a normal vaccine trial where researchers have to wait months or years for people to be exposed to pathogens.

“We were very, very optimistic that this could be revolutionary for acne therapy,” says Gallo. “We’ll just have to see if it pans out in the human population.”

Meanwhile, Armora is targeting a different protein, called hyaluronidase, based on work by George Liu at the University of California, San Diego. Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, a large sugar secreted into the spaces between cells. These terms might be familiar because hyaluronic acid is often used as a filler for cosmetic purposes, while hyaluronidase is injected to break down filler that is no longer wanted or if things go wrong.

We are finally working out what happens to the skin and gut microbiome when someone gets acne, giving us new targets for treatments

Some bacteria such as strep B (Streptococcus agalactiae) produce hyaluronidase for similar purposes, to help them invade tissues. There are two main types of hyaluronidase, it turns out. Some break down hyaluronic acid into simple sugars. Others break it up into large chunks that act as an alarm signal to the immune system.

When it became clear that there were two types, Liu’s team searched genetic databases to see which type is found in which bacteria. They found the “simple sugars” type was the most common. The “large chunks” type was limited to a few free-living bacteria, which makes sense because they don’t need to worry about immune systems.

“The exception was acne,” says Liu. C. acnes jumped out to the researchers because it produces both types of hyaluronidase. More precisely, some strains of C. acne produce the simple-sugars type, while other produce the large-chunks one – none produce both, he says.

That made Liu wonder if this was connected to acne. Sure enough, the team showed in mouse studies that large-chunks strains of C. acnes cause acne-related inflammation, while the simple-sugars one slightly reduces inflammation. The team then went to show that a vaccine that stimulates the production of antibodies targeting only the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase could reduce acne in mice, as could inhibiting the enzyme with a small protein.

What isn’t clear is why some strains of C. acnes have evolved to trigger an immune response. One possibility is that it is a way to kill off some of their competitors, says Liu.

He thinks that in people, a vaccine against the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase would be most effective against the “more severe, red, angry type of acne lesion”.

“The ones that are hard to treat right now, those are the ones that we would target with a vaccine,” he says.

Shingles vaccine may lower risk of stroke and heart failure

His findings might also help explain why antibiotics, which are commonly prescribed for acne, don’t work that well: they kill off the helpful C. acnes strains as well as the harmful ones. The other issue with antibiotics, of course, is that resistance can develop.

Another acne treatment called isotretinoin (Roaccutane) is more effective than antibiotics but has a long list of nasty side effects including causing birth defects, impotence and dry, itchy skin. How it works isn’t clear, though there is some evidence it alters the skin microbiome.

Acne vaccines promise to solve all these issues. They shouldn’t have any lasting side effects, nor should there be any issue with resistance, because the vaccines are targeting secreted proteins rather than directly targeting bacteria.

The fact that two competing approaches are being developed is great news for those with acne. If one vaccine doesn’t work, perhaps the other will. And it could be that both will work, or that targeting both CAMP and hyaluronidase simultaneously will prove even more effective than either alone. Maybe, just maybe, adolescence is about to get a little easier.

New Scientist October 26, 2026

Wind turbines have killed nearly 19 million bats in the US over the past four decades, according to the most comprehensive analysis of its kind to date. The problem seems to have worsened in recent years, with more than 1.5 million deaths now occurring annually.

But there may be ways to make this green energy source safer for wildlife without overly affecting energy production. This data can help “advance research to really support effective conservation measures and science-driven decision-making in the future”, says Charles Labuzzetta at Fort Collins Science Center in Colorado.

Endearing photos of bats show clever adaptations like long tongues

Bats play a vital role in ecosystems, particularly by controlling insects like mosquitoes and moths that produce crop-killing caterpillars. But many species face growing threats from habitat loss, disease and human activities, with some now classified as threatened or endangered.

Advertisement

These human-activity threats include pesticide use and the building of skyscrapers. Researchers have also previously found large numbers of dead bats at wind farms during required monitoring to comply with wildlife protection regulations. But not all wind farms share their results, and monitoring methods vary from site to site, says team member Bethany Straw, also at Fort Collins Science Center.

“We know bats are being impacted, but could we change the engineering or sites of a turbine to minimise those impacts?” she asks. “There’s been an increasing interest in this, but we just haven’t had the appropriate data yet.”

Free newsletter

Now, Straw, Labuzzetta and their colleagues have analysed 499 reports from wind farms across the 48 adjoining US states to estimate how many bats were killed by turbines from 1981 to 2024, focusing on 10 species. They used a statistical model that considered differences in how wind farms searched for dead bats, the size and design of their turbines, and the surrounding environment.

Their results suggest that wind turbines killed an estimated 18.7 million bats between 1981 and 2024. Annual deaths seem to have exceeded 1.5 million from 2021 onwards, which may be the result of more wind turbines being installed.

Hoary bats (Lasiurus cinereus) had the greatest losses, with an estimated 6.7 million deaths, followed by 5.8 million deaths among eastern red bats (Lasiurus borealis), 3.4 million among silver-haired bats (Lasionycteris noctivagans) and 1.5 million among big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus).

Wind farms near rivers and turbines with longer blades were linked to more deaths among certain species, while having more space between the blades and the ground may reduce the risk.

As newer homes are built or older homes are renovated, empty attic spaces are disappearing – this eliminates a vital refuge for birds and bats during a biodiversity crisis

The researchers aren’t sure why bats fly so close to wind turbines. Previous work suggests that migratory bats mistake the structures for trees and approach them in search of food, shelter or mates. A recent European study also found that male bats sometimes sing courtship songs around turbines, potentially attracting females into the path of spinning blades. Differences in species prevalence and behaviours may partly explain why some seem to be more at risk than others.

The researchers hope their findings will help wind farm developers protect bats by choosing safer locations and adjusting turbine designs. For example, research suggests that stripy wind turbines could prevent seabird collisions.

Changing when turbines operate might also help. Research shows that temporarily shutting them down during periods of high bat activity, particularly in low winds, can substantially reduce fatalities with limited loss of electricity production.

‘Oddball’ test lets us glimpse how monkeys see the world

New Scientist October 26, 2026

We can never know what it is like to be a bat, philosopher Thomas Nagel famously agued. But what about monkeys? Do they see the world in the same way we do?

To find out, neuroscientists in India used an “oddball” test to compare visual performances between people and macaques. They found that, although the different species scored similarly on many aspects of perception, there were two intriguing differences: the monkeys were less phased by images being flipped upside down and they seemed far more focused on fine details.

Chimps, bonobos and orangutans grasp how others view the world

There have been previous attempts to compare human and monkey vision, but the tests often require extensive training, says S. P. Arun at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. “The worry becomes: did their perception change because of all that training?” Different aspects of vision have also been studied using different tests, so it is hard to compare the results.

Advertisement

Now, Arun and his colleagues have chosen just one test, the oddball search task, which can be adapted to different visual features. Subjects are shown a set of pictures on a screen, identical apart from one, and must identify the odd one out by touching it.

When the oddball appears more similar to the other images, “it takes us longer to find the odd one out”, says Arun, providing an objective measure of perception. The researchers taught the test to three monkeys, using juice as a reward, and 24 people.

Free newsletter

In several tasks, the people and monkeys performed similarly. For instance, they both categorised inanimate objects (such as a mushroom or leaf) as more similar to each other than to animate items (such as a bird or cat).

They also both obeyed Weber’s law, which states that the smallest noticeable change in a stimulus depends on its baseline magnitude. In this case, the researchers showed that the brighter a spot was, the bigger any change in brightness had to be before either monkeys or humans could perceive it.

But there were also intriguing differences. The researchers tested a phenomenon in which people find it harder to differentiate mirror images flipped across a vertical axis compared with a horizontal one. An example of this is when young children confuse the letters “b” and “d”. This “mirror confusion” is thought to arise because we often see the things around us, such as trees or chairs, from different angles around a vertical axis, so we perceive these images as more interchangeable. We more rarely come across them upside down, so images flipped across a horizontal axis seem more different and therefore easier to tell apart.

It is impossible for us to know exactly how another person’s experience of the world compares to our own, but a new experiment is helping to reveal that colour is indeed a shared phenomenon

This is exactly what happened among the human participants in the oddball test: they took longer to identify outlier images if they were flipped around a vertical axis compared with a horizontal one. But the monkeys didn’t experience mirror confusion, and consistently showed similar performances whether images were flipped vertically or horizontally. Arun suggests this might be because these agile creatures are more used to seeing familiar objects from a range of angles. “They are swinging across stuff, and sometimes they’ll hang upside down.”

The monkeys were also highly attuned to small features, yet seemed oblivious to larger shapes. The researchers tested this using large shapes – a diamond, circle or X – made up of smaller shapes. People find it easier to tell when the overall shape changes, compared with the smaller units. “You can see the forest before you see the trees,” says Arun. But the monkeys only seemed interested in the details, and were no faster on the task when the overall shape changed as well. It isn’t clear why this is, says Arun.

This question was posed as part of New Scientist’s Last Word series, in which readers give scientific answers to each other’s questions. Here’s what our readers had to say

Rufin Vogels at KU Leuven in Belgium says the differences identified in the study are “striking”, although he cautions the results could be affected by differences in attention as well as perception.

As well as providing a glimpse into the monkey visual world, the study could have broader implications for research, says Arun, as these animals are often used as models for human vision. Although they are similar in many respects, he says, “it may not be OK to assume they see everything the way we do”.

Arun hopes the oddball approach could be used to chart vision in other systems, too. The test is so simple, even birds and bees could be trained to do it, he says. His team is now using it to investigate vision in children of different ages, including those with ADHD and autism, to understand how they might perceive the world differently than adults.

Predatory amphibians swam the seas 237 million years ago

New Scientist October 26, 2026

The Late Triassic seas contained a multitude of marine reptiles, but lurking on the sea floor was something different: a marine amphibian. A fossil of the large, bottom-dwelling ambush predator discovered in China is the first evidence that amphibians once found a way to adapt to life in the ocean.

The researchers who studied the fossil think that its secret to survival in salt water, which is normally fatal to amphibians because of their permeable skin, probably lay in its strong body armour.

Advertisement

Stunning early mammal fossil sheds light on the evolution of suckling

“It was a flat animal that lived on the sea floor,” says Ryosuke Motani at the University of California, Davis, who was part of the team that analysed the fossil. It was probably an ambush feeder, he says, as its wide mouth and the strong hyoid bone in its neck suggest it used suction feeding, as is seen in some modern bottom-dwelling predators of a similar size that use an ambush strategy, such as wobbegong sharks.

As soon as the researchers began to study the fossil, they knew it was neither fish nor reptile. It had to be an early amphibian because of its tell-tale anatomy, which included its four legs and gills.

There is, however, no evidence that the creature underwent metamorphosis, as many modern amphibians do, such as when tadpoles become frogs, says Motani.

Subscriber-only newsletter

To prove that the animal was indeed marine and not just a land-based creature washed into the sea after death, the researchers studied the strontium isotope ratios of the fossil bones.

They found that the remains of the new species had a clear signature of sea water, meaning G. maritimus grew to adulthood while in the ocean. Palaeogeographic reconstructions also suggest that, 237 million years ago in the Late Triassic Period, the location in which the fossil was discovered was at least 30 kilometres away from land.

The fossil was also recovered alongside that of a large marine reptile: an ichthyosaur called Guizhouichthyosaurus, which reached lengths of 7 metres.

Fossil mammal with reptile-like teeth changes picture of our evolution

Interestingly, the closest relative to G. maritimus lived in freshwater environments. A fossil of this amphibian, Gerrothorax pulcherrimus, was first described nearly a century ago.

This has led the researchers to suggest the marine lifestyle of G. maritimus was an accident of evolution. “There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonise the sea – the body armour,” says Motani.

The armour originally protected the Gerrothorax genus from predators in fresh water. But because it formed an impermeable barrier, it could also help the amphibians survive in seawater, he says.

Although it is commonly believed that “amphibious” means the ability to be on land or in the water, this is a misconception, says Motani. There are many modern newts that never leave the water, yet they are amphibians, he says.

A stunningly intact marine reptile named Austronaga minuta that lived around 245 million years ago may have looked like a miniature version of more famous later ocean predators, like plesiosaurs

“My take is that it is similar to calling a snake a tetrapod, when it does not have limbs,” says Motani.

John Long at Flinders University, Australia, says the fossil is a first, given that none of the 8000 or so living species of amphibians today is fully adapted for life in the sea.

“If not for the marine invasion by many groups of reptiles at the same time, they might have even had a chance at diversifying in this niche, but that clearly didn’t occur,” he says. “It shows us that amphibians closely related to modern forms were able to adapt to different environments, like seawater, in ways we never thought possible.”

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

New Scientist October 26, 2026

For seven years, molecular biologist Ionut Dumitru and his colleagues played what felt like the world’s most exhausting game of hide-and-seek.

Yet instead of peeking around doors or under beds, they were examining brain tissue in a lab at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, looking for something that had long evaded neuroscientists: concrete proof that the adult brain can form new neurons via a process called neurogenesis. Scientists have spent decades debating whether this is possible. As soon as one paper turned up positive clues, another would yield nothing at all.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

But it seems the search may finally be over. A slew of new findings, including those from Dumitru and his team, have revealed near-certain evidence that adult neurogenesis occurs in the human hippocampus, part of the brain central to learning and memory. The discovery is forcing us to rethink long-held assumptions about our most indispensable organ, from how it functions to how it changes with age.

Advertisement

Even more exciting is the potential neurogenesis holds for brain regeneration. Some of our most devastating medical conditions, including Alzheimer’s, stroke and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), involve neurons dying at massive scale. If the brain is capable of replacing some of those lost neurons, we may be able to harness and enhance that ability, stimulating neurogenesis to help treat neurological conditions that are currently incurable.

“To many of us, we think the question is no longer whether it exists or not,” says neuroscientist Hongjun Song at the University of Pennsylvania. “It’s, how can we take advantage of that?”

Neurons are the brain’s key messengers, transmitting the signals that underpin our most basic functions, from moving and talking to thinking and dreaming. They form when a stem cell – which can morph into other cell types – transforms into a “parent” progenitor cell, which then births an immature neuron that eventually matures.

Scientists long believed this process played out only during development in the womb and, to a lesser degree, during childhood and adolescence. In other words, humans were born with essentially all the neurons they would ever have. The brain would change in many ways over one’s lifetime – forming new connections between neurons and pruning away those that were no longer necessary – but it wasn’t going to get a windfall of new neurons. Or at least, so we thought.

In the early 1960s, Joseph Altman, a biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, went against the grain by looking for signs of neurogenesis in adult rats. He injected the animals with a radioactive tracer used to track cell division, then identified cells bearing it in the rodents’ brains, revealing what appeared to be freshly generated neurons.

But the finding was widely panned by the neuroscience community. The idea that adult neurogenesis was impossible “had really been embedded within the scientific literature”, says Fred “Rusty” Gage, a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California.

Altman was apparently undeterred, replicating his findings in the brains of additional rats and then cats. Other researchers eventually joined in, finding adult neurogenesis in species such as canaries and monkeys, and discovering that it seemed to play a role in learning and memory – helping birds learn new songs, for instance.

But whether human brains also pump out new neurons remained an open question. You can’t ethically crack open a living person’s skull and dig around in their brain tissue.

Free newsletter

Gage and his colleagues found an ingenious workaround to that problem. In the 1990s, some people being treated for cancer received injections of a chemical called BrdU, which flagged dividing cells so that doctors could monitor disease spread. When five such patients had died, Gage and his colleagues were able to autopsy their brains. Lo and behold, they found BrdU in hippocampal cells – a sign of neurogenesis.

The trouble is that BrdU can sometimes flag cells undergoing repair, not necessarily division. And subsequent studies that used different markers yielded results all over the map. Some showed next to no neurogenesis in the adult brain; others, that the adult hippocampus adds 700 new neurons every single day, on a par with that of a much younger brain.

So, Song and his colleagues pioneered a different approach. Instead of looking for immature neurons with just one or two markers, they analysed the full genetic profile of individual brain cells, searching for the genetic characteristics of freshly generated cells. They discovered immature neurons in people who had died across all stages of life, even up to age 92.

But spotting a young neuron still isn’t enough to prove the adult brain is generating new ones. Neurons can linger in an immature state for a long time, perhaps even an entire lifespan. These Peter Pans of the brain aren’t necessarily created in adulthood; they just aren’t growing up.

The real challenge in proving adult neurogenesis occurs was to capture each stage of the process – and one remained elusive. “Nobody had identified the proliferating progenitors,” says Dumitru. “They could identify immature neurons, they could identify maybe stem cells – so the cells that are at the beginning and end of the trajectory – but nobody identified the proliferating ones.”

To identify these cells, which actually birth new neurons, Dumitru and his colleagues genetically analysed roughly 400,000 brain cells from the hippocampi of people who had died between infancy and adulthood. They used a machine learning model – a type of artificial intelligence – to pinpoint genetic patterns that resembled those seen in progenitors from animals and developing infants.

The overlooked power of diet for improving your mental health

The researchers almost couldn’t believe it when they spotted the first few progenitors. “It was so difficult to convince ourselves,” says team member Marta Paterlini, a molecular biologist also at the Karolinska Institute.

But after years of testing and re-testing, they finally felt confident their search was over. They found only about 350 progenitor cells – and they weren’t present in all the brains sampled. But by finding any at all, “we showed that there is active neurogenesis” in the hippocampus, says Dumitru. “That cannot be contested.”

Except that, well, some scientists still do. Developmental neurobiologist Arturo Alvarez-Buylla at the University of California, San Francisco, isn’t convinced that machine learning models can reliably categorise cell types. He says the only way to know for certain that adult neurogenesis happens would be to track a stem cell as it transforms into a neuron – a nearly impossible task to do in a living human.

But sceptics like Alvarez-Buylla are increasingly finding themselves outside a coalescing consensus. At least 38 clinical trials related to adult neurogenesis are now under way. “It’s there,” says Sandrine Thuret, a neuroscientist at King’s College London. “The new debate is, what is it for?”

One of the first clues to answering that question comes from the fact that adult neurogenesis appears almost exclusive to the hippocampus, the brain’s headquarters of learning and memory. This region is highly plastic, meaning it can easily reorganise itself and form new connections, helping us to take in and remember new information.

In a study from earlier this year, neuroscientist Orly Lazarov at the University of Illinois College of Medicine and her colleagues found that neurogenesis may play a role in this process. They examined post-mortem hippocampus samples from adults who had Alzheimer’s and adults without cognitive impairments, including “superagers” – people in their eighties or older who had outperformed younger adults on a memory test. On average, superagers had roughly twice as many immature neurons in their hippocampus as adults without cognitive impairments. People with Alzheimer’s had almost none at all.

In our efforts to keep our brains healthy, how do we know what is working? Helen Thomson explores a new generation of tests that can reveal whether our efforts are paying off

The finding suggests that neurogenesis is closely linked with cognition and may even stave off its decline. Some of the superagers with an abundance of immature neurons also showed signs of Alzheimer’s in their brains, including the condition’s characteristic plaques and tangles. It is possible that enhanced neurogenesis allows the brain to bypass or overcome what would otherwise contribute to cognitive decline, says Lazarov.

Several studies within the past year have also found neurogenesis is impaired in other conditions like Parkinson’s and depression. The latter finding comes from the lab of René Hen, a neuroscientist at Columbia University, New York, who has spent the past 20 years trying to understand the connection between neurogenesis and depression.

His interest began after coming across a study that showed rats dosed with antidepressants had increased rates of neurogenesis. Curious about whether this could explain how antidepressants work, Hen ran a follow-up experiment and found that if he manipulated rodents’ brains to stop producing new neurons, they also stopped responding to antidepressants. Hen was hooked and has been investigating the link ever since.

He and his colleagues have shown that, at least in animals, hippocampal neurogenesis seems crucial for pattern separation – the ability to distinguish between different objects, situations and emotions and remember them appropriately. This process is impaired in depression, as well as other psychiatric conditions in which neurogenesis may go awry, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It may explain why people with depression can tend to overgeneralise, for example, interpreting one bad day as evidence that things will always be bad, says Hen.

Like Alzheimer’s disease, these mental health conditions are also associated with smaller hippocampal volumes. While there are probably multiple factors that contribute to this, it is possible that impaired neurogenesis is one of them, says Hen.

Finding a way to stimulate neurogenesis could, therefore, be a promising treatment approach. Several studies have indicated that already available medications, such as antidepressants and the diabetes medication metformin, could stoke neurogenesis.

But there could be more advanced ways of manipulating the process. For instance, if we can pinpoint why superagers have increased neurogenesis, and why it seems to be protective, we could potentially develop therapies that mimic these effects. “We might be able to provide some kind of shield [against cognitive decline],” says Lazarov.

Harnessing neurogenesis could even treat conditions it isn’t directly involved in, such as traumatic brain injury or stroke. A 2025 study showed that transplanting neural progenitor cells into the brains of mice after a stroke led to the production of new neurons and helped the animals regain lost movement.

Still, it will take years to determine whether any neurogenesis interventions work, and even longer to bring them to market if they do. Song and his team are trying to speed up the process by developing miniature models, or organoids, of the human hippocampus. Because these organoids capture what happens in the living human brain more accurately than animal models, they could make it easier to identify therapies that boost neurogenesis, says Song. Other researchers are trying to develop non-invasive brain-imaging techniques to measure neurogenesis in living people, with similar goals.

There may be simpler interventions, too. “Lifestyle is an easy way of modulating, potentially, neurogenesis,” says Thuret.

Research has long shown that neurogenesis increases in rats when they are mentally stimulated, such as by having roommates or fun toys in their cages; people may similarly benefit from enriching activities like socialising or learning a new skill.

Exercise also shows promise, at least in rodents. Gage and his colleagues found that when adult rats run on exercise wheels, they produce more immature neurons than sedentary rodents. They also do a better job navigating a maze, signifying enhanced cognitive performance.

Thuret was curious whether the same could be true for humans. So earlier this year, she and her team exposed human hippocampal stem cells to blood serum taken from adults who had completed a three-month exercise programme and those who hadn’t. But instead of stoking neurogenesis, blood from the exercisers actually reduced the number of stem cells ready to become new neurons.

Thuret is still trying to unravel what this means. But given that it is well established that exercise benefits brain health, it may not necessarily be a negative outcome. It is possible that physical activity helps regulate the pace at which stem cells transform into neurons, reserving some for future development, she says.

It is intuitive to think that if impaired neurogenesis is bad, cranking it up to 11 would be good. But too much neurogenesis could backfire, says Thuret. Cancer, a disease of unchecked cell growth, is a prime example of how more isn’t always better when it comes to the human body.

This is just one reason why indiscriminately turning up neurogenesis probably isn’t a viable treatment option. It is more likely that therapies of the future will be targeted, tweaking neurogenesis in different ways and to different levels to treat various conditions, rather than having an across-the-board fix, says Thuret.

To gain the benefits of sleep, it was thought that the whole brain must switch off. But experiments suggest the right kind of rest can encourage our brain to improve memory and learning while we’re awake.

Plus, as far as researchers have been able to tell, neurogenesis is mostly confined to the hippocampus. Many cognitive and psychiatric symptoms originate there, but not all of them. For example, a completely different brain region mediates anhedonia – the inability to feel joy, which is a hallmark of depression. “I don’t think that a drug that stimulates neurogenesis is going to cure anhedonia,” says Hen. “The medicine of the future is probably going to be a medicine where we use multiple drugs, each one targeting specific symptoms.”

Unless, of course, neurogenesis isn’t limited to the hippocampus at all.

After finding progenitor cells in the hippocampus, Dumitru, Paterlini and their colleagues didn’t celebrate for long. Instead, they embarked on a new search, turning their attention to the subventricular zone, another part of the brain that some studies suggest is capable of neurogenesis well into adulthood. The work is in early stages, says Dumitru, but already they have spotted signs of progenitor cells in adult samples of this area – a new game of hide-and-seek has begun.

Robotic dog controlled with a computer powered by human blood cells

New Scientist October 26, 2026

Living cells have been used to create a biological computer that can control the movements of a robotic dog. Its creators say using cells to replicate the digital neural networks of AI models like ChatGPT – which are themselves modelled on biological brains – could create more efficient and adaptable computers.

The start-up Cortical Labs has created and commercialised a biological computer called CL1, which can be trained to navigate towards a target in a simulated 2D environment. In later tests, this training data was used to control the movements of a real robotic dog.

Ferrante Neri at the Education University of Hong Kong, who wasn’t involved in the research, says that a paper published by the company that is yet to be peer-reviewed shows experiments where the neural network improved as time passed, even as it was fed the same digital data – suggesting it was being successfully trained to do the task.

Advertisement

A glob of jelly can play Pong thanks to a basic kind of memory

“That is promising evidence of learning from limited experience under these experimental conditions,” says Neri. “Establishing an advantage on this task is an early step towards handling the complexity of real-world navigation.”

Cortical Labs has already used living cells to perform computations: in 2021, it showed that its technology could play the computer game Pong.

But the company’s latest experiments show there may also be applications in robotics in the physical world. Cortical Labs says that a biological computer could be less energy-intensive to run than a digital alternative, which would be an advantage in robotics where battery life is a key limitation.

Brett Kagan at Cortical Labs says the cells used in CL1 computers are created from stem cells that are generated from blood donated by people who have given their consent. “There is no evidence that these systems experience pain or suffering, but we recognise that this possibility requires careful monitoring and are addressing it with independent groups.”

“Despite the best advances in [digital] robotics, having them avoid running into obstacles remains a challenge. And that’s because there is still work to be done in areas such as higher order control, navigation and pathfinding,” says Kagan. “Biology and AI have different strengths; biology has evolved to adapt and respond to the world in real time.”

Waiōuru fire: Smoke clearing, but could still have effects in Napier and Hastings

New Zealand Herald October 27, 2026

Thick clouds of smoke billow into the sky as a vegetation fire burns through the Waiōuru Military Area near the Desert Rd.

Smoke from a vegetation fire burning about 150km away is dissipating, but a Health New Zealand health warning for Napier and Hastings remains in place.

Health NZ announced on its Hawke’s Bay Facebook page on Tuesday evening that smoke from the Waiōuru fire was expected to affect air quality in Hawke’s Bay’s twin cities on Wednesday.

The vegetation fire that burned about 230ha on Monday was ignited during live-fire training in the Waiōuru Military Training Area.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand firefighters were continuing their work to contain the blaze on Wednesday.

Fire and Emergency NZ incident controller Nigel Dravitzki said a perimeter flight in the morning confirmed the fire had covered 3700ha.

“Steep terrain and vegetation where the fire is still burning, as well as variable weather conditions including a forecast increase in wind speed today, continue to make this a challenging fire to contain and extinguish.”

Medical officer of health Dr Nick Jones said air quality modelling provided by Fire and Emergency NZ predicted potentially medium to high levels of smoke pollution from early morning in Napier, with conditions expected to improve across Napier and Hastings throughout the day.

People sensitive to smoke, including those with heart or lung conditions, pregnant women, young children and older people may experience symptoms such as coughing, shortness of breath or irritation of the eyes, nose and throat.

Jones said exposure to smoke can worsen pre-existing health conditions such as asthma and heart disease.

“Residents should be aware that smoke may affect air quality and are advised to keep windows and doors closed and limit outdoor physical activity while smoky conditions persist.”

Anyone with health concerns could call Healthline 24/7 on 0800 611 116 for free health advice, or their family doctor.

In its post, Health NZ – Hawke’s Bay wrote if smoke is seen or smelt, stay inside if it’s safe to do so, keeping windows and doors shut and switching air conditioning to recirculate. Once the smoke cleared outside, air out homes.

Keep an eye on children, older people and others at risk while keeping pets inside with clear water and food, with the pets’ bedding inside if possible.

People she has spoken to said they either did not enrol or update their details on time because they were unaware of the new rules.

"I spoke to someone who'd just moved back from Australia, their kids were coming next week. They've been back and forth a couple of times because of work.

Mitchell said the changes were made so "Kiwis weren't waiting around in the seats for the election results".

Wayne Brown wants to wrest control of Auckland’s motorway and rail network from central government

New Zealand Herald October 27, 2026

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown wants to wrest control of the city's entire motorway network and rail system from central government.

Mayor Wayne Brown is gunning his city’s entire motorway network and rail system just weeks after forcing Auckland Transport back into council hands.

Brown has today released his Manifesto 2026 just nine days out from the general election.

The City Rail Link (CRL) has transformed Auckland’s rail network but the city’s transport challenges have not disappeared, Brown’s document said.

Auckland was poised to have two million people and needed to tackle congestion and boost public transport to move people and goods efficiently across the city.

However, the current cost of transport governance was stalling real progress, Brown wrote.

To avoid the mistakes of the past, Auckland’s transport network needed a “single point of control” to improve standardisation and value for money, and prevent costly roading projects being foisted on the city “for little benefit to Auckland”.

“This means one agency – Auckland Council – being responsible for running our region’s entire road and rail network, guided by the agreed 30-year plan. It is the obvious next step for transport reform in Auckland.”

Brown said his expectation for a future government was to progressively shift control of state highways and the rail network to Auckland Council.

Other expectations included:

As revealed by the Herald this morning, a new primary school for Auckland’s city centre is also being proposed by Brown as part of his ambitions for 100,000 more residents living in town.

Brown’s manifesto and desire to take control of the city’s road and rail network comes just weeks after the council stripped Auckland Transport of its core policy, planning and road control functions.

The council-controlled organisation has been reconfigured into a smaller agency which is now responsible for public transport.

While transport is a key focus in Brown’s manifesto, the document also canvasses other priorities for the city.

Supporting growth “in the right places” is also highlighted. Brown said housing development needed to be targeted where necessary infrastructure and transport connections already existed - not “sprawling endlessly into paddocks and productive rural land”.

This appears to be a dig at recent out-of-sequence developments submitted or approved under the controversial fast-track legislation.

“If the city continues to sprawl, we will lock in low levels of productivity, disconnected communities, more pressure on infrastructure and slower economic growth. That is not the kind of Auckland I want us to build for future generations.

“Aucklanders, not Wellington politicians or bureaucrats, should plan what kind of city we want, and any future government must commit to ending the constant cycle of plan changes we have been subjected to in recent years.”

Brown wanted Wellington to butt out of Auckland’s spatial planning, which he said had created uncertainty and concern.

He also called for developers to pay their share of infrastructure costs rather than ratepayers and taxpayers being forced to foot the bill.

“Put simply, if a development cannot pay for the roads, pipes, schools and transport it requires, then it is not economical and shouldn’t proceed.”

He called on a future government to commit to removing greenfield housing developments from the fast-track system, and to match Auckland’s commitment “dollar-for-dollar to assemble land in priority areas like Maungawhau to Morningside and the city centre.

Other priorities included committing to Brown’s tourism funding charter for a visitor levy or tourism dividend, enabling councils to fairly rate short-term accommodation like Airbnbs, and reviewing “draconian visa and migration settings that acted as barriers to visitors and talent.

He called on the Government to sort out Fire and Emergency and “overzealous” fire safety rules, fix the Dog Control Act to help Auckland manage roaming dogs and remove the exemption from government properties paying rates.

Brown is unveiling his manifesto at an event in Auckland this morning.

Lane Nichols is Auckland Desk Editor and a senior journalist for the New Zealand Herald with more than 20 years’ experience in the industry.

Kaikōura dairy farmers help protect Hutton’s shearwaters with dark sky lighting

New Zealand Herald October 27, 2026

Before ... light spill from floodlights at a Kaikōura dairy shed. The lights have since been upgraded. Photo / Kaikōura Dark Sky Trust

Kaikōura dairy farmers are doing their bit to protect the night sky and endangered seabirds.

A collaboration between local farmers and the Kaikōura Dark Sky Trust has shown dairy shed lighting can be upgraded to reduce light pollution, while providing the lighting needed to allow workers to operate safely at night.

The project follows the Kaikōura district being granted international dark sky sanctuary status in September 2024 and the council passing new lighting rules in the Kaikōura District Plan in the same year.

The motivation behind gaining dark sky status was to protect the Hutton’s shearwater/kaikōura tītī, which can become disoriented by bright lights.

Kaikōura District Council chief executive Will Doughty said small changes can make a big difference.

“It’s been fantastic to see local farmers willing to get behind this initiative and trial a different approach.

“The results speak for themselves and demonstrate what can be achieved when our community works together to protect Kaikōura’s special night sky.”

Kaikōura Dark Sky Trust project co-ordinator Colette Doughty said she has been amazed by the support from local farmers.

“We’ve also discovered that some farmers have stopped using their outdoor lights altogether, with no impact on their operations.”

The project employed three basic principles, including directing lighting down, using warm light and avoiding unnecessary light spill.

Fully shielded fittings helped to keep light below the horizontal, while 3000 Kelvin LED fittings were used, which met the council’s outdoor lighting provisions.

The result was a reduced amount of light spilling into the sky and surrounding areas.

Fonterra Tasman Marlborough regional manager Sam McCulloch said the initiative was an example of how simple changes can deliver positive environmental outcomes.

“By demonstrating what can be achieved in a real farming environment, we hope the project encourages other farmers to consider whether small changes to their outdoor lighting could make a difference too.”

Local electrician Dan Farr, of Dan The Sparky, was engaged to source and install replacement lights at the participating farms.

“Retrofitting existing farm lighting to meet the dark sky standards doesn’t need to be a big or expensive job.

“In many cases it’s simply a matter of replacing the existing floodlight with a fully shielded, warm LED fitting.”

Participating farms included Sequoia Dairy Shed and Rockwood Dairy Shed, which are both owned by Mylor Dairy, and the Boyd Dairy Shed on Old Beach Rd.

Mylor Dairy operations manager Justin Hocking said he was impressed with the results.

“This project has done a fantastic job at reducing the light pollution from our two dairy sheds without hindering our operations.

“In fact, there are a couple of hidden benefits such as reduced electricity usage and a far less intrusive light, which the workers and cows enjoy.”

Another local dairy farmer, Simon Mackle, said he used to think the cows needed to be illuminated out in the cowshed yard.

On foggy mornings, he could see hundreds of Hutton’s shearwaters “circling above the lights” in their confusion.

Turning the outside lights off had made no difference to the cow flow, he said.

“I feel the lights were causing light pollution, affecting our neighbours and how well people in Kaikōura can see the night sky.”

Matakana Island emergency landing: Pilot escapes injury after propeller breaks mid-flight

New Zealand Herald October 27, 2026

Veteran pilot Evan Wheeler made a desperate dash for a safe landing.

A veteran pilot escaped unscathed after being forced to make an emergency landing on a remote Bay of Plenty beach when part of his propeller snapped off mid-flight.

Evan Wheeler, 72, told the Herald he had hoped to clock 1000 flying hours without an incident, but fell just 12 hours short.

He was flying his two-seater Murphy Rebel bush plane back to Whitianga after a barbecue hosted by the Ōpōtiki Aero Club on Sunday afternoon when part of its wooden propeller suddenly broke off.

“My initial thought was, is it the engine, is the engine blowing up?” he said.

“There was just an instantaneous massive vibration, horrible, serious vibrations,” he said, comparing the sensation to an unbalanced car wheel spinning at speed.

“If it’s spinning, it just shakes, shakes the hell out of it. And that’s what the propeller was doing.”

Wheeler, who has 26 years of flying experience, immediately reduced the throttle, knowing the vibrations could cause serious damage to the plane.

As the engine slowed, the vibrations subsided, leading him to realise the problem was likely with the propeller.

He estimated he was five minutes from an airfield at Waihī but soon realised that was too far.

“I was only at 1200 feet, so you don’t have a lot of time. You’ve got about a minute to get on the ground.”

With time ticking away, he turned his attention to the shoreline of Matakana Island, where he hoped to bring the plane down safely.

Wheeler said his training kicked in and he remained calm, asking himself: “Where am I, what are my options?”

He said his priority was reaching the sand, knowing a landing in the water “could create a number of problems”.

“I just managed to coax it in, just nudged it along with a little bit of throttle ... And that just gave me enough to get over the sand.”

He believed he would have been forced to land in the sea had he been just 500m to 1km further offshore, potentially causing the aircraft to overturn in the water.

But even reaching the beach carried risks, with Wheeler fearing the soft sand could cause the plane to flip onto its roof.

“I turned, pulled the motor off so it cut out and let her land, just glided it in, just a few bounces then we were all right.”

“A very big relief,” he said.

Wheeler escaped without so much as a bruise, while the aircraft was also undamaged, apart from the broken propeller.

The force of the vibrations had automatically activated his emergency locator beacon, alerting the Rescue Coordination Centre in Wellington, which called him within minutes of landing.

The Matakana Island fire chief later helped Wheeler reach the mainland, where a fellow pilot collected him and flew him home.

The following day, Wheeler returned with friends and a replacement propeller, which they fitted after checking the aircraft for further damage, allowing him to fly it back home.

“It’s home now in the hangar, all good,” he said.

The Civil Aviation Authority said it was aware of the incident and would conduct preliminary inquiries to establish what happened and whether further action was required.

Wheeler suspects a small component covering the propeller bolts may have come loose and struck one of the blades.

Wheeler, who also serves as president of the Whitianga Aero Club, credited his survival to the emergency training he had received, including regular exercises in which instructors simulated engine failures.

“You’re in a situation where if you want to survive, you’ve just got to stay calm.

“You’re taught the procedures to follow when it hits the fan, you’ve just got to do it.”

Despite the close call, Wheeler said he was still learning after almost 1000 hours in the air.

“I’m still learning. I’m always learning and I’m happy to be told ‘do this better’.”

Former Met officer who served in same unit as David Carrick and Wayne Couzens found guilty of sexual offences

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 20:34:59 GMT

Mark Tyrrell convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice at Southwark crown court

A former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.

A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.

The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”

Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.

He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.

Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.

The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.

The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.

In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.

Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.

In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.

Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.

“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”

Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.

The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.

Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.

Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 20:02:34 GMT

Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows

Should any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.

Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

Docherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.

Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.

Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.

Ferguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador until Sir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipend in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021 when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo, loose talk escaping to social media.

Ferguson’s part in Ronaldo’s disastrous return to Old Trafford evidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss. The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game, left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.

A Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Not that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to the Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.

Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, that he was being replaced. His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.

Using the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the fact he turned United down in 2013. The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leave David Moyes, the immediate successor painted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.

Moyes’s reputation is another enhanced by failures that followed, including Mourinho’s grumpy, fractious tenure. When emerging reluctantly from his Lowry Hotel bolthole, the Portuguese reduced himself to mocking club history with “football heritage” rants. Such a scorched-earth policy was echoed by Ruben Amorim, while Erik ten Hag’s retention by Ineos in summer 2024 was as confusing to Ten Hag as to everyone else.

An unmanageable club? Busby and Ferguson showed it can be done, though the chance of another empire recedes the longer the vanity, plotting and self-interest that personify United continues. And for that, Busby and Ferguson deserve a share of the blame.

Unpaid carers say chancellor’s plan to scrap allowance cliff edge falls short

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 19:48:53 GMT

Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with overpayments will still have to pay

“On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,” says unpaid carer Guy Shahar of the government’s decision to abolish the notorious carer’s allowance cliff edge.

But Shahar is angry that most carers hit with unjust overpayments in the past will still have to repay them, for all the promise of a different future. And he notes that the cliff edge remains in place for four more years, potentially catching out more carers.

“They are effectively saying: ‘We know that the system was unfair but we will still punish you for having been the victim of an unfair system,’” he says.

The chancellor is expected to announce the introduction of a new digital taper system into the carer’s allowance benefit in the budget, in effect ending a rule that has landed hundreds of thousands of carers with life-shattering financial penalties.

Unpaid carers have broadly welcomed the move – and there is a general acknowledgment that ministers are moving positively, if slowly, to reform a system with inbuilt injustices and terrible management that birthed what became known as the carer’s allowance scandal.

But there is also disbelief that the new system – which must be built from scratch – will be live before 2030, and a feeling that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has a lot more to do to regain the trust of unpaid carers.

Shahar and his wife, Oksana, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were victims of the cliff edge. This rule meant that a carer who earns more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – will forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, now £86.45.

A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40. Last year, the Shahars were landed with a £10,000 repayment bill for relatively trivial earnings breaches dating back five years.

Oksana had earned more than the allowed limit by just £1.92 a week on average while juggling caring with part-time minimum wage jobs. In some weeks, she was paid just 38p more than the carer’s allowance earnings threshold.

Over the period, she earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed – but was duly issued with a bill for £10,130.45 – plus a £50 civil penalty. The Shahars are challenging the charge at tribunal but the stress is real and ongoing.

Unpaid carer Elizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, is staggered that the taper system is years away: “We live in the age of tech; it is ludicrous it is going to take so long. They need to make it a priority.”

Tait, a former teacher and now a private tutor and educational consultant who ended up with a bill for £1,623 after unwittingly breaching the earnings threshold, says the carer’s allowance cliff edge symbolises a “whole crazy system”.

Reforming carer’s allowance is essential but it needs to be part of a wider examination of the crucial role of unpaid care in propping up England’s social care arrangements, she says: “We care willingly and lovingly, and yet we end up a casualty of the system.”

Andrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, is one of a handful of carers to challenge a cliff edge penalty and win, successfully overturning a £4,600 overpayment at a tribunal in February 2025.

As a result, she did not have to repay the money, although she suffered months of stress along the way. She welcomes the decision to introduce a taper but believes carers punished unfairly by draconian rules should be compensated.

“People repaying overpayments should no longer have to, and they should be given back what they have already paid,” she says.

Tucker recalls how for years she carefully monitored her monthly earnings from her part-time charity shop role to stay under the limit. Some weeks she would work six hours for nothing so as not to risk losing carer’s allowance.

Even so, she was hit with an overpayment when DWP officials decided – unlawfully – that she could not average her earnings over a one-year period.

There is raw bitterness among carers about the cliff edge, she says. “My friend is paying back their overpayment at £10 a month. She went £12.50 over as a result of receiving holiday pay. She always tells me: ‘I hope I die before I have paid it all back.’”

RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 19:24:29 GMT

Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told

A group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.

One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.

Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.

Abdulkarim, of London, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service. He is accused of buying the vans used in the Fairford incident on the instruction of Ali.

Essghir, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, after initially being arrested at the scene near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September and then re-arrested on 20 October. He is accused of visiting RAF Fairford and filming around the facility on a video call with Ali before returning a month later in the convoy of vans.

Abdulkarim has been released on bail under conditions including the surrender of his passport, and Essghir has been remanded in custody. They will appear at the Old Bailey on 20 November.

Prosecutor Louise Gray alleged the defendants were in contact with an individual known as Ali who is now believed to be abroad.

She said that during the events of 27 September at the RAF Fairford base, five men who were arrested travelled in vans, parked and got out “and were told to do so by someone known as Mr Ali”.

One of them, she said, had claimed they were told there was a bomb in the van and called 999.

The court heard that the person calling stated that they were from London and that he was one of a group of five males. The caller told the police that they had been tasked to drive vans to the location for the purpose of a new business venture. When the vans arrived at the location, the organiser was in communication with them over the telephone.

Gray alleged he then told them to park the vans and to walk away from them. After they did that, the organiser told them to run as he had planted a bomb in the van. The caller indicated that he and his colleagues had run away from the vans and were now calling the police for help.

The defendants are believed to have known Ali for “a number of years”, she said.

Essghir is accused of travelling to RAF Fairford on 22 August and contacting Ali.

Abdulkarim is accused of buying mobile phones and collecting cash for Ali, as well as buying five vans including the three that were driven to RAF Fairford.

The court heard he had known Ali for 10 years and it was claimed the latter had been linked to a drone incident at the Israeli embassy.

Counter Terror Policing said they believed the foreign intelligence service involved in the case was Iranian.

The assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said: “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat.

“The public can help us with this, and as always I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”

A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national who was also arrested on 20 October on suspicion of aiding Iran’s intelligence service has been released without charge but remains on police bail after being arrested on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.

Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford. We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”

Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 19:17:55 GMT

Emissions from exported oil would not count against carbon budget, insiders say – reasoning likely to draw dismay from climate campaigners

The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.

The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.

Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.

A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.

On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.

But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.

“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”

Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.

But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”

Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.

A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.

Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.

Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.

In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.

Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.

Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.

He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.

Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.

Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment.

In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.

The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”
