England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blow

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 19:09:54 GMT

Bath flanker Pepper injured ankle at Gloucester on Friday

Bristol’s Van Rensburg advised to rest after two concussions

England’s head coach, Steve Borthwick, said he will be monitoring this weekend’s domestic Prem games with some trepidation. Already he has lost at least two potentially key squad members for the entire autumn period in the form of Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg, with doubts still hanging over his first-choice fly-half, Fin Smith, and fresh injury uncertainty emerging on virtually a daily basis.

Pepper’s involvement always looked improbable from the moment he sustained a nasty-looking ankle injury against Gloucester last Friday. The young Bath flanker will be sidelined for several weeks, as will the Bristol centre Van Rensburg who has been advised to rest and recuperate after two heavy concussions within the past three months.

Smith, meanwhile, is still being treated for the calf problem he sustained against Leicester last Saturday. Borthwick says it remains “unclear at this stage” whether the Northampton fly-half will be available to face Australia next week. Calf injuries and kicking are not a great combination and England also need their tactical hub to be at the heart of their preparations.

Borthwick, accordingly, will effectively want to make a call by the end of this week although England are slightly helped by the fact the Wallaby fixture is on a Sunday rather than 24 hours earlier. “Typically I would name the team for a Sunday game around the Wednesday, so that would still be my aim,” said Borthwick. “But if Fin’s not available for selection we also have some quality fly-halves in George Ford and Marcus Smith.”

The Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu has also limped away from training in Bagshot with a leg injury that will now be assessed, but there is more encouraging news regarding Seb Atkinson (knee) and Manny Feyi-Waboso (hamstring), both of whom should be available to play for Gloucester and Exeter respectively this weekend.

Borthwick’s preference would probably be for both players to be tucked up on their sofas but under the terms of the joint agreement between the Rugby Football Union and the clubs, the latter can pick their international players once they are cleared by England’s medical staff. “If they’re fit then they’re available for selection,” said Borthwick. “That then comes down to the head coach or director of rugby of the club.”

Either way it is a tense time for the national management who are having to do without their customary full extra week of training because of the need to shoehorn the new Nations Championship finals weekend into the calendar. Rugby players need to play rugby but, invariably, it comes with an element of risk attached. “Certainly there is a part of me watching these games and hoping the players get through the 80 minutes and are fit and available for next week,” said Borthwick.

The stakes are further heightened by next year’s looming World Cup, with Borthwick having pointedly reminded his players that only nine Tests remain before England’s World Cup preparations enter their final stages. The primary message is that, for those intending to be on the plane to Australia, performing at the requisite level starts now. “This series of games this autumn is the last opportunity we have playing southern hemisphere opposition before we’re at that World Cup,” said Borthwick.

“I’m looking forward to seeing players compete and perform against this calibre of opposition. You look at the power many of these southern hemisphere teams have. That’s a different challenge. When they come into camp again on Monday night, having recovered from their games, all that matters is performing the way we want to against Australia.”

“I actually think it’s a real strength of the game to be able to compete like that in that kind of full-blooded encounter – and then they’re perfectly fine. It’s a strength of English rugby that the players have such pride in their clubs … in modern day sport I see that as a positive. But when you come in [here] it’s all about the England team.”

Michal Stasiak and Kinga Wydrzynska pleaded not guilty to 11 counts relating to death of 13-month-old Isabella Stasiak

A 13-month-old girl was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of her parents before she was fatally injured by her mother, a court has heard.

Michal Stasiak, 28, and Kinga Wydrzynska, 26, appeared at Warwick crown court on Tuesday, where they pleaded not guilty to 11 counts related to the death of Isabella Stasiak.

Wydrzynska is charged with Isabella’s murder, while both parents have been charged with one count of causing or allowing the death of a child, four counts of causing or allowing serious physical harm to a child, two counts related to the sexual assault of a child and three counts of child cruelty.

The court heard both parents were known to social services and the police.

Isabella died in hospital after sustaining a series of injuries including a fractured skull and ribs, a broken arm and a burn to her entire face, the court was told.

In her opening statement to the court on Tuesday, Annabel Darlow KC said emergency services were called to the Wydrzynska’s home in the early hours of 7 January 2025 where Isabella was found “grey and lifeless”.

Medical experts later concluded Isabella died “because she suffered injuries consistent with a forceful direct impact to her head against a hard surface”, Darlow told the court.

Darlow said Wydrzynska was the only adult present at the home when Isabella was found by police and the injuries were the “devastating culmination of systematic physical abuse”.

“The prosecution say, by the time Isabella died, there was an entrenched pattern of abuse, neglect and mistreatment of the little girl of which both parents were entirely aware,” Darlow told the court.

“Before she died, Isabella was subjected to physical and sexual abuse at the hands of both her mother and father,” Darlow added. “Neither defendant has ever provided any explanation for those injuries to their daughter.”

Jurors were told Isabella was born in December 2023 and immediately taken into the care of social services. After being placed in emergency accommodation, Isabella was looked after by foster parents for four months before she was returned to her parents in April 2024 – nine months before her death, the court was told.

Members of the jury were also told Stasiak was arrested by police for common assault after a report was made by Wydrzynska on 14 December 2024, less than a month before Isabella’s death.

Wydrzynska made repeated attempts to withdraw the report, jurors were told. However, Stasiak was placed on police bail and prohibited from living at the family home or contacting Wydrzynska.

In addition, the court was told police officers had attended the family home after a complaint was made by a neighbour in October 2024.

Officers attended the property and were only responded to when the police threatened to force entry, Darlow said. Officers spoke to the parents and saw Isabella and “did not have any immediate safeguarding concerns” after the visit, the court was told.

The trial continues.

Russell Brand told police he led a ‘very promiscuous’ life, trial hears

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 18:32:46 GMT

Comedian accused of sexual offences against six women said consensual encounters were ‘unfavourably reframed decades later’

Russell Brand told police he had led a “very promiscuous” life and consensual sexual encounters had been “unfavourably reframed decades later”, his trial has heard.

The 51-year-old comedian blamed the allegations on “defamatory and fictitious” media reports. He said in a statement that he had had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios and kissed hundreds of people in public while trying to be “friendly, consensual and warm”.

Brand is accused of seven offences against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Wearing a grey suit and pale blue shirt, he sat in the dock on Tuesday as his statements to police were read to Southwark crown court in London.

The jury was told Brand was interviewed four times between November 2023 and July 2025, when he read prepared statements in which he insisted he had “never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity”.

“I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I have spent years openly denouncing,” he said in his first statement on 16 November 2023.

Referencing joint reporting by Channel 4, the Times and the Sunday Times, Brand added: “On 16 September 2023, a defamatory and fictitious documentary was broadcast in conjunction with the publication of two national newspapers containing false, anonymised allegations which led to unprecedented media reporting.

“Subsequently, both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which resulted in further encounters being invented or reimagined.”

Addressing an allegation that he had touched an MTV worker’s breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her in 2004, he said he did not recall meeting the woman.

“At no point would I have touched [her] breasts unless it was consensual,” he said. “I have had consensual sex in toilet cubicles during parties. I have never forced anyone into a toilet and I have never forced my penis into anyone’s mouth.”

In a statement on 14 December 2023, Brand said he did not remember the women who had come forward to accuse him.

But he added: “It is entirely possible that I may have encountered them and that we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that has since been reimagined.”

Brand described aspects of his past celebrity lifestyle, saying: “My engagement with interested members of the public was friendly, consensual and warm. There was often physical contact. At live shows, press events, junkets and book signings I did my best to be accessible, non-discriminatory and loving. I spent a lot of time at these events.

“I have shared kisses with hundreds of members of the public during press events and photos of many such kisses, in front of hundreds of people, are available online. Everything I did in public once I was famous could be photographed or recorded and end up in the tabloids – I was aware of this.

“I routinely made provocative jokes or comments both with members of the public and during live performances and broadcasts.”

He also went on to detail his promiscuity, saying: “I did on occasion find reasons for leaving, or for asking partners in casual sexual encounters to leave, shortly after the experience had concluded.

“I had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios often with people I had just met. The way of life that I have described, the magnitude of the promiscuity, deceptively rendered in recent media attacks, accompanied by advertisements for complainants, have caused consensual encounters to be unfavourably reframed decades later.”

Brand gave similar statements to police in his subsequent interviews on 17 January 2024 and 17 July 2025. In response to police questions after each statement, Brand said: “I have nothing further to add at this time.”

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

The trial continues.

The Guardian view on supporting carers: the DWP’s problem is deeper than IT

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 18:30:40 GMT

A taper is much better than a cliff-edge. But problems with carer’s allowance should have been solved years ago

The reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit paid to people who spend 35 or more hours a week caring for a disabled relative – is overdue and welcome. The cliff-edge design that forces claimants in England and Wales to forfeit their entire payment if they breach an earnings limit of £204 a week by as little as a penny is wrong in principle and made much worse by the appalling way in which rules have been applied.

A Guardian investigation revealed that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) failed to warn thousands of people who it knew were being overpaid. This resulted in debts and hardship, and hundreds of criminal convictions for fraud. Carers in already difficult personal circumstances described feeling driven to desperation and illness by what one called a “catch-out culture”. Most claimants are women on low incomes; the allowance is £86.45 a week.

The plan to replace this outdated, blunt tool with a taper is a good one. The disincentive to employment built into the existing system is perverse. Adults with caring responsibilities should be encouraged to do paid work in addition to their roles at home if they can. As with child benefit, the promised taper will mean that earnings over the threshold lead to a diminution rather than a loss of the allowance. Demands for repayment should be drastically reduced. Thousands of low-income households with disabled members will gain more freedom as a result.

Details of the policy’s implementation have yet to be set out. But after years of delay and inaction, the main concern is timing. A DWP whistleblower first raised the overpayment issue a decade ago, only for their complaint to be shut down. Successive Conservative governments did nothing despite a detailed 2020 report from the work and pensions committee. Finally, last November, Liz Sayce’s independent review led to the recruitment of extra staff and a new approach. Ministers committed to correcting past errors, including the way that claimants had been unlawfully blocked from averaging their earnings. But progress has been slow, and with the taper expected to be rolled out in 2030-31, the injustice of the current situation looks set to continue for several more years.

The benefit system is complicated, and it is better to make changes properly than to rush through a botched job. But the overhaul of carer’s allowance should not be mistaken for an IT problem. The deeper issue is the ongoing failure to get to grips with the fundamental challenge of care in our society, and to take on board the extent to which millions of people’s lives are shaped by the needs of dependent adult relatives.

Louise Casey has made it clear that her social care commission will deliver recommendations about what it is reasonable to expect of families, as well as the state. There are grounds to hope that her forthright style and years of experience, combined with Andy Burnham’s strong commitment to reform, will finally lead to a breakthrough. In the meantime, the DWP must do all it can to put right the wrongs done to carer’s allowance claimants. There has still been no satisfactory explanation about how such a punitive culture developed. But the new commitment to tapered support is an encouraging indication that the government is now moving in a more compassionate direction.

Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 18:27:32 GMT

Far-right senator on plane to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.

Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.

Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.

“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.

The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.

Lawmakers from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.

Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.

A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.

A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.

Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.

The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.

Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”

One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.

The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.

As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.

The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.

Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.

The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.

Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.

“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.

Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.

Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.

“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.

Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.

Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.

Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.

Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.

Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.

“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.

The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 18:25:40 GMT

If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.

Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.

Similar ideas have long circulated in far-right thinktanks. But they are now in the programmes of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany – Europe’s historic engines of integration. Ms Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland.

Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight. Mario Draghi, the former head of the European Central Bank, has warned that without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. But other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leader speaking with the same sense of urgency.

Ms Le Pen and Ms Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defence, the moves towards European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin (and any Maga successor to Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit.

As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counter-arguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming. But it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms. For the time being, to paraphrase WB Yeats, the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.

Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 18:15:29 GMT

From tackling the youth jobs crisis to repairing Brexit’s economic damage, John Healey has his work cut out for him

John Healey will deliver his first budget on Wednesday as UK households and businesses come under pressure from the unfolding economic shock caused by the war in the Middle East.

Against a febrile backdrop in global markets, the chancellor is facing a delicate balancing act to provide “breathing space” measures to ease the cost of living crisis while increasing growth and sticking to the fiscal rules.

Healey will also flesh out Andy Burnham’s pledge to deliver “good growth in every postcode”, with measures to hand local leaders more money and power.

Here are six charts that will underpin the chancellor’s decisions.

At the spring statement, Healey’s immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, left herself £23.6bn of “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be matched by receipts by the end of this parliament. However, the buffer is widely expected to have been slashed by a surge in debt interest costs, as the war in the Middle East causes a global inflation shock that is rattling the bond markets.

The Resolution Foundation estimates headroom has been halved to about £12bn. Much will depend on the judgment of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the independent Treasury watchdog, which will take into account the hit from rising debt costs, but also other positive and negative developments for the public finances – including inflation, pay growth, employment and productivity.

Healey is thought to be willing to allow the buffer to take a hit. However, jittery bond investors will be looking for him to retain some headroom to guard against further negative shocks, with at least £14bn thought to be needed to avoid provoking a bond market reaction.

The chancellor has pledged “breathing space” measures for households and businesses grappling with the cost of living crisis, as the energy price shock fuelled by the Iran conflict hits consumers.

Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills are forecast to increase to £2,000 a year from January for the typical household. Since 2021, consumers have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.

Healey is thought to have earmarked more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which will go on increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. He has also vowed to help businesses, and has been urged to extend a cut in fuel duty.

Alongside energy support, Andy Burnham has already promised Labour will cut living costs through other measures – including a new mortgage scheme for first-time buyers, and a pledge to build more social homes.

Burnham has made “growth in every postcode” his top political slogan since becoming prime minister. With devolution likely to be a central theme of the budget, a raft of measures are expected to add some substance to the rhetoric.

Central to the devolution package will be plans to allow local leaders in England to retain a share of income tax, alongside a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for directly elected mayors.

Britain is the most centralised G7 country for tax and spending policy, and is among the most economically unequal, according to the Centre for Cities thinktank. The aim of redrawing the political map – including establishing a new hub for No 10 in the north, based in Manchester – is to increase regional economic growth, and with it the performance of the UK economy at large.

Burnham has also signalled that a strengthened industrial strategy will be key to his agenda, as well as measures to support high streets and towns.

The prime minister has said Britain is facing an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” after a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million.

Tackling the youth jobs crisis will be a key budget theme. Business leaders have pressed Healey for tax cuts and help with labour costs to encourage youth recruitment, while ministers have explored options for overhauling the benefits system and making changes to apprenticeships.

Healey has indicated that welfare reform will be critical. There could though be costs attached – as any savings from changes to the system could be offset by higher spending on employment support. The government is handling the process carefully to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion faced by Keir Starmer, and is still awaiting recommendations from two key reviews – by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn and the Department for Work and Pensions minister Stephen Timms.

The government is understood to favour handing local leaders more power and money to support young people as part of the solution. Analysis from the Youth Futures Foundation, a charity, shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is geographically uneven: rates are significantly higher in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford than in Bath, Harrogate or Guildford.

Having resigned as Starmer’s defence secretary over funding, Healey is widely tipped to use his budget to find more cash for the military. Burnham has also spoken of the importance of the defence sector for his reindustrialisation plans.

First, the chancellor will need to find an additional £1bn a year to fund Labour’s defence investment plan. Announced by Starmer in his final weeks in office, that put defence spending on track to reach 2.7% of gross domestic product by 2029.

However, Healey has expressed an ambition to spend 3% by 2030. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates an extra £11bn would be needed in that year. Longer term, the government is targeting spending of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. This is equivalent to a £25bn increase in today’s terms.

Burnham reopened the debate over Brexit in his speech to Labour conference in Liverpool, arguing that leaving the EU had damaged the UK economy and failed to bring the benefits promised.

This week’s budget is expected to underscore the economic hit, including from a drop in net migration.

Net migration to the UK has fallen sharply from a record peak of almost a million in 2023. Earlier this year, the Office for National Statistics downgraded its estimate for the long-run figure to settle at about 230,000 annually, down from a previous assumption of 340,000.

On average, immigrants are net contributors to the exchequer, and so how the OBR accounts for this drop in its forecasts will be critical. Should it adopt a similar approach to the ONS, the Resolution Foundation thinktank estimates this could lead to a drop in tax receipts of £4.7bn by 2029-30 relative to previous forecasts.

Lack of a ‘protective ring’ around care homes meant our loved ones died of Covid

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:55:11 GMT

Diane La Rosa and Teresa Pacey-Devlin on the deaths of their fathers during the pandemic. Plus more letters responding to the Covid inquiry from John Robinson, David Flood and James Townsend

My dad was in a care home when Covid hit in March 2020 and visits were stopped (UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry finds, 20 October). It was heartbreaking not being able to see him, and talking to him via phone was almost impossible. I couldn’t see how Covid wouldn’t spread to the home as there wasn’t any testing at that point. He was a sitting duck and there was nothing I could do.

In late April 2020, when I had been calling all day, eventually someone answered and told me they were too busy to talk. The next day when I called, I was told Dad wasn’t feeling very well. I asked if there was Covid in the home: they were honest and said there was. I was distraught.

I then received the inevitable call in the early hours next morning from the home, saying my father had been taken to hospital with suspected Covid. My conversation with the hospital was soul-destroying. They would make Dad as comfortable as possible, he wouldn’t be given oxygen and no resuscitation would be given. The only positive was that I’d be able to go in and see him when he was close to death – they would call me.

In a way I felt as though I was one of the lucky ones, being with my father as he passed away, convulsing and gasping for his last breath. I will never forget it. Diane La Rosa Tottenham, London

My father died in a care home during Covid, surrounded by close family. For many weeks before that we couldn’t touch him or hold his hand. Restrictions were still in place, as others in government were partying. It was only when he was dying, and a kind nurse telephoned us to say he’d taken a sudden turn for the worse, that we all ignored the rules and rushed to the nursing home to be with him, speak to him, tell him he could let go – give him permission to take his last breath.

Until then only my mother and I had spent any time with him, and that was 10 minutes in a cold segregation room where he looked at us blankly as a tear rolled down his cheek. All other times it was waving through the window of the care home to him. He had dementia and didn’t understand why his family was deserting him.

As agency staff entered the care home – strangers to my dad and possibly carriers of the virus – we, his family, were locked out. We took the tests, we wore the PPE, we pleaded with the care home, we promised to be extremely vigilant; anything to allow us to see our loved ones while doing everything we could to safeguard them against the virus.

Please support Gloria’s Law, which would give everyone a right to a care supporter when using health or care services. Allow care givers and loved ones access during any future pandemic so that people don’t die scared, lonely and alone. Teresa Pacey-Devlin Bassingfield, Nottinghamshire

Boris Johnson apologised to me in parliament on 19 April 2022 for his partying in Downing Street while my wife and thousands of others were dying from Covid (Letters, 14 April 2022).

Many of us had already suspected the unimaginable, that Johnson and the health secretary were prepared to let us older people die. Now we know the awful truth: there was no “protective ring”, no “ring of steel” around care homes, just a ring of lies. John Robinson Lichfield

Sadly, it comes as no surprise that Lady Hallett rejected Matt Hancock’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic, saying it was “unfounded”. I was working as a nurse in a large acute hospital at the time of Covid, in particular within the interface between the NHS and social care. I kept a diary.

This is what I noted on 31 March 2020: “So we are starting to see the fallout from poor policy/guidance from DH/NHSE. Discharge plans to care homes etc causing huge amount of understandable confusion and even possible cross-infection across the sector. Care home managers saying no to at risk patients ‘ready’ for d/c as too many unknown factors/risk in terms of Covid. Really is a mess. Watch this space as the impact in care home sector could be huge.”

I look back with anger, sadness and shame at how our colleagues in the care sector and their residents/clients (and respective families) were treated. Never again, please. David Flood Wimbledon, London

The Covid inquiry’s report on the care sector finds that about 5.8 million people were caring unpaid for a family member or friend during the pandemic. Many did so for months without a break, buying their own protective equipment and taking on medication, injections, dressings and end-of-life care at home with little or no training. In 2021, almost three in four had still not had a single break since the pandemic began.

Yet none of the report’s eight recommendations is about them. Their experience gets a chapter section of findings, a short paragraph in the executive summary, and nothing the four governments must formally answer.

The report is clear about why help failed to reach them: nobody knew who they were. There is no register of unpaid carers anywhere in the UK. A minister at the time told the inquiry the government had limited knowledge of who was caring. Northern Ireland resorted to leafleting every household.

This is fixable. The government’s Pandemic Preparedness Strategy, published in March, already commits to identifying unpaid carers in England by digital means, and the report points to GP records and health apps as practical routes. What is missing is a deadline and someone accountable for meeting it.

When ministers respond to this report, they should add the recommendation it lacks: that everyone caring for someone they love can be found, told what help exists and offered a break, well before the next pandemic arrives. James Townsend Chief executive and co-founder, Mobilise

Pablo Escobar tried to bomb me in Bogotá. To stop the cartels infiltrating Europe, we should legalise cocaine

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:55:04 GMT

Responding to a Guardian investigation into trafficking, former British ambassador to Colombia Keith Morris says the ‘war on drugs’ has failed

I congratulate the Guardian on this investigation (Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’, 13 October). It has already prompted a strong call from the former Colombian vice-president Marta Lucía Ramírez for effective international cooperation to counter the transnational criminal threat.

I have followed the “war on drugs” pretty closely since I was the British ambassador to Colombia in the heyday of Pablo Escobar, but I was still shocked to learn of the scale of the Latin American criminal presence in Europe, including supposedly political insurgents such as the Colombian ELN and various Farc dissident factions. The fivefold increase in the cocaine trade in the last decade has boosted organised crime on both sides of the Atlantic. It underlines dramatically the failure of the “war on drugs”.

In 2001 you published an opinion piece by me saying that this war was unwinnable and that state supervision of legalised drugs would be preferable. I argued that aggressive law enforcement had greatly damaged producer and transit countries without reducing the flow of drugs to consumer countries. Prohibition ensured that the incentive of high prices for cheaply produced drugs was simply too great. So it has remained.

However, legalised cannabis regimes are now working in Canada, Uruguay and more than 20 US states, providing possible models for cocaine. The situation has been complicated by the development of extremely strong synthetic drugs, such as fentanyl. Of around 80,000 drug overdose deaths in the United States in 2024, 22,000 were cocaine users, while 48,000 had used fentanyl. It strikes me that the availability of such dangerous drugs would make the alternative of legally controlled and safer cocaine worth an experiment, on top of the reduction of violence and corruption that legalisation should bring.

I will soon be 92, and owe that to the good fortune that I and fellow members of our chamber of commerce board walked out of a meeting in Bogotá in January 1993, just 15 minutes before an Escobar-ordered car bomb destroyed our boardroom. I have an obligation to continue making this case. Keith Morris Ambassador to Colombia, 1990-94

Radio 4 Extra sustains a major part of our cultural heritage. Save it from the BBC cuts

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:54:58 GMT

Stephen McKenna argues against the axing of the station to cut the BBC’s costs

My father was the actor TP McKenna, who died in 2011. A boon of his years in that great radio studio in the skies is the regular messages I get from friends who have heard him of late on BBC Radio 4 Extra in such programmes as Ballylenon and Baldi. If I tune in myself, it’s as if he’s in the room with me.

Of itself, that’s hardly a reason to save this important channel from plans to scrap it (BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next year, 20 October), and yet it is. Not to mention the astonishing roll call of British actors that could be cited, including Paul Daneman, John Moffatt, Robert Hardy, Robert Lang, Richard Pasco, Norman Rodway, Anna Massey, Stephanie Cole, Elizabeth Spriggs, Joanna David, Maggie Steed, Melinda Walker, Geraldine McEwan, and the words of our finest writers from Alan Ayckbourn to George Bernard Shaw. Just a few out of so many.

The fact is, the BBC’s radio archive is to our ears as the National Trust is to our Sunday afternoon excursions. It is a major part of our cultural heritage, and far too important to be stuffed away in some corner of BBC Sounds. An all too pertinent reminder these days that there is hardly anyone remaining in the BBC’s management who was ever a part of its former culture. Stephen McKenna Blackheath, London

Britain’s fridge disposal crisis and what to do about it

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:54:53 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Sam Wollaston about Norfolk’s fridge mountain

Sam Wollaston (What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain, 21 October) highlights an urgent issue, but misses a key underlying driver: the reality of climate change and increasingly hot UK summers.

Many standard UK fridge-freezers are only built to normal (N) ambient climate classes, rated to operate in temperatures up to +32C. During recent heatwaves, indoor temperatures in many homes regularly exceed this limit. Even subtropical (ST) rated units fail when ambient temperatures push past 38C. When ambient limits are exceeded, cooling systems fail, leading to compressor breakdown, spoiled food and premature appliance disposal.

We need higher regulatory standards requiring manufacturers to produce more durable, resilient appliances rated for higher ambient temperature classes (such as Tropical T or SN-T). Until manufacturers are held to these standards, UK consumers will continue to be left with failing fridges and our landfill waste will keep growing. Alistair Beattie London

The problem of fridge disposal needs government action. A “polluter pays” levy should apply to all new fridges, and should go proportionally to local authorities responsible for waste management. They could use the levy to commission companies to recycle fridges in an environment-friendly way. Steve Rowell Solihull

There is a simple solution when fridges and freezers are being thrown away simply because the owner wanted an “upgrade”. Appliances in working order can be given away to others via apps such as Olio and Freecycle, or community Facebook pages or WhatsApp groups. This is how I disposed of all my functional white goods when my house was renovated. Jacky Rowland London

I have just had to buy a new fridge as I can’t find replacements for the door seals on the the old one. Fridges should be repairable. Now the old one, which still functions in a rattly sort of way, has to join the recycling queue simply because of a bit of perished rubber. Diana Dalasini Molesey, Surrey

Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:43:02 GMT

Frontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuation

A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians.

The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022.

Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation.

Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.

The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.

The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid.

Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe.

Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it.

Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles.

Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia.

Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.

“People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press.

The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russia bombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire.

The bridge remains closed to traffic, but some commuters walked across it to get to work. Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it.

He said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote.

The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole.

European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, given Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a candidate.

The divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said.

She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.”

Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process.

This month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces.

Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in an interview with ABC News. He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian.

The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:41:03 GMT

A regulator to keep the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank on mission is starting to look essential

Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy.

The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn.

Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing.

Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules. Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt.

To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse.

Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies in a report last week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-era private finance initiative did. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped.

Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions.

In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new. Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful.

There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out.

The line can appear blurry at times. This column has questioned the £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”? Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising.

Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans?

To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’s follow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

And, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities. In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell: last year’s return on equity was -2.6% but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful.

But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in its impact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholder, the Treasury.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.”

That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundation argues that, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets.

Schrödinger’s racism, Nige’s latest wheeze to try to dodge his associates’ bigotry

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:29:26 GMT

We are apparently to believe Raheem Kassam calling Kemi a ‘Nigerian scammer’ was racist and not racist at the same time

Back to the future. Some of us can remember the days when the key to surviving a nuclear war was to kneel down under the kitchen table and keep your eyes closed till you were incinerated or died of radiation poisoning. Now the government wants you to hoard some baked beans and a few litres of water in the hope of getting through the next three days.

But when the apocalypse does come, you can bank on there being one survivor. The politician with seemingly limitless powers of regeneration. As one party of his dies, so another rises from the ashes. Fuelled not by water and tinned food, but by alcohol and grievance. Somehow, Nigel Farage is always the victim in his own story. The man who is forever misunderstood.

Nige must be the unluckiest politician alive. The man who has only ever wanted the best for everybody – deporting immigrants is clearly in their own best interests, even if it involves death or torture – keeps getting mired in scandal. There’s the money. Of course there is. Plenty of it from – how shall we put this? – unorthodox sources. But there’s also the racism. Why is it that so many who are close to Farage and his organisation turn out to be bigots? How can his message of love and peace to all men be so tainted? It’s happened so often now that you could forgive Nige for being a little grumpy.

Last week one of his closest friends was at it again. Raheem Kassam, touted as Reform’s next chief of staff, called Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”. You and I know exactly what he meant. The leader of the opposition was like a West African phonejacker who rang you up and tried to scam your bank accounts. It was a fairly obvious racist slur. One designed to denigrate.

Only it wasn’t quite so obviously racist to Reform MPs themselves. Robert Jenrick called it a bit of forensic journalism. At least that’s what he implied by describing Kassam as a journalist. Danny Kruger was even more confused. There again, he often is. He’s meant to be the intellectual and moral compass of Reform, but just appears dim-witted and spinning helplessly in space. He thought “Nigerian scammer” couldn’t be racist because he couldn’t conceive of any of Nigel’s friends being racist. Try a little harder, Danny.

It was third time unlucky – that word again – as Nige took on his first proper morning media round in months. It didn’t end well for him. Car-crash TV. On BBC Breakfast, the presenter Sally Nugent quickly cut to the chase and it soon became clear that Nige doesn’t take it well when an intelligent woman asks him tricky questions. He likes to think of himself very much as a man’s man. Somehow being interviewed by a woman is a sign of disrespect. Or maybe he’s still tetchy about having given a press conference to a near-empty hall the day before.

First Nige tried to claim Kassam had not been a former chief of staff – he had in one of Farage’s previous lives – and was on the point of saying he wasn’t even a friend. But then he had a brainwave. “He’s Indian,” he said. “He’s of Indian heritage.” As if that somehow precluded all Indians – all black and brown people, for that matter – from being racist. A suggestion, dare one say it, that is racist in itself. Nige clearly believes in a hierarchy of racism. If he believes in racism at all. Maybe we’re just all stuck in a doom loop of cultural relativism. We just need to chill out a bit.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Next Farage tried to play the word dissociation game. Just because Kassam had used the words “Nigerian scammer” in conjunction with one another, it didn’t necessarily mean the words were in any way connected to form a single image. All he had done was to state two truths. Kemi was of Nigerian descent, though for the purposes of this conversation he was prepared to concede that she might also be part British. And she was a scammer, because she had said things that were demonstrably untrue. Much the same could be said of Nige, mind. Maybe in his own mind he also longs to be outed as a scammer.

Back in the BBC studio, Nugent wasn’t having any of this and kept at him. Did he think it was racist? “No, I don’t,” said Nige. Perhaps a bit over the top, but definitely not intentionally racist. Farage had spoken, Schrödinger’s racism. Something could be racist and not racist at the same time. In any case, he couldn’t be held responsible for any of the social media posts his friends and supporters made. It was his curse that so many in Reform expressed themselves in racist language. He had no idea why he had become the last refuge for so many bigots.

Things took on a more surreal turn later that morning when Kassam emailed a Guardian journalist to give an update on the situation. In it, he said that Nige had given him a ticking off for a tweet that was neither “clever nor funny”. Just a shame Farage couldn’t have used his position as the leader of Reform to make that same point on the BBC hours earlier. Kassam went on to say that, in hindsight, his tweet could have been better phrased and timed. He also claimed Kemi was a con artist for turning the Tories into a version of the Lib Dems. That will come as news to both the Tories and the Lib Dems. The Tories have been shadowing Reform to the right for the last two years.

The real sorry-not-sorry moment came when Kassam suggested he had spent too much time in the US recently. Over there, out-and-out racism was an acceptable rite of political discourse. People could say what they want. The trouble is that we Brits had lost our sense of humour. It was now a thought crime even to make a racist joke. Time we all lightened up. What was needed was more politicians who called Kemi a “Nigerian scammer” not fewer.

This isn’t quite the end of it. Because Kassam’s new found contrition may not be all it seems. On Tuesday morning he was again posting about “Kemi Scammenoch” on X. A post that has been subsequently deleted. As has his pinned “Nigerian scammer” tweet. If this is remorse, it’s still in its early days. Maybe one should treat Kassam and Farage as one and the same. When they show you what they are, believe them.

‘Well-known’ public figure in bid to stop publication of allegations of inappropriate sexual activities

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:09:13 GMT

Individual seeks permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN to block claims, citing high risk of suicide

A “well-known individual” attempting to block two media outlets from publishing allegations about him has been accused of inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities with girls and young women, the high court has heard.

The individual, referred to in court as PPT, is seeking a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies. His legal team argued that publishing them would “highly likely lead him to commit suicide”.

In written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a “wide-ranging and rigorous investigation”.

However, at the opening of a two-day trial, PPT’s legal team argued it was a “highly exceptional” case in which publishing was likely to lead to the death of the claimant.

In a written submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team said that he suffered from “very severe mental health problems”.

“It is important to understand that this drastic effect on the claimant is not from guilt of the wrongdoing alleged (which is denied) but because of shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of ‘trial by media’,” it stated.

Sara Mansoori KC, PPT’s lead barrister, said that he had first attempted to commit suicide in May, when the Guardian and ITN contacted him to give him the chance to respond to the allegations. He was admitted to hospital that afternoon as a voluntary patient.

The court was told PPT made a second attempt to take his life in July, “on that occasion absconding from a secure hospital to do so”.

Submissions to the court by PPT’s legal team stated he is detained in a psychiatric hospital for his own safety and has no intention of returning to public life.

The claimant is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life, article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment” and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

Setting out the claimant’s case, Mansoori pointed to medical evidence that PPT’s life would be endangered should the allegations be published.

“It would be a travesty if the court didn’t step in to act in these circumstances,” Mansoori said.

According to written submissions from the news outlets, they will argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never required a state to prevent publication of journalism in order to protect against the risk of suicide by an individual.

The written submissions argue that any duties the state has towards PPT should come in the form of NHS mental health treatment and its powers under the Mental Health Act.

The news outlets will set out their case to the court on Wednesday.

An independent expert assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing stated that “community arrangements” would not be sufficient to manage the immediate suicide risk around the prospect of publishing the allegations.

“Publication while the claimant remains in an inpatient psychiatric setting would be significantly safer in terms of reducing the likelihood of a successful suicide,” the expert concluded, according to a summary of his findings.

“The expert does not conclude either that suicide is inevitable if publication occurs, or that psychiatric treatment can eliminate all risk,” the expert’s report states.

Mr Justice Nicklin, the judge overseeing the case, opened the trial with a warning about online speculation over PPT’s identity.

“That speculation has named several different individuals,” he said. “This is a difficult and important case. The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions, while respecting both the principle of open justice and the protective purpose of the orders already made.

“I ask that the court be allowed to perform that task without further attempts to identify PPT or any other person whose identity is protected.”

The trial continues.

Australia fight back in rollercoaster start to deciding Test against South Africa

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:04:06 GMT

Decision to bowl first looked like backfiring

But hosts all out for 329 after being 140-0 at lunch

For a time, it was heading up there with the worst. David Gower at Leeds in 1989, when Australia topped 600 and declared. Nasser Hussain in Brisbane, 2002, when Australia were 364 for two by the end of the day. Edgbaston 2005, where England lamped 407 from 80 overs. Those were the looming comparisons for captains deciding to bowl at the toss, after Pat Cummins did the same in the third Test at Cape Town, only for South Africa’s openers to smash 140 by lunch. Yet, by day’s end, Australia had taken 10 for a further 189, Mitchell Starc destroying the tail with four wickets in six balls, 329 all out constituting a serious Australian comeback.

What a rollercoaster. The Australian setup has looked frazzled on this tour: confused player selections for the squad, then for the XIs, confused shot selection in the middle, players bouncing around the order with nightwatch duties and injury absences. Here they chose to leave out their best player from the second Test, Scott Boland, for Nathan Lyon, and were forced to leave out their best player of the last decade, Steve Smith, for Josh Inglis, as well as dropping Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster for Cameron Green and Cooper Connolly. The last time a touring Australian side made four non-disciplinary changes was in the West Indies in 1984.

So it tracked that there was confusion in the decision by Cummins as well. He has been a bowl-first enthusiast relative to captaincy convention, this being the ninth time he has made that call in 25 opportunities, and perhaps was banking on there being more juice in the surface on the first morning than on the second afternoon. But with locals describing a Cape Town surface that is known to run easy, and on a morning of bright sunshine with plenty more predicted, surely the safest move was to try to build a score?

That is what Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman did, Markram setting the tone with some early blows, then Ackerman following his lead until surpassing it.

Starc and Josh Hazlewood bowled poorly, too short and too wide on too many occasions, and with no swing and no lateral movement from the pitch, Markram laid into front-foot drives, back-foot punches, and even a shockingly audacious smash from Hazlewood on the up. When Cummins came on to play enforcer, Markram pulled him for six. Lyon, the spinner, was bowling by the 12th over rather than waiting to influence day five.

Before long, Ackerman took over. Happy to hook whenever the opportunity came, he cleared fine leg for six from Cummins and belted Lyon out of the arena over midwicket. When Starc returned for a later spell, Ackerman smashed 18 off one over, hitting four boundaries in a row. Australia were shambolic, Travis Head dropping one of the easiest catches of his life at cover, spliced to him by Markram from Starc, then Lyon letting a return catch go through in the first over after lunch. With the score on 158, South Africa were 13 short of the record opening stand against Australia for a team being sent in, and the tourists looked set for a dismal day.

It was Lyon who found a way through. With Ackerman determined not to temper his approach on 95, he ran at Lyon only to be outfoxed, a wider and slower ball evading his bat to bring about his stumping. Markram also perished while forging on, pulling a Hazlewood ball that had bounced nowhere high enough out to long leg, the first of many false shorts to short balls that found the hands of a fielder. That opened the door for Lyon to bowl Temba Bavuma, past the defensive outside edge, and Connolly to get his first Test wicket by burrowing past Matthew Breetzke’s inside edge, lbw on review.

David Bedingham had played beautifully, driving with precision, and finally reached 50 having been out for 46 and 49 earlier in the series. But he went no further, also caught at fine leg hooking, Hazlewood dancing over the boundary and back to complete it, followed by Wiaan Mulder top-edging a hook off Starc for nought. Wicketless for 158 had become 216 for six.

So it was time for South Africa’s rollercoaster to climb up again. Marco Jansen, so often the Australians’ chief cause of frustration, took them on once more, flaying the ageing ball for another half-century after his match-turning 85 in the second Test. With Ryan Rickelton alongside him, they added 95 in good time.

after newsletter promotion

But the first over with the new ball brought about the rollercoaster’s death-drop finale. Now with cloud cover at the end of the day, the ball began to swing, and Starc went back to his roots. No wobble-seam, no bouncers, just left-arm, over the wicket, inswinging menace. Rickelton nailed on the back pad, fourth ball of the over, for 42. Jansen two balls later, trying to drive, curling back to kiss the outside of off-stump, bowled for 52.

First ball of Starc’s next over, Gerald Coetzee was bowled off his pads, backing away from that inswing, and while Kagiso Rabada survived the hat-trick ball, he was smashed in line with leg-stump from the one that followed. South Africa had lost four wickets for two runs, Starc finished with six for 72 and a day of Test cricket containing almost everything one could ask for was called to a close. The jury might remain out overnight if asked to decide who should be happier. Look for a verdict later this week.

A group of restaurants in Sardinia are banning families from using smartphones and other devices at the table in a quest to encourage conversation.

The initiative, called A tavola senza schermi or At the table without screens, is being spearheaded by Anna Cau, the children’s ombudsman for the Italian island. It is part of a campaign to curtail excessive screen use among children and inspire interaction during meals.

Parents and their children will be required to put their phones away when dining at any of the 15 restaurants that have volunteered to participate in the scheme during a one-month pilot exercise beginning next week.

Cau, a former juvenile magistrate, said: “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others.

“We need real-world settings that strengthen and accommodate the lives of both adults and children. This initiative is a small step within a broader philosophy that guides my approach to this highly complex issue.”

After families hand in their devices, restaurant staff will give them a “reunion kit” containing games and drawings. The kit, which has been designed by the Italian federation of paediatricians, is aimed at helping under-18s start conversations with their parents, such as sharing stories about their day.

The kit includes a brochure outlining the risks of digital overexposure and tips on managing social media use at home.

“The restaurants will offer an alternative activity in the form of a game which is intended to foster interaction,” said Cau. “Obviously, the games are structured with time limits within the context of a restaurant lunch or dinner.”

Cau worked on the scheme with the Sardinian wing of Fipe-Confcommercio, an association uniting the catering, tourism and entertainment sectors.

Emanuele Frongia, president of the federation on the island, said the 15 restaurants had readily agreed to participate. The plan is to expand the initiative on a voluntary basis.

“Restaurants play a vital role in fostering the intimacy that families rediscover when they dine out,” said Frongia. “Yet we increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices. Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.”

Maplin said sales of torches had almost quadrupled and sales of power banks and radios had doubled. One brand of emergency wind-up radio sold out on Friday.

Ollie Marshall, the managing director of Maplin, said: “Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics – a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank.

The grocery chain Iceland said sales of tinned products were up 40% over the weekend and it had also seen strong sales of bottled water. A spokesperson said: “It’s clear consumers have listened to the government’s message. Our supplies of these products remain healthy.”

The online grocer Ocado said demand for some products was up and it would “continue to work with suppliers to ensure there is stock for customers to gradually add items to their shops”.

Several major supermarkets said they had seen no material change in demand in tinned goods and that the cooler, stormy weather was more likely to influence demand for soups and beans.

Jim Bligh, food policy director at the British Retail Consortium, said: “While some retailers have seen a small uptick in sales for some products, food availability remains strong and retailers remain well stocked with all essential products.”

Name: The Babydoll trend.

Age: Older than you think.

Meaning? Let’s come back to that.

OK. Appearance? Everywhere. TikTok, Insta, all your socials. Also on the radio, if you still do that.

I call it the wireless. A song, right? More than a song, but we’ll come to that too. But yes, a song, currently No 1 in the UK singles charts, by Jamie Miller.

That name rings a bell. He was on The Voice in 2017.

From Wales, no? From Wales, yes! He grew up in Pontprennau in the north of Cardiff. Now he’s the first Welsh solo male artist to top the singles chart since …

Tom Jones? Not quite that far back. No, since Shakin’ Stevens’ festive hit Merry Christmas Everyone in 1985.

So after The Voice, Jamie’s career took off? Not really. He only came third, for a start. And even the aforementioned Sir Tom didn’t “spin his chair” for his fellow Welshman. Since then he’s played venues such as The Globe in Cardiff, and brought out a few records, but he has hardly taken the world by storm. He was considering quitting music altogether.

Until now, and Babydoll? Sort of. It was originally released in early August.

A slow burn, as they say. Correct, though now smoking hot. It really got going after Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos of herself singing along and doing the dance routine.

There’s a dance? Oh yes.

How do I do it? Start with a chug, stepping on your right foot, raising your left knee and heel, then switching sides. Do eight of them, while rolling your shoulders.

[Chugging, kind of.] Got it! Next you’re going to go out with your right foot, and back, then out with the left, and back, and so on. Times eight again, while popping your arms.

This is getting complicated. Maybe it would be easier if you found a tutorial video.

[Having found a tutorial video] OK, now I’m pulling my arm up, with a little finger-click, five, six, seven, eight … Maybe I’m too old for Babydoll. Nonsense. Look around, everyone’s doing it: the very young, very old, dogs, more slebs …

Who? Antonio Cipriano (off Off Campus), who recorded a version with Miller. And Alison Hammond did it, with Miller – very well, until she fell over a boulder and injured her wrist.

I knew it was dangerous. Anyway, are we declaring it a viral dance craze? To the extent that Miller and Cipriano were on Strictly at the weekend, doing it with the entire cast.

I’d call that viral. It’s really catching on. “If you’re gonna leave me broken-hearted / Then maybe, baby, we should just get started …”

Do say: “Who’s laughing now, Sir Tom?”

Don’t say: “And now shall we do … the Macarena?”
