‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the Telephone

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:25:55 GMT

They gigged wildly, helped other groups to fame and their songwriting brilliance gave Blondie a signature track. Could a deathbed wish now see the Nerves finally making it big?

The Nerves should have had it all. Formed in 1974 and gifted with earworm melodies, good looks and a painstaking work ethic, the trio of Jack Lee (guitar, vocals), Peter Case (bass, vocals) and Paul Collins (drums, vocals) wrote, rehearsed and gigged as if their lives depended on it. Not quite punk and dismissive of the description “power pop”, they aimed to cram epic brilliance into effervescent, two-minute songs.

When the music industry ignored them, the Nerves opted to make their own luck, pressing their own EP and booking a gruelling nationwide tour that saw them share stages with Devo and the Ramones. After they split in 1978, a bittersweet coda to their brief career swiftly followed: Parallel Lines, Blondie’s smash-hit third album, opened with a cover version of their song Hanging on the Telephone. Previously a Nerves calling card, the Blondie take seemed to scrub them from history.

“I figured it would be two weeks, or a month tops, before we were famous,” smiles Paul Collins from his New York home today. A Juilliard student with a bohemian upbringing and an overriding love of rock’n’roll, Collins dropped out and headed for the west coast. “I was barely 18, I had 80 bucks in my pocket and I was scared to death,” he recalls. Within three days of arriving in San Francisco, he found an ad tacked to the wall of a record store which led him to the enigmatic Jack Lee, a transplant from Sitka, Alaska.

Peter Case proved harder to woo. Baling on school at 15 and ditching Buffalo for San Francisco, he played blues and country standards on the street to pay for food. “I slept in a beat-up van parked down by the water,” says Case. “It wasn’t even my van.” Lee and Case struck up a friendship when the latter was busking. When Collins came on board, the Nerves were transformed from idea to actuality. “You just couldn’t find people that wanted to do something that was that out of joint,” Case recalls. “There was nobody else like Jack around – someone who had a vision, wanted to go with it and could write.”

The band set up shop in a three-storey flophouse, immersing themselves in practice sessions that could last up to 16 hours. “It was like being in boot camp,” says Collins. “My snare drum would be covered with blood because we were playing so fast. It was three people acting as one person, and it was a 24-hour endeavour. There was no on and off.”

For all their commitment, it soon became apparent that the Nerves were going nowhere. With no peers beyond the Flamin’ Groovies and the aloof, leather-clad Crime, the trio saw no future playing to barflies and fist-swinging off-duty servicemen. After Lee recovered from a near-fatal stabbing, the band left for LA. There they rubbed shoulders with scenesters such as Kim Fowley and Rodney Bingenheimer, and organised early shows for punk bands the Germs and the Weirdos. “It turned out to be a bitter pill to swallow, because they instantly became much more popular than we did!” says Collins.

Unperturbed, the band concocted a national tour in 1977 that spanned 71 days, 39 gigs and 16 cities, during which they connected with the Dead Boys and Cheap Trick, and played a series of dates with the Ramones. “The Ramones’ work ethic was even more stringent than ours,” recalls Collins. “They’d be practising before the show, and afterwards they’d go back to the hotel and work on songs. I remember sitting at this big wooden table with them after a show, and Dee Dee goes, ‘May I be excused? I have to go to the bathroom.’ It was like he was at the dinner table with his parents!”

If the Ramones were a picture of politeness, other soon to be stars were less welcoming. “We played Boston, and when we were loading in, there were these four guys completely dressed in leather,” says Collins. “One of them goes, ‘What the fuck do you think you’re doing? You’re touring all over the country. You don’t have a manager. You don’t have an agent. It’s bullshit. We know what we’re fucking doing. We’re going to be huge.’ So we look at them and say, ‘Yeah, well what’s the name of your band? The Cars? What a stupid name…’”

Inevitably, travelling thousands of miles in a station wagon and booking gigs on the fly took its toll. “It’s like a plant,” says Collins. “You don’t give it water, you don’t give it sunlight, it’s gonna die. We couldn’t get any industry acceptance, and I think we’d taken all we could.”

After a stint in the Breakaways, Collins and Case respectively formed the Beat and the Plimsouls, with both bands enjoying the success that eluded the Nerves. Lee, meanwhile, worked on a solo career, self-funding two albums and encountering more proxy success when Come Back and Stay became a hit for Paul Young. While Hanging on the Telephone would be covered by everyone from L7 and Def Leppard to Girls Aloud, the Nerves remained perennially under the radar, never achieving the same cut-through as the bands they’d served with in the trenches.

Fifty years on, a new anthology may redress the balance. “My dad tasked me with this on his deathbed,” says Lee’s daughter, Cynthia Cook. “His dream was to be on Jack White’s label Third Man Records.” While Cook may have grown up writing songs with her father – their first was titled Rock’n’Roll Rabbit, penned when she was five – the music industry wasn’t her home turf. “My dad was all about the long shot,” she smiles. “You know, I’m a mom who works in real estate … but I should go get a deal with Third Man.”

The long shot eventually paid off, however, and Cook seems both overwhelmed and overjoyed by the challenge of sifting through a lifetime’s worth of songs. “I have cassettes from the 70s, 80s, 90s and 2000s,” she says. “There’s about three albums’ worth of releasable material.” Her finds to date include a swiftly junked MySpace cut preserved by a fan, and a live tape recorded by an off-duty Whiskey a Go Go waitress and unearthed in a closet 50 years later.

As for the Nerves’ legacy, the surviving members are philosophical. “It makes me realise that we did everything wrong in certain ways, and everything right in others,” says Case. “It didn’t work out well at the time, but the music is here now, 50 years later. Who would have ever thought that?”

The Nerves: Best Collection is out now on Third Man Records

Elon Musk says he has ‘cyber psychosis’. Do you too?

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:01:14 GMT

Whether using chatbots for childcare or taking up smoking, a new affliction is sweeping through the tech world. Here are the signs

In the least surprising news you’ll hear all week, Elon Musk has said he’s not entirely right in the head. “I’ve got a little bit of cyber psychosis,” the world’s richest and most irritating man explained during an event this month. “Maybe a lot actually.” Musk added that, over “various points this year”, he’s had “AI or SI psychosis probably half a dozen times”. SI, in case you missed the super-important memo, stands for “superintelligence” and it’s what Donald Trump wants everyone to call AI now, for reasons too stupid to explain.

While the phrase SI is still being used 0nly by weaselly tech bros desperate for Trump’s approval, you’ll probably have heard the term “AI psychosis” bandied around a lot. On the most serious level, it refers to delusional thinking induced or exacerbated by sycophantic chatbots. People who have ploughed their life savings into a ridiculous business idea, for example, because computer code told them they were the next Jeff Bezos. But the phrase has also been used more jokingly to describe overexuberance around artificial intelligence, and that seems to be how Musk was using it. The comments about his self-diagnosed bouts of cyber psychosis came as the tech mogul waxed lyrical about how great AI music videos have become, and how he believes artificial intelligence now “understands beauty and harmony”.

I don’t know if Musk gushing over the beauty and harmony of AI slop is down to cyber psychosis or possibly his widely reported enthusiasm for the benefits of ketamine and psychedelics. But I can tell you that large swathes of Silicon Valley are dangerously high on their own supply of AI bullshit. And the sickness is rapidly spreading to the populace. So, I’m taking it on myself to help you spot a couple of signs that demonstrate someone has become over attached to AI or grown too credulous when it comes to the puffery around the industry.

A sudden cigarette habit is one of the more unusual signals something is afoot. This month, Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar told CBS that numerous AI researchers “have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers” that they believe AI is going to cure cancer soon. Sankar provided no data to back up this extraordinary claim, which he said was emblematic of “this mass psychosis, social delusion” around AI. But tech executives don’t need to prove things any more, do they? They just make grandiose statements and watch the investor dollars roll in.

Another signal your brain may have been fried by AI? An inability to interact with your small children without the help of a large language model. “I cannot imagine having gone through figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT,” OpenAI CEO and new dad Sam Altman said on Jimmy Fallon last year. Try to imagine, Sam! People have been doing it for a while. Earlier this year, Altman also informed us that AI is a great way to bond with your kids. “cool use case of chatgpt work i heard last night: connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests,” Altman tweeted. “every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc.”

While Altman’s parenting tip didn’t land well with normies, Marissa Mayer probably appreciated it. Mayer made her name (and tons of money) as the first female engineer at Google and the CEO of Yahoo; now she’s flogging an AI assistant called Dazzle. In a new interview with the New York Times, Mayer told a story about how, when her daughter Marielle was turning 10, her teacher wanted three bullet points about what made Marielle special. Mayer “felt overwhelmed”, and asked Dazzle for help. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer told the Times. I don’t know how much AI Kool Aid Mayer has drunk, but it’s clearly enough to have made her believe asking AI for insights about your kid is sweet, not downright dystopian.

Unfortunately, I do not have the cure for AI psychosis. But as the gold rush continues, let me point you to a sobering reality check from American asset management firm Apollo Global Management. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype … [AI] has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” stated an insight it published on Saturday. While AI is obviously a transformative technology, I suspect we’re in the middle of a bubble that’s about to burst. After all the mass exuberance, we’re due a very nasty comedown.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:00:34 GMT

Student supporters of Reform UK at Oxford college have organised evening with Nathan Cofnas discussing DEI

The University of Oxford’s Oriel College has been urged to cancel an event featuring Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas that has been organised by student supporters of Reform UK.

Arday, 41, was found dead in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship. He had faced intense media scrutiny after Cofnas made unproven accusations of plagiarism against him and said there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims.

Cofnas, a blogger and academic who has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, is expected to appear at an event called “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: Is DEI undermining higher education?” at Oriel’s Harris lecture theatre on 17 November.

The event has been organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society (OURS), a student group set up this year to support Reform UK.

Oxford campaign groups, British academics, members of the public and Oxford alumni have signed an open letter urging Oriel to “withdraw its facilities from the event”.

The signatories say the event “risks creating a hostile and exclusionary environment for students, particularly those of ethnic minorities” and “risks undermining Oriel’s role as a world-class educational institution” in 2026, the year of the 700th anniversary of its royal charter.

The letter accuses Cofnas of using his platform to assert discriminatory beliefs, and claims his blogging played a significant role in the coverage Arday faced.

Days before Arday’s death, Kehinde Andrews, the author and the UK’s first professor of Black studies, told the Guardian Arday was facing a “dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge”.

Responding to news of the Oriel event, Andrews said in a post online that it was “despicable and disgusting”.

Oriel College said in a statement: “Oriel College is committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive. We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination.

“The college considers events booked by students who are committee members of registered societies according to our code of practice on freedom of speech. When an event is permitted, this does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers.

“When considering booking requests, the college takes seriously the security implications of events and the safety of its members.”

‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey film

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:08:41 GMT

Tesla tycoon launched Grok project after criticising Christoper Nolan’s diverse casting for his Homeric blockbuster

Elon Musk has released an AI-generated rival to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey after pledging to make a version “true to the art of Homer”.

Having criticised the hit movie in the summer, the tycoon said he would use Grok Imagine to make a “historically accurate” adaptation.

The initial results have been released on X in the form of a seven-minute episode made in conjunction with Wonder Studios, a London-based startup.

Musk had objected to Nolan’s casting choices – such as black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy – and used the blockbuster as a vehicle for reciting his views on diversity, equity and inclusion.

The Tesla tycoon had promised to make a “full-length movie” version of Homer’s poem before the year ends but is sticking to a film released in episodes.

The first episode starts with Odysseus agonising over whether to join the Greek forces in their attempt to sack Troy. He then sails from Ithaca, his home island, with his men crying out for “vengeance” before they make land and start fighting.

The episode ends after 10 years of conflict, with Odysseus holding, ominously, a wooden figurine of a horse.

Xavier Collins, the co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the first episode was made in less than two weeks with a creative team of three, including the US-based director Dev Walker. It is understood to have cost tens of thousands of dollars. Nolan’s version cost $250m (£188m) and was shot in multiple locations over 91 days with a vast crew. It has made $1.8bn at the box office.

Despite Musk’s criticisms of Nolan’s film, the creative team behind the latest take on Homer are supporters of the summer blockbuster.

Collins said he was a “huge fan” and told the Guardian: “We were not given any direction to make it [Musk’s version] anti-woke or anything like that. We were given the opportunity by one of the world’s best frontier labs to work on one of the best stories ever told.

“The brief was ‘help us understand the technology, where it’s strong, where it could use improvement’.”

The episode on the Grok Imagine X account has received 7.3m views and some harsh feedback, with a reviewer in the Telegraph saying: “You can feel your eyeballs twitch as it unfolds in all its sloppy gruesomeness.”

Collins said Wonder aimed to make the next episode an improvement on the first and would address criticism, including the historical accuracy of its boats and rapid pacing.

“We are going to take a look at all of the comments and all of the things we could have done better and see if we can improve it. The goal is that the last episode we make is radically better than the first,” he said.

How has Andy Burnham used his first 100 days in power?

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street promising to transform the way Britain works, restore hope and bring an end to years of political division. One hundred days later, the prime minister has announced a series of measures aimed at making everyday life easier, he’s reopened the debate over Britain’s relationship with the EU and set out plans to overhaul public services. He has also managed to maintain an unusually visible public profile, appearing regularly on social media and even taking part in a charity edition of Channel 4’s Gogglebox. Burnham has said he’s been surprised by the public’s appetite for change, insisting his first budget on Wednesday would offer some breathing space for households and businesses.

But the early weeks of his premiership have also exposed tensions between immediate political wins and the structural changes he has promised. Here is how his first 100 days have unfolded in six key ways.

Burnham made a series of what Downing Street calls “everyday fixes” central to his premiership, targeting everything from electricity bills and bus fares to misleading discounts, subscription traps and antisocial behaviour on public transport. One of his first announcements, the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills across Britain, took effect on 1 October. The government estimates an annualised saving of £45 for a typical household, although the temporary measure is funded only until March. Other announcements have yet to take effect. A £2 cap on participating bus services in England outside London and new rules making subscriptions easier to cancel are due to start in January.

The bus measure also involves trade-offs. It is partly funded by switching international climate finance from grants to loans, a decision criticised by development charities. The strategy is intended to demonstrate that the government understands ordinary frustrations and can respond quickly. Yet questions remain about whether a collection of relatively modest interventions can significantly improve living standards. The VAT cut on electricity bills is not likely to help struggling households, who are more likely to be reliant on gas than electricity.

Ending rough sleeping was among Burnham’s earliest commitments, drawing on his experience as the mayor of Greater Manchester. The government initially allocated £442m to tackle the problem, and announced a further £432m on Sunday, bringing its commitment to £874m over different funding periods.

Burnham wants everyone sleeping rough in England to be offered a route off the streets or appropriate support before Christmas. But the success of the initiative will depend on whether people can access suitable accommodation and the services needed to help them remain housed. And it remains unclear how exactly the prime minister hopes to keep people from going back on to the streets and not staying permanently in temporary accommodation.

A big proposal is Burnham’s plan for a national care service in England, which he intends to help finance by reforming the state pension triple lock from 2030. The government plans to legislate during this parliament, while maintaining the existing guarantee until then. But the savings from changing pension uprating are uncertain and depend heavily on future economic conditions. Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, welcomed Burnham’s proposed changes of the triple lock but said “it will not be the answer to funding universal social care”.

Burnham promised a more open approach to managing Labour, with greater consultation and less reliance on party discipline to suppress debate. His appointments have included members of the Socialist Campaign Group, bringing MPs from Labour’s left into government roles. But he has disappointed a lot of soft-left MPs who campaigned for him after the Labour conference in 2025, when he made a number of media appearances attempting to prove he could replace Keir Starmer. His failure to include many of those from Mainstream, Open Labour and larger soft-left factions has been noted from MPs in the new intake, and those who have been in the parliamentary Labour party for a long time.

Disagreements have emerged, particularly over immigration. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, faces opposition from Labour MPs and some cabinet colleagues over proposals that could require some migrant workers to wait 15 years before securing permanent residence. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, declined to endorse the specific proposal before being forced to clarify her support for the government’s broader approach. Burnham backed the principle of earned settlement but stopped short of committing to every detail of Mahmood’s proposals.

A government source believes Burnham has avoided public rows so far because he is “taking his time to get policy right”, but they added, “isn’t it strange that a sitting cabinet minister had to apologise for making a joke … clearly we’re not one big happy family”.

Beyond the everyday fixes, Burnham has begun confronting choices that divide opinion within his own party. He has reopened discussion of Britain’s relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has damaged economic growth and weakened immigration control. On Monday, he revealed his personal desire to see Britain rejoin the EU during his lifetime, while ruling out abandoning Labour’s manifesto red lines during this parliament.

Energy policy has presented another dilemma. Last week, the government approved the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield, arguing that domestic production would support energy security and employment. The development is expected to create only 27 new direct jobs and safeguard 273 existing positions. Environmental groups argue that further fossil fuel production undermines Britain’s climate commitments, while domestic gas does not automatically reduce household bills.

Burnham has drastically changed the way Downing Street presents itself. The prime minister’s social media updates, which are pretty much daily, his collaborations with public figures including Mo Farah and online creators, and his appearance alongside Steve Rotheram on Gogglebox have taken his message beyond the traditional Westminster audience or those who avidly follow politics. His approach has attracted substantial online attention and made short, accessible explanations of government announcements a recognisable feature of his premiership. Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University, has described Burnham’s collaborations with influencers as generating a “constructed sense of authenticity”.

But there is a big difference between attracting audiences, of all ages and backgrounds, and explaining policy and persuading voters that measures will actually help them.

Labour has recovered ground in the polls, although the measures of how satisfied the public are seem slightly more complicated. As soon as Burnham entered No 10, the party’s ratings rose to 23% then reached 26%, overtaking Reform UK on 24%.

After the Labour conference, an Ipsos survey conducted between 15 and 22 October put the party on 32%, eight points ahead of the Conservatives, with Reform UK on 20%. But 66% of those surveyed expressed dissatisfaction with the government’s performance, against 23% who were satisfied.

Meanwhile, YouGov polling conducted earlier this month revealed 46% viewed Burnham favourably and 42% unfavourably. His net favourability rating had fallen from 13 points in August to four points.

Despite this, Opinium pollsters declared: “Burnham remains the only party leader with a positive net approval rating and holds a commanding lead over both Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage on who would make the better prime minister.”

‘How on earth is this man not sweating?’ The director who spent 10 years painstakingly remastering Bowie’s ‘greatest filmed performance’

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:00:36 GMT

Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgan has turned lost footage of two 1978 concerts into an arena spectacular. ‘You can feel the danger and excitement’, he says

‘Lost’ 1978 David Bowie tour film to play arenas in 2027, remastered by Moonage Daydream director Brett Morgen

In 2017, when Brett Morgen began work on his acclaimed 2022 David Bowie documentary, Moonage Daydream, he was given complete access to the late star’s entire, cavernous archive. “My eyes were immediately drawn to a stack of gleaming 35mm cans with the word ‘Stage’ written on them,” he remembers.

At first, the director – whose work also includes Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck and the Rolling Stones documentary Crossfire Hurricane – assumed the cans might contain some sort of footage shot around Bowie’s 1978 live album, Stage, recorded in mostly in Philadelphia. However, he soon realised they actually contained the holy grail of Bowie artefacts: footage of the legendary Earl’s Court shows later that year, which had remained unseen for almost 50 years. “Making Moonage Daydream, I had access to every filmed performance in existence of David Bowie,” he says, “but when I saw this one I knew this was without question the greatest filmed performance of his career.”

In 1978, Bowie had commissioned Just a Gigolo director David Hemmings to film two of the three sold-out summer shows at the venue – where the star was touring Low and “Heroes” – with a view to showing the film in theatres in lieu of a physical tour (he wouldn’t take the road again until 1983). However, the singer subsequently started making the Lodger album, moved to Switzerland, was reportedly unhappy with the film’s editing and the entire project was subsequently left behind. “He was moving on to other things at the speed of light,” Morgen explains. “So at that point I think the idea of looking backwards was distasteful to him.”

Before his death in 2016, though, Bowie had floated the idea of finally putting it out. In the new year it will debut in arenas – not cinemas – almost half a century after it was made. Morgen and team spent nearly 10 years readying it for 2027 as a multimedia experience. “It became something of an obsession,” he admits. “We spent over 1,000 hours colour-grading the footage, which I believe is some sort of record, but we really wanted it to look and feel like something you would experience today.”

It helped that the footage had been beautifully shot and perfectly preserved in Bowie’s storage unit, with excellent sound recorded by Bowie’s producer, Tony Visconti. Missing from Morgen’s film will be the extraneous stuff Hemmings added to the concerts. “I found a lot of footage of a young boy playing David that I was a bit confused by,” the director grins. “That’s not in the film.” Instead, it focuses on Bowie – in wonderfully billowing trousers and makeup – at the peak of his performance powers. “He looks amazing,” Morgen smiles. “I’ve looked at close-ups and I think: how on earth is this man not sweating?”

By the time the Isolar II tour reached Earl’s Court, Bowie and band were at the pinnacle of their game, signposting the future. “To have an electric violin, a piano and a synth player in a rock show in 1978 was extraordinary,” says Morgen, whose film combines songs from both nights because “It was very improvisational. Different arrangements two nights running. You can feel the danger and excitement that it could have gone off the rails at any moment and David was very charged by that.

“The audacity of starting the show with Warszawa, perhaps the lowest-energy first song of any rock concert ever – but that’s Bowie. By the end of the first set he’s reeled them in and by the end of the second set the place is just insane. The performance of Station to Station is incredible.”

During the second show, on 1 July, Bowie quips, “OK, this will be interesting”, and performs Sound and Vision for the first time ever. “And he’s cracking up throughout the song because I think the electric violin was trying to do the horn section, which David thought was kind of amusing. It’s a great moment. Then the camera stays with David when he goes off to the sides, having a glass of beer or smoking a cigarette, and he’s so engaged, dancing and smiling. It’s very joyous. I think this was the first time he’d performed without a mask, or ‘character’, so to speak.”

Morgen isn’t giving everything away but promises “surprises” as well as “a new medium of entertainment”.

“It’s not a movie that’s being shown in arenas,” he insists. “There’s multiple screens, a fully integrated lighting package, a 7.1 [surround sound] sound mix. The performance is 1978 but the presentation is 2027. The audience is invited to gaze where they want to gaze: choose your own adventure. Eleven years after his passing, it makes perfect sense that Bowie will be trailblazing again.”

Stage premieres at the Berlin film festival, Germany, in February 2027, before touring.

A year after the ‘ceasefire’ in Gaza, this is what our lives look like: no privacy, no peace

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:00:34 GMT

I look at myself and my neighbours queueing for water, and dream of a lost normality. We are now strangers even to ourselves

Every morning, I look at myself and my neighbours standing in the queue for water, and remember how each of us once had a life of our own, our privacy, our own toothbrush, our own home and our own bathroom. How we used to wash our faces and drink clean water without ever imagining that a day would come when these simple routines would become a battle with ourselves and with every drop of water. Even standing beneath a hot shower has become a dream postponed until further notice.

A year has passed since the announcement of the “ceasefire” in Gaza, yet the spectre of war, bombardment and death has never left our lives.

War is not simply the bombing of buildings or the evacuation of a residential neighbourhood. There are small wars inside this one enormous war. The tent is a war. The surveillance drone – the zannana, as we call it, for its incessant buzzing – is a war. Queueing for water is a war. Waiting to use the toilet is a war. The death of privacy is a war. Thirty people crammed into a single room is a war.

Every morning, the same question follows me: what will happen today? Will my children return from what remains of their school to what remains of our home, having walked along what remains of a street, when bombardment could take them from me at any moment?

They walk long distances because transport is difficult and expensive amid fuel shortages, repeated border crossing closures and the trickle of essential supplies into Gaza. It is as though life itself is being rationed to us, drop by drop.

In Gaza, waking up alive is not enough. You must also make sure that the place where you slept is still somewhere you can spend the following night. You must hope that your children can dream of an ordinary day – one in which obtaining a loaf of bread, an education or medical treatment is not an achievement worthy of celebration.

It is as though the ceasefire never happened. The sounds of bombardment, explosions and surveillance drones have continued to accompany our days and nights. What remains of our homes and tents trembles – and so do our hearts.

In Gaza, to be alive is to live on the edge of death. As though we are still trapped in October 2023, when the course of our lives was redrawn into a new geography, and evacuation became a matter of Israeli orders dropped from the sky on leaflets – orders to flee from one place to another, from one tent to another disappointment, from one dangerous patch of land to a corner that seemed slightly less dangerous.

On the morning of Friday 13 October 2023, the skies over Gaza rained down evacuation leaflets ordering us to leave our homes and head south.

We left the north, broken, and entered madness.

We left, but we have never truly returned to ourselves. We lost the people we were before the war. We are no longer who we used to be. The war has turned us into strangers, unfamiliar even to ourselves.

We left everything behind.

We left the stairwell, the curtains and the windows. The sofas, the router, the 55in television, the pressure cooker on the stove, the unwashed dishes – and half a lemon that, for some ridiculous reason, we always insisted on keeping in the fridge door.

We left behind conversations, arguments, disagreements, embraces and unfinished secrets. Stories told after dinner. A bunch of keys, and a never-ending chain of household troubles.

We left our photo albums, our wedding pictures, and the hairstyle that irritated me on my wedding night because of all the hairpins; the clutter in the storeroom, the gas lighter, the bathrobe hanging behind the bathroom door, the dining table, the backgammon table, and the water, electricity and internet bills.

And we left behind a precious set of drinking glasses, imprisoned in the display cabinet since 1997 on the charge of being “far too good to bring out for guests”.

After the bombing, they ended up out in the street.

And it turned out we had been wrong to punish our little boy for breaking a cup.

We never imagined that we, too, would be broken.

All of us were.

Three years have passed, yet we still fear hearing again the announcement that changed our lives: “Leave your homes immediately and head south.”

Three years of displacement, tents and fear. Three years in which school years have begun and ended without our children experiencing anything resembling a normal education.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

For the first time, school years are no longer measured in grades and certificates, but in the number of years children have spent displaced.

Third year of tent school.

It is as though the words I wrote years ago had been waiting for me in the present. As though I had written an early warning that I myself failed to take seriously.

I once wrote, in my 2017 book What’s That:

“A tent that lets us down.”

And in a Facebook post that same year I wrote:

“We are all beggars in the making.”

I never imagined that the words I had written in satire would one day become the details of our daily lives.

From Gaza to Khan Younis, to Rafah, to al-Mawasi, to al-Zawayda, to Deir al-Balah, from a tent to what remains of our home, we have arrived safely in the unknown.

Our dreams have yet to arrive. Our hopes have yet to arrive. I fear they may have evaporated somewhere along the way.

And today, a year after the announcement of the “ceasefire”, I am still standing in queues: for aid, for cooking gas, for water – and in the endless queue of those waiting for the unknown.

I wait for my children to return from school, and I try to recover something of the life we left behind.

The name of this chapter has changed. But fear has not changed its address.

There is more to tell – if there is anything left of our minds, or our lives, to tell it.

Akram Al-Sourani is a writer and poet from Gaza City, and the author of A Homeland Out of Coverage, Half-Baked Homeland and What’s That

Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey review – the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 13:01:46 GMT

It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t

Think back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and without having seen the film, condemned the supposed wokery in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, for getting Elliot Page to play Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen of Troy? As the plaudits and the box-office receipts for Nolan’s Odyssey piled stratospherically up, Musk showed that being a good loser is not among his qualities. He petulantly exclaimed that he could do his own better and more authentic Odyssey on Grok AI. And now he has released the first online seven-minute “episode” to a world that has long since forgotten about this claim and didn’t care in the first place.

In Musk’s version, as the tale begins Odysseus is – off screen – pretending to be mad to avoid fighting in the Trojan war. Grim-faced Palamedes and Agamemnon are shown testing this ruse by taking his baby boy Telemachus and placing him in the harm’s way of a plough in a field; Odysseus instantly rushes to save his child, showing that he isn’t mad, and agrees to fight. We see him join the armada, with Penelope and Telemachus (soon to grow to a little boy) left behind. This, effectively, is a prologue sequence that is not in Nolan. The expeditionary force arrives at Troy, and an intertitle tells us we have cut to a 10-years-later flashforward; the siege is about to escalate into the fake-horse attack.

As ever, the AI footage is ponderous and inert, demonstrating its familiar uncanny-valley stock-footage quality with classical-age Call of Duty graphics. Every single dramatic moment – Odysseus’s cod-insanity and his agreeing to fight, taking leave of his family, the hardship and adventure of the sea journey and the climactic decision – is all as motiveless and meaningless as the movement of shapes on a laptop screensaver. The ships are lined up on the sea like a row of high-def space invaders. Perhaps the worst thing about it is the deadly audio and digital-robot voice work. Every character speaks with that even, over-emphatic, declamatory tone.

Who cares? Certainly not Musk. He has no passion to tell us this story, only to win an argument that he long since lost. Perhaps he will now do his Grok AI version of Digger, in which Tom Cruise’s oil baron in fact saves the universe by drilling for more and yet more oil. Or maybe he will release his own Grok AI version of You Can See Everything in which glassy-eyed Elizabeth Holmes will prove her little blood-diagnosis box actually does work before she zooms off with Elon in his flying car.

Of course, as we are always being told, AI is continuously improving. With succeeding episodes, this boring and pointless series may look better. But if Elon’s AI-Odyssey is of any value at all, it is to underscore the basic truth: nobody believes AI has any artistic merit, only financial merit. In terms of quality, it is a pitiful fraction of the real thing, but a zillionth of a zillionth of a zillionth of the cost. It is time for Elon to make his own inglorious retreat from this phoney AI Dull-yssey.

Rule of thumb: why don’t we use weight measures for fresh ginger?

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 13:00:31 GMT

When it comes to ginger, personal taste often trumps strict precision, say our experts as they get to the root of the issue

Why do so many recipes state the amount of fresh ginger in “thumbs” or centimetres. With it being so variable in shape, why don’t you use weight? Nick, by email Let’s gather some of the Guardian food troops and ask them to explain themselves. First up in front of the class is our own perfectionist, Felicity Cloake: “That’s a very good question, and I don’t think there is a very good answer,” she says. “Maybe it’s just convention, because sometimes it feels a bit fussy to give a precise weight for the likes of ginger, onions and other staples if you’re not, say, Heston Blumenthal.” Often, it doesn’t really matter that much, either: “If you give a precise weight, people will perhaps think it’s very important and worry if they’re a few grams out,” she adds. In other words, if Nick were to use a smidge more (or less) ginger than Cloake in, say, her dal, it’s unlikely to make or break it.

Cloake’s fellow columnist Georgina Hayden agrees: “Unlike measuring a ratio of risotto rice to stock, or making a cake, the typical recipes I use ginger in, such as curries, don’t have to be precise,” she says. “After all, cooking should be as instinctive as possible, rather than relying on digital scales.” However, Nick is right in that ginger does vary hugely in shape, Cloake says: “If it was a very thick piece, or it wasn’t thumb-shaped, I’d cut it so the cumulative flesh of the ginger was roughly the same as the cumulative flesh of a thumb. You’re just trying to give a rough amount, without being too prescriptive. But he’s right, we should probably move to grams.”

In that same spirit, another columnist, Ravinder Bhogal, nails down the thumb measurement even further, taking it to mean a piece that’s about 5cm long, the length of an average adult thumb, and weighing about 15g. “I get that ‘a thumb’ as a measurement is not exactly scientific, but how much ginger you put in a dish is also up to you – more if you like it stronger and less if you don’t,” Bhogal says. If, for example, a recipe were to call for garlic as well as ginger, she would be inclined to use the same weight of each, although, she adds: “Remember the flavour of ginger softens as it cooks. But a centimetre here or there is not going to make a huge difference, so go with your own personal taste.”

After all, that’s a big part of cooking, right? When Hayden writes a recipe, she says, its purpose is also to empower home cooks to take a bit of creative licence: “A knob of butter, a pinch of salt, a bunch of herbs … sometimes, vague measurements are a good thing. Also, it’s mad to get out the scales for something as small as ginger.”

Cloake, however, imagines Nick “to be a more scientifically minded cook” than she is, so here are some final words: “Essentially, there’s no good reason for it, except to say that it gives an idea that you don’t have to worry too much. It’s just a guideline.” And there’s plenty enough to worry about in this world already right now.

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”

I struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to her

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:00:37 GMT

My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away

It was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey. Watching the slightly choppy sea from a boat, the last thing I felt like doing was embarking on another 5km (3-mile) swim. Mind fog had sapped my energy, and my mood was decidedly Eeyore-like. But as I pulled on my cap and flippers, adjusted my goggles and took the plunge, something shifted.

Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen. Breathing came properly. There was respite.

My swimming is far from sophisticated – my strokes are messy and I am mostly kicking from the knees. Still, I manage to move forward, albeit slowly, hugging the coastline of Turkey’s Lycian Way, turning a corner and entering an area of calm. The water is blue-green. Fish glide purposefully beneath, and I’m uplifted when I see a turtle navigating around a rock on the seabed.

I came to Turkey with SwimTrek, a Brighton-based company offering guided open-water swim tours. The plan is to complete 25km over five days. On the one hand, it is a holiday; but for me, the combination of swimming and the sea has become something more than that.

It began in Croatia in June 2024, eight months after my mother died unexpectedly, when a friend persuaded me to sign up to swim 3km a day for a week.

I had been feeling lost as I tried to come to terms with my mum not being here any more, and generally anxious, made worse by sleepless nights. Even on calm days, at times it felt difficult to breathe, the tightness in the throat unrelenting.

The only thing that seemed to help was swimming, especially with the focus on the Croatia challenge. My preparation was mostly in the pool, pretty much all of it breaststroke.

I had a rude awakening on the first day of the trip when I tried to swim either breast or backstroke – the latter steering me wildly off course. On day two I was kitted out with flippers and one of the SwimTrek guides taught me the basic front crawl technique. From that point, my confidence in the sea grew.

The sensation of being immersed in the open water is difficult to describe, but it brings me instant relief. I feel weightless yet anchored by the buoyancy. The rhythmic movement while watching the sea life helps to clear my mind of clutter.

This is a far cry from my early experience of swimming. Growing up in the south London town of Croydon, the closest I got to the water was a municipal pool. I was taken there by my mum. I would bob around in the freezing water of the children’s pool while she would swim laps in the adult one.

Going swimming in those days – the 1980s – was synonymous with verrucas and posters featuring cartoon images warning against “bombing” and “heavy petting”. The latter made me and other children giggle although none of us really knew what it meant.

The changing rooms were grim and you would travel home with wet hair, laden down by a damp towel and stink of chlorine for days. The highlight was a post-pool Curly Wurly from the snack machine.

On a hot summer’s day, my mum would take us on the train to Brighton. I would go reluctantly, more enthused by amusement arcades than the sea.

But I was lucky. There were glimmers of the sea winning me over. With an Italian father, every two years we would go on holiday to Italy, travelling by train from the UK to see relatives in Turin and then along the Mediterranean coast to see those in Sicily, where my dad was born.

When we were at the beach, my mum would swim up and down, seemingly for hours. I would look out for her now and then from the shore.

It is only now, since I have started swimming myself, that I wonder what those swims meant to her.

My mum lived with depression and anxiety, and I believe the sea might have given her the same kind of respite it has given me.

I don’t know because we never spoke about it. The only time we really talked about her swimming was when she called needing help to buy a cap, which had to be of a particular variety, or goggles, online.

My mum, who was 73 when she died, did other things to keep active, too – going to the gym every morning, at least until Covid, and she loved playing tennis and walking.

After years of talking about it, my parents moved to Bexhill-on-Sea in East Sussex a few years before she died. So now, whenever I return to the UK from Italy, Bexhill is where I go. I appreciate the UK coastline much more and find that walking by the sea when there, or even just listening to it for a few minutes, helps to centre me. Now and then, I brave a cold-water dip.

But it is the swim tours that have become a powerful source of all-round wellbeing, helped also by a welcoming swimming community and new friendships made. A year after Croatia, I did a 4km-a-day trip in Greece, where I celebrated my 50th birthday.

I managed to complete the Turkey one, too, feeling a huge sense of achievement and absolutely no shame about being the slowest in the group.

I’m already planning next year’s swim. And even though I’m sad that I can’t tell my mum about it, the sea makes me feel connected to her.

Want to know what you’re really like? Just ask the people who see you twice a year

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:00:37 GMT

Apparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is?

The worst kind of professional relationship is with the person you see twice a year, in a variety of different locations, because whatever they notice about you from that tiny observational sample, that’s what you’re like. So on the first rainy day in folk memory, the opening bars of Storm Austen, I turned up to a job with a photographer, soaked. I’d been on my bike and had tucked my trousers into my socks, so the accumulated water in the ankle area had seeped upwards, giving me a confusing wet leg-warmer effect, then a couple of dry inches, then an unbelievably wet rest of body. I was so wet that when I went to hug the studio’s labrador, he backed away from me like I was trying to give him a bath.

“You were really wet last time!” the photographer exclaimed, remembering our previous meeting back in March. “Well, it’s a wet country,” I replied, before the person we were there to shoot chipped in: “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” Then the photographer asked, “Have you thought about getting some wet-weather clothes, if you’re going to cycle?” and I said, “Obviously this is the first time that’s occurred to me, otherwise it would have happened at some point between March and now,” except she didn’t hear me because I had my mouth full of Haribo chewy sours.

“You ate all the Haribos last time,” my colleague observed, and I’ll skip the denials because even though I can’t remember that, it sounds true. Something about getting soaked on a bike makes me powerfully hungry – I think the sense of grievance messes with my blood sugar. “Have you ever thought of having breakfast?” came the next bolt of blue-sky thinking. It’s a great ice-breaker, making such a fist of your life choices that you become a human suggestions box, everyone mucking in with some basic improvements. But this, I insist, was two freak days of 2026; all the others have panned out fine.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 10:00:09 GMT

Whether you favour spooky fairtales, satanic card games or infernal hijinks at the chip shop there are all manner of fresh top scarers at large this witching season

Tis almost All Hallows’ Eve and naturally, the thoughts of all good video game players are turning to horror. 2026 has already been a bloody good year for the genre with Resident Evil Requiem and Silent Hill: Townfall leading the rabble. But this autumn sees a festering surge of indie horror releases, featuring everything from cursed card games to Nazi-hunting penguins. Here are eight terrifying titles we think you should sample while jack-o-lanterns burn and spirits walk the moonlit streets.

Allogloom (PC)

Mixing dark fairytales with classic point-and-click adventure gameplay, Allogloom follows a young girl who must leave her isolated village alone to hunt for her lost mother. The game’s eerie picture book aesthetic and doll-like characters have the feel of a 1970s Czech animation, making for a surreal and disquieting experience.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival (PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox)

This latest extension of Barker’s seminal horror novella The Hellbound Heart received mixed reviews, but then so did the Hellraiser films, and they were largely awesome. You play as Aidan, looking to rescue his girlfriend from the nightmarish realm of the Cenobites and their S&M obsessed followers. Gory, kinky and ridiculous it is quite literally a hell of a ride.

Grease Trap 99 (PC)

You’re working in a quiet Scottish takeaway, frying and serving fish, chips and pizza, when your boss asks you to start serving a “special” dish. But what is it, and what’s that strange gurgling noise coming from the cellar? Created by lone developer James Muirhead with dialogue in Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig), this is more of a short interactive horror movie than a game, but its glitch-ridden, low-poly visuals and dark humour keep you serving until the gruesome finale.

Hunter’s Moon (PS5)

Based on the real-life witch-hunts of the 17th century, this atmospheric immersive adventure has you playing as a young woman accused of devilry and now running for her life through woods, rivers and abandoned mines as her hunters pursue. Poetic and strangely beguiling, fans of the classic folk horror movie Witchfinder General, will feel oddly at home.

The Killing Stone (PC, PS5, Xbox)

Fans of deck-building card battlers are spoiled for choice these days, but The Killing Stone is the perfect choice for Halloween. Set in a remote 17th-century mansion, you must play an ancient card game against the devil to win back the soul of your beloved mistress. The set-up is familiar but there are lovely occult touches, and you get to explore the gloomy house in first-person between bouts, leaning its dark lore. An engrossing fireside treat.

Penguin Colony (PC)

A Nazi base in the desolate Antarctic is beset by Lovecraftian entities, driving its inhabitants to madness. But in a neat twist, you play as a penguin observing the chaos and exploring the wilderness, discovering weird obelisks and winding labyrinths as the cosmic horrors threaten your colony. Read our review.

Silver Pines (PC, PS5, Xbox, Switch 2)

On the trail of a missing singer, troubled private investigator Red Walker finds himself in an abandoned town, but quickly discovers he is far from alone. Influenced by Twin Peaks, Silent Hill and Alan Wake, this haunting 2D adventure is rich in atmosphere and crammed with intriguing puzzles. Read our review.

Tenebris Somnia (Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox)

When a young actor visits her estranged boyfriend, she discovers that his apartment has been trashed and he’s nowhere to be seen. Where is he and what are those weird symbols daubed on the wall? Heavily inspired by early 90s point-and-click adventures as well as interactive movie games such as Night Trap, Tenebris Somnia mixes beautiful pixelated visuals and FMV sequences to eerie effect.

‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assault

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 10:00:09 GMT

In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success

Cynthia Erivo is contemplating her favourite crisps, the ridged American brand Ruffles, as we sit talking in a quiet corner of a west London restaurant. Dressed all in black and sporting her signature elongated nails, she is known for her healthy lifestyle, but everyone, it seems, has their vices. “Ruffles are just perfect,” she says. “When you get a good batch, and the salt-to-potato ratio is perfect … it’s amazing.”

Erivo has just touched down after singing in Phoenix, Arizona, the night before, and has been running me through the health routine that helps her maintain her frantic schedule. Before her concert, there was the Dior front row at Paris fashion week, and she has just been announced as a guest host on SNL UK. Erivo doesn’t drink alcohol (today she orders some peppermint tea); she’s vegan; she doesn’t eat airline food, only her own prepacked meals. She even has an infra-red sauna “to help me heal from the inside”. Earlier this year she ran the London Marathon before jumping on stage to perform Dracula, where she played all 23 parts; she had rehearsed her lines while going on gruelling marathon training runs. All that requires discipline – and snacks – to keep the show on the road.

She has flown in this morning to promote her new film, the legal drama Prima Facie, an adaptation of the one-woman Suzie Miller play about sexual assault, in which Jodie Comer wowed audiences in 2022. Erivo bristles when I ask if she was hesitant about picking up a role so associated with someone else. “I get asked that question a lot,” she says. The pair actually met at a fashion dinner and spoke about the role – “Not asking any tips or anything” – and Erivo insists she was always going to make Tessa her own. “I’m never worried about what someone else has done,” she says. “I try to be respectful.”

Erivo plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual assault. Tessa knows how to dance around the courtroom – and the victim – raising inconsistencies that mean convicting a man “beyond reasonable doubt” becomes almost impossible. When Tessa is raped by a colleague, her world implodes and it’s made clear just how brutal the British justice system can be for women, who, according to Rape Crisis, have a one in four chance of being sexually assaulted, while only 2.7% of reported rapes result in charges being brought.

Miller, a former barrister herself, said the inspiration for the story came from her realisation that: “It’s almost impossible to actually run a sexual assault case and win it.” Tessa, says Erivo, doesn’t see how hard it is for anyone to recall traumatic events in detail, or how lopsided the system is, until it’s swallowing her whole. “I don’t think she realises that until she’s on the other side. I think it’s only then she realises what she’s been asking other people to do – when it comes to recall – is actually impossible.”

Is Erivo hopeful the film can have a lasting impact? “We have had judges see it, we’ve had lawyers see it, [but] one of the major issues is the way we view consent,” says Erivo. “I hope that as this film filters out, we start to have a conversation not just among us as people, but within law.”

The film’s central struggle is twofold: the legal system victims have to navigate, and the bigger question of consent, which is something Erivo thinks is often far simpler than it seems. “I think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t be,” she says, leaning forward. “It’s very clear what consent is: if a person isn’t conscious, or conscious enough to say yes, they’re not saying yes. If a person doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes. If the body language doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes.”

Tessa’s rise through the legal ranks as a working-class Black woman mirrors Erivo’s ascent through the West End, Broadway and Hollywood. After arriving at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada), Erivo had to traverse a strange world, deeply rooted in tradition and privilege that she wasn’t exposed to growing up in south London.

When I ask Erivo what it was like navigating that space she gives a one-word answer: “Hard.” She held down three jobs, including working every imaginable role at the Stratford East theatre, while classmates with means simply had to turn up. “I was exhausted all the time,” she says. “We’re in the classes, and it’s a Monday; I’ve worked all day on a Sunday, and probably done a gig at night, and I’ve come in. I’m falling asleep in class, so people were like: ‘She doesn’t care.’”

Erivo tells me the story about how she had to turn down a backing singer gig with Westlife that would have lasted two weeks and paid her £10,000 – enough for a couple of years’ tuition. “When I went to the registrar to say, ‘Hey, can I take these two weeks to go and do this? It will pay for my fees,’ they said, ‘No, you can’t. If you go, you leave. If you stay, you stay.’” Erivo says the incident showed how at Rada there could often be “a deep misunderstanding of what it is like to need money”, which is something she is trying to address in the role she has held since 2024 as vice-president of the institution.

“I want it to be different,” she says. “Rada is not an easy place to go to school. It asks a lot of you. If you’re a kid who is just really talented, but you’ve not picked up a Shakespeare before, you now have to learn a new language. If you’ve never read a Greek before, now you have to understand what anything means with the Greeks. That’s a big shift from doing plays at school.”

James Norton was in Erivo’s year at Rada and recently recalled how she would occasionally burst into song, something she had been doing since her school days in Clapham, where she’d perform Brandy and Monica’s The Boy Is Mine in the playground. “The room would go completely silent,” said Norton, which is no surprise because despite Erivo being little over 5ft tall, she possesses a gigantic voice. It’s a tool capable of the grandstanding volume needed for musical theatre, but also the subtler demands of R&B. In her forthcoming memoir, Erivo recalls being asked at Rada to sing the parts of a white student who was ill, but rather than being replaced was allowed to mime along. “The powers that be took my voice away and gave it to someone else,” is how she described it. In 2020 Rada apologised for institutional racism, later publishing an anti-racism action plan and appointing David Harewood president alongside Erivo.

Erivo set about reclaiming that voice in her post-Rada career, at first mostly on the stage, including a star-making Broadway turn in 2015 as Celie in The Color Purple. The New Yorker’s Hilton Als went to see the production not expecting much (he’d been disappointed by the film adaptation) but remembers Erivo’s Celie as being a revelation. “It was like listening to Judy Garland when she first started out,” he told me. “She keeps you marvelling at what is surely a God-given talent.” Erivo says that show was pivotal for her. “The Color Purple was one of those moments where I went from a jobbing actress and just pleased to be there to someone who was known for this particular piece. My life looked different after that.”

Before Broadway she’d had fleeting TV roles in Michaela Coel’s Chewing Gum and in Mr Selfridge, but things shifted again in 2018 when Erivo starred in Steve McQueen’s take on the Lynda La Plante, all-female heist story Widows. Hollywood took notice and she was cast as two African-American icons: the soul star Aretha Franklin and the abolitionist activist Harriet Tubman. But playing Tubman triggered a backlash. Some argued that because she is British-Nigerian, the casting was “disrespectful to African Americans” and part of a wider trend of Black British actors – including Daniel Kaluuya (who played Fred Hampton in Judas and the Black Messiah) and David Oyelowo (who played Dr Martin Luther King in Selma) – bagging roles that some felt should be reserved for Black Americans.

The criticism stung Erivo, and at the time she told the Guardian: “Before I’m British, I’m a Black woman. The first things people see are the colour of my skin and my sex.” I’m interested in her thoughts now, almost a decade on. “I still think it’s happening,” she says, answering almost before I’m able to get the question out. “And I think it’s a waste of everyone’s time.

“I think we could all just sit in a room and be like: ‘OK, so what’s the problem? What’s going on? How do we fix this? How do we stop doing this?’ Because nobody else does this. Nobody else is having this conversation. The Australians and the Americans and the English white folk are not having this conversation. They don’t care.” Does she have sympathy with the argument that African Americans do face – on average – more inbuilt disadvantages than some other Black immigrant groups who move to the US? “I have empathy,” she says. “But I also think that it’s hard for a Black English kid from London to also make it.”

In person, Erivo can be measured and precise, her arms and adorned fingernails spreading out wide when she wants to make a point. As we talk, she really comes alive when we discuss her experiences after the release of Wicked: For Good in 2025, the sequel to the 2024 adaptation of the long-running Wizard of Oz musical Wicked.

The film, a heartwarming story of friendship between Ariana Grande’s good witch, Glinda, and Erivo’s bad witch, Elphaba, swiftly became the highest-grossing movie adaptation of a stage musical. For Erivo, it was another new high-water mark, one which shot her into the upper echelons of fame.

The Wicked: For Good press tour became a must-follow, not just for fans of the film but for a meme-hungry internet, which feasted on any interview where Erivo and Grande were paired together. Erivo and Grande sat cheek by jowl; they hugged, cried, and – famously – “held space” for each other while holding each other’s index fingers in micro embrace. Erivo says she has seen most of the gifs and loves many. But there was a point at which it seemed to tip into something else, something darker.

Commentators started to ask why the pair were apparently so close. Was it all faked as part of a Hollywood psyop? What was really going on here between Erivo – a queer star – and Grande? “It was interesting that there were many people who had become psychologists from their couches,” says Erivo. “There was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friends. Like, why are they friends? Why are they connected? There must be something wrong with them.”

She leans forward and takes off her glasses, before beginning to sound like Tessa, the barrister. “Why are they showing emotion? How dare they cry? And how dare they laugh? And how dare they be emotive and alive?” she asks, sounding both hurt and confused. “It’s a double-edged sword,” she adds. “Because if we were dead behind the eyes and showing no emotion, there would have been something else to say about it. I wish there was someone who could have been like, ‘Right, this is the proper balance of emotion that you should show. Don’t show this. Don’t show that. Just this amount,’” she says, pinching her fingers together.

The speculation and online hysteria became even more heightened after an Australian prankster, Johnson Wen, jumped on to the red carpet in Singapore, grabbing Grande in an attempt to get a selfie with her. Erivo, who was by her side, immediately confronted him and put her arm around Grande. The moment was terrifying, says Erivo. “No one else was moving. We were on a carpet. We were exposed. My immediate response was: ‘Get this man away from us now.’”

The internet’s response was to give thinly veiled praise to Erivo, who was recast as Grande’s “bodyguard” – something she took exception to, arguing that her “humanity had been bastardised” after the incident. Today, Erivo says the reaction was one cloaked in a mix of misogyny and misogynoir – with people seemingly taking great joy in mocking a queer, muscular, bald, Black woman looking out for her friend. Erivo was asked by a journalist on another red carpet whether she was a “protector”, a question that still rankles. “I was like: ‘Oh, you think because I look like this that you could talk to me this way about something that was a human thing that I would have done for any friend, and hopefully a friend would have done for me,’” she says. “But I must be a bodyguard.

“I think the idea that it’s OK to rip a person to shreds in that way when they’re doing something that’s a naturally human thing to do just felt crazy,” she says. People in the public eye are supposed to just take abuse, she continues. “I think that this particular moment went just too far.”

I wonder if that experience made Erivo reconsider her career. She has often talked about wanting to push the limits of what’s possible – does she still feel that way? She reverts to her Tessa barrister mode, firing rhetorical questions like darts. “What else have I not discovered about myself as a person, as an artist, as a friend? Like what can I do? If I’m working towards what could be a possible limit, then it means I’m never doing the same thing over and over again. In order to push a limit, it’s gonna hurt a little bit. It’s gonna feel uncomfortable, which means I’m never staying the same. I’m always having to build.” To this very average human, that sounds exhausting, but for Erivo, perhaps it’s nothing a few Ruffles can’t fix.

Prima Facie is in UK cinemas from 13 November and Australian cinemas on 14 January.

Why won’t MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 10:00:09 GMT

Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue

In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table. Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.

Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters. We know that wealth inequality – with the richest 50 families in the UK possessing more wealth than half of the UK population – is weakening our economy, eroding our social fabric and undermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?

To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source. We interviewed 30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.

The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully tricking ordinary homeowners into thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actually left a decade ago – and quote “millionaire flight” figures from a seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.

Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.

Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”

Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”

When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.

For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.

One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.

First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Ultimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.

Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.

Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UK
