Defund Elon Musk

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 10:00:08 GMT

No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine

He’s Exhibit A on why billionaire wealth should be taxed, why we must get big money out of politics, why billionaires shouldn’t be allowed to buy up major media, and why our government shouldn’t give them huge military contracts.

I’m talking about Elon Musk, of course.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Musk “ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine”. The decision “sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration, U. S. officials and people familiar with the matter said”.

Musk and Trump, the Journal noted, have both “expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices” – although the high prices are really due to Trump’s war in Iran.

This month, Musk slowed “the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network … rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless”.

According to the Journal, “Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.”

Who gave Musk authority to slow his satellite service in the first place? Musk finally admitted this weekend that he had pulled the plug because, he wrote on Twitter/X: “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

So Musk can decide on his own when a foreign country working alongside the United States against a brutal dictator can have access to vital US intelligence?

Every time I list another of Musk’s outrages, someone says: “Yes, but he’s an innovator!”

He’s not. As is made clear in Alex Gibney’s smart new documentary, Musk, Elon didn’t invent Tesla. He didn’t invent X. He got plenty of help founding SpaceX.

Musk is to innovation what Trump is to governing.

Both are conmen. Both are megalomaniacs. Both love authoritarians and detest democracy. Neither believes in (or harbors an ounce of) empathy toward anyone. Both think nothing of corrupting governments for personal gain.

Both spout bigoted filth all hours of the day and night to hundreds of millions of people.

OK, let me just say it out loud: both Musk and Trump are loathsome human beings.

Someday historians will come up with an explanation of how two such awful people could have become the two most powerful people in the US, if not the world (what was it about the US in the early 21st century?).

But for now, the goal of all sane people must be to defund both and get them as far away from politics as possible.

That will be difficult, to be sure. Musk has so far sunk roughly $445m into the 2026 midterm election cycle – all to help Republicans retain control of Congress. That makes him the largest single known donor in the entire midterm elections. Will he expect a return on his investment?

Sign up to How We Win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

Hell, he spent a quarter of a billion dollars in 2024 to help Trump win re-election and ended up with access to vast troves of government data, along with billions of dollars’ worth of no-bid contracts with the Pentagon.

His Starlink satellite system is now key to the military strategy of the United States as well as that of Ukraine. He was also rewarded with a chainsaw inaptly named “department of government efficiency”, which he used to destroy USAID and slash other government agencies he doesn’t like.

Musk has given at least $168m to Texas Super Pacs seeking to elect Republican Ken Paxton to the Senate, despite (or is it because of?) Paxton’s long record of ethical lapses and legal controversies. Musk’s businesses are headquartered in Texas, so he needs friends there.

Musk recently pushed the false story to his 242 million followers on X that James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, was absent from the campaign trail because he had suffered a mental breakdown and was receiving counseling at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Ohio.

That story has been thoroughly debunked. Security camera footage shows Talarico at home, not at an Ohio mental health facility. (Meanwhile, according to the Wall Street Journal, on New Year’s Eve 2024, Paxton partied in Dubai with his extramarital girlfriend and two fugitives from charges of about $300m in healthcare fraud in the US. One of the men donated $190,000 to Paxton, $25,000 of it after he was indicted.)

The project of defunding Musk will probably have to wait until after 20 January 2029, when, let’s pray, we have a sane administration in Washington that will end all government contracts with him (his support for rightwing extremists around the world makes him a security risk), bust up his monopolies (a reinvigorated Federal Trade Commission and Federal Communications Commission will see to it), and impose a significant wealth tax on him.

No private individual should have the power to determine US foreign policy, as Musk has attempted to do in Ukraine.

If Musk’s Starlink system has become so central to military strategy that its Pentagon contracts can’t be cancelled, it should be nationalized. (After I suggested this on my podcast last Saturday, Musk posted: “Stealing companies is a serious crime. Prison for Reich.”

But you don’t have to wait until Musk is officially defunded. Stop buying Teslas. Don’t use X. Don’t sign up for Starlink. And support politicians who promise to defund him.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. England need to unearth World Cup core despite derby friction and injury chaos

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 09:57:07 GMT

Nations Championship games against Australia and Japan should be the end of experimentation for Steve Borthwick

Even on the most serene days no one would describe coaching England as a relaxing gig. With his side’s opening November Test looming on Sunday week, Steve Borthwick is already faced with assorted injury-related complications at precisely the moment he needs to start finding lasting answers to a range of fundamental selection questions.

The untimely training field absence of Fin Smith, pencilled in to be England’s starting No 10, is a prime example. With the two leading midfield candidates to face Australia – Seb Atkinson and Bernhard Janse van Rensburg – also unable to train this week, Smith’s calf injury has materialised at the worst possible moment. Add the Bath flanker Guy Pepper, who limped off against Gloucester last Friday, and suddenly there is a hint of pre-Halloween gloom hanging over England’s preparations.

There is also the bigger picture. At various times, Borthwick has been urged to base his selections around dominant club sides in Northampton, Bath and Saracens. How unfortunate, then, that all three went down in a sodden, windblown heap at the weekend. Nor does it help that the two most effervescent England‑qualified back-rowers this season, Jack and Tom Willis, ply their trade in France and are ineligible.

On top of everything else, there is the small matter of Borthwick being required to manage the increasing number of squad members itching to punch Henry Pollock’s lights out. To say Ollie Chessum and the other Leicester players who squared up to the Saints back‑rower during the East Midlands derby on Saturday were unhappy with their England “buddy” would be putting it mildly. Competitive tension is an inevitable part of the game, but, from Borthwick’s perspective, a “them and us” split within the national squad would be ruinous.

Because, in the end, there is only one overarching question that matters: how can England win the World Cup next year? The debate then becomes less about week-to-week contingencies and necessitates some longsighted vision. This next month is effectively Borthwick’s last chance to identify his preferred combinations before the World Cup and that opportunity absolutely cannot be wasted.

Nor can England afford a repeat of the turmoil that compromised their plans before the last World Cup. In the semi-final against South Africa, there were a mere seven surviving starters – Freddie Steward, Jonny May, Manu Tuilagi, Owen Farrell, Jamie George, Maro Itoje and Tom Curry – and 10 of the matchday 23 from Eddie Jones’s last hurrah as head coach against the Boks less than a year earlier. Given the circumstances, England did well to scramble as far as they did.

Compare that with England’s World Cup-winning squad in 2003 when only two players – Josh Lewsey and Trevor Woodman – were not involved in a thrilling victory against the Wallabies at Twickenham 11 months previously. While there was movement on the bench, where injuries played their part, 17 of Sir Clive Woodward’s 22-man squad from November 2002 featured at the World Cup.

Hence why this autumn matters so much in terms of nailing down certain positions. There has been some judicious filleting with Theo Dan, Ben Spencer, Ollie Lawrence and Elliot Daly nowhere to be seen. Charlie Ewels, similarly, finds himself on the outer. Kepu Tuipulotu, Noah Caluori and Arthur Clark have earned the nod, with Cadan Murley and Ben Curry seeing off the respective challenges of the unlucky George Hendy and Fitz Harding.

Tom Pearson, similarly, has profited from the injury to Chandler Cunningham‑South and Borthwick’s reluctance, for now, to summon Max Hicks, Courtney Lawes, Hoskins Sotutu, Ethan Roots or Jack Clement, among others. The Bracken brothers, Jack and Charlie, must be close too. At least there is an A international to encourage the aforementioned, but, equally, those not required in Bagshot this week now know something truly special is required.

Borthwick has to settle, as a matter or urgency, on who should wear six, seven, eight, nine, 12 and 13 this time next year – not guys who might conceivably have the highest ceiling at some unspecified future date, but individuals capable of turbocharging an England side that, lest we forget, have lost five of their past seven Tests.

With any luck, then, Borthwick is not just thinking about the Australia game in isolation, but the opening two weekends as a package. If all 36 players in training this week have some involvement against Australia and Japan it would also help to separate the wheat from the chaff: the management then can identify a 23-man squad to face New Zealand that, ideally, mirrors the one that will kick off the knockout stages of the World Cup less than 12 months from now.

Admittedly, that strategy becomes harder if Smith, Atkinson, Janse Van Rensburg and Pepper are unavailable. On the other hand, Marcus Smith is back in form while Sale’s Joe Marchant, if required, has plenty of experience. Alternatively, Gloucester’s fleet-footed Will Joseph could just prove the answer to England’s endless midfield conundrum; a partnership with his clubmate Atkinson would certainly work in terms of cohesion, pace and balance.

Anyone who has watched Northampton attack will also be eager to see the alert Archie McParland in an England No 9 shirt sooner rather than later. Then, suddenly, with Itoje, Chessum, George Martin and Alex Coles all scrapping for a start at lock and Pollock, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Greg Fisilau vying for back-row prominence, England could be in clover. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 08:00:06 GMT

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 06:00:03 GMT

Bankers have barely begun to repay the billions they cost the country after 2008. In this PM they may have met their match

Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.

This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from capping bus fares to that small but resonant sum of £45 VAT on average off electricity bills – get people talking, alongside bigger plans for a national care service, electoral reform and a possible journey back to the EU.

Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused, banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.

UK profits from the country’s four biggest banks were reportedly £13bn for the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.

Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Finance writes to the chancellor saying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries. Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him to scrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, and announced the tower go-ahead only after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.

Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists his net worth as $3.1bn, and he took home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir, Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.

This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islam recounts that episode as told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.

The bank payroll tax raised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?

Officially the bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP; others suggest double that amount.

Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take. Dimon visited No 10 last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.

So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, from the 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

TUC polling finds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.

Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.

Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so is employment, growth, business investment and average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest way to raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.

A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Would you pay to have the ‘best baby’? Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection

The Guardian Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:00:04 GMT

For decades the idea of eugenics has been taboo. Now it is returning in a new commercial guise

For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more.

It is hard to be young and to know that you are growing weaker rather than stronger. I had all the same aspirations that my nondisabled friends did, but I lived in fear of the future in a way they did not. I spent a lot of time thinking about what my life would have been like if I didn’t have SMA. The images in my head were of something like a double: myself, only rid of this one deficit, imprecisely defined, but encoded somewhere in my body.

In the 1990s, the human genome began to be mapped. Medical genetics grew ever more precise. I was vaguely aware of this, of the fact that genetic conditions such as mine were being better understood with every year. With that understanding came the possibility, however faint, that there might be some form of treatment for me beyond the interminable hours of painful, barely-worth-it physical therapy I took after school.

At some point, it did strike me that before medical genetics could even begin to pursue a treatment, an SMA gene would be identifiable in embryos. My other self might be me, cured. Or he might be someone living in my stead, while I’d never been born at all.

As science progressed, this other self came to seem more concrete, more knowable than ever. It was an immensely attractive image. In almost every other respect, I was happy to be me. I didn’t bother to ask who I might have been if my eyes were blue, like my sister’s, instead of brown. I didn’t ask whether I’d have been happier with a talent for music instead of languages. Only this one error in my genome would need to have been corrected, and I would have been me, only better.

Eventually, this perfect shadow-self faded away, for many reasons. But last year it came back to haunt me, as I read about a series of adverts placed by a company called Nucleus Genomics. Throughout the New York City subway system, Nucleus promised prospective parents that they could now have their “best baby”. By way of posters claiming that “height is 80% genetic” and “intelligence is 50%”, potential customers were led to a website detailing an expensive, comprehensive IVF procedure. Up to 20 embryos would be screened for every genetic disorder under the sun, but also for eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male-pattern baldness.

It was a sales pitch perfectly tailored to the present moment. We already seek to optimise ourselves in every way, through healthy, precisely monitored living. Through the measurement and quantification of exercise routines, nutrition and even sleep patterns, we can assess whether we are living our lives in the best possible way, so why not have the best baby as well? Although we may not be immortality-seeking billionaires, we are all constantly living under the relentless imperative to strive for human perfection, in our own generation and the next. And although it has taken on a new, consumerist form, centred on the individual self, that imperative has a familiar name: eugenics.

Genomics companies tend to avoid the label eugenics, and for good reason. Although the word derives from the Greek for “good birth”, in the wake of the second world war, eugenics was broadly disavowed as a racist, pseudo-scientific movement. Its stated aim was to improve the human species, but its most tangible results were the involuntary sterilisation and forcible institutionalisation of “inferior” people in many countries and, in Nazi Germany, the mass murder of people deemed a threat to the master race.

In the preceding decades, however, eugenics was popular among scientists, politicians and the general public. Although many of its champions were elitist, sexist and racist reactionaries, there were eugenic progressives, eugenic socialists and eugenically minded feminists. While some eugenicists advocated the forced sterilisation of people deemed unfit to reproduce, some advocated women’s right to birth control as a means of social improvement. After all, the belief that many traits in human beings were strongly hereditary was not incompatible with the belief that humans also needed good sanitary conditions, public health and welfare systems, and access to education if they were to realise their full potential.

It is impossible to understand the appeal of eugenics without realising that it held both utopian and dystopian elements. This is particularly important, because the return of eugenics also involves both. And eugenics really has returned, including under its old name. What may be called the neo-eugenic revival sometimes takes an explicitly racist, white-supremacist form. It talks about birthrates, IQ levels and the impending “civilisational collapse” of the west. It focuses on what it sees as distinct, unequal racial groups. It harkens back to classical eugenic dystopias, such as the influential American writer Madison Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race, published in 1916, an inspiration for Tom Buchanan’s racist rants in The Great Gatsby.

This form of neo-eugenics is easy to dismiss for people who think of themselves as enlightened. However, another form of neo-eugenics is arguably much more pervasive. It is careful about words and labels, and it eschews the state management of populations for a focus on individual freedom of choice. In one sense, this form of eugenics never really went away.

Towards the end of the last century, some philosophers and bioethicists began to defend what they called “liberal eugenics”. Nicholas Agar and Julian Savulescu are among the figures who have argued that this form of eugenics, driven by parental freedom of choice, is something entirely different from the repressive eugenics of the past, which sought to mobilise the state to marginalise or even exterminate entire groups.

The origins of this reorientation are much earlier. According to the historian Nathaniel Comfort, eugenics was already beginning to shift its attention from the population to the individual during the middle of the 20th century, in tandem with the rise of medical genetics. This was partly because repressive eugenic policies were controversial, and partly because medical genetics was a burgeoning science, very different from the pseudo-scientific assumptions of the past. In the US, eugenic records offices kept a hodgepodge of observations based on prejudices about race, class and gender. Medical genetics clinics were building knowledge and tools with actual, and growing, predictive power. Today, prenatal screening procedures have been part of standard medical practice for decades, mostly directed at the identification of disabilities and illnesses. Down syndrome is becoming very rare in countries that facilitate screening. Denmark, for instance, now sees the termination of over 95% of pregnancies where Down has been identified.

Of course we want the best for our children. In a neoliberal society, one obsessed with maxxing every aspect of life, the “best” might easily come to mean competitive advantage. A company such as Nucleus knows this. Playing on the term “generational wealth”, its website suggests that customers can purchase “generational health”, providing a kind of embodied insurance policy against deteriorating public health and social services. In the 20th century, eugenics was a project for the nation state; in the 21st century, it has reinvented itself as the logical extension of capitalist individualism.

There are still problems with the science. Nucleus’s claims about height and intelligence being genetic to a particular degree refer to population-level estimates of how much of the variation in a group is due to genetics (and are contested, at that). They do not mean “you can reliably decide how smart and tall your child will be”, even if that was a likely takeaway for some people. But in a way, applying population-level logic to individuals makes perfect sense. States need to manage their populations for instrumental purposes – to keep the economy growing, to avoid public health emergencies and to have enough soldiers available to fight wars.

For a long time, this management was carried out in paternalistic or authoritarian ways. But, as the philosopher Michel Foucault argued, a signal feature of the modern state is that it operates through governmentality – by providing the incentives for citizens to manage themselves in ways that align with state interests. If we, as individuals, freely decide to treat ourselves and our families as miniature populations to be optimised for health and productivity, that saves the state quite a lot of effort. But what does this mean for our sense of ourselves?

As the biologist and historian Adam Rutherford has pointed out, eugenics was always about control. The word itself was coined in 1883 by Francis Galton, a cousin of Charles Darwin who saw evolution as a process to be managed and directed. With the discovery of natural selection, it seemed obvious to Galton that “what nature does blindly, slowly, and ruthlessly, man may do providently, quickly, and kindly”, as he put it in his seminal 1904 essay, Eugenics: Its Definition, Scope, and Aims.

An enduring image from the early decades of the movement is the “eugenics tree” commissioned for the Second International Congress of Eugenics, held in New York City in 1921. Growing from roots labelled with disciplines across the natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, the tree is surrounded by the words “eugenics is the self direction of human evolution”. In that image, the accumulation of knowledge as well as biological processes are provided with a teleology. But what are their goals? What is all the control, management and optimisation really for?

To Galton, and to the generations of committed eugenicists who succeeded him, eugenics was politically and morally necessary in order to prevent societal disaster due to degeneration. Following earlier thinkers such as Thomas Malthus, they worried that too many poor and undesirable people were reproducing. In a short time, the superior peoples, whether defined as the upper class or as “Anglo-Saxons”, “Nordic types” or “Aryans”, would be outbred and outcompeted by their natural inferiors.

Eugenics’ proposal of wholesale management of the population was thus made in service of a particular ideal of humanity, where the universal “best” was defined in a strikingly narrow way. Through the notion of “hereditary genius”, Galton presented the privileges of wealth and class as innate qualities; while he explained undesirable traits such as “vagrancy” and “criminality” as the causes, rather than the consequences, of poverty, deprivation and marginalisation. Galton’s eugenic utopia was an idea that reflected the prejudices of a particular place and time.

The same is true of liberal eugenics in our own time. We may question whether the genomics companies’ promises of “best babies” are credible. But it may be more important to ask what their notion of the “best” is. What do they see as valuable and worthless in a human life?

Liberal eugenics accentuates the positive. In an attempt to distance itself from the forced sterilisations of the past, it prefers to focus, as Nucleus does, on human improvement and enhancement. But as Rutherford notes, in biology you cannot select for something without selecting against something else. Positive eugenics and negative eugenics are two sides of the same coin; without an idea of what is undesired, there can be no notion of the desirable.

For the Victorian eugenicists, the “best” was an amalgam of racial fantasies about “Nordic” or “Aryan” types conflated with the privileges of the upper classes, defined against the undesirable character of brown and black people, and the underclass. For the new eugenics in its liberal form, positive qualities coalesce around productivity and competitive advantage. The ideal human is strikingly close to the ideal worker, someone who is smart, efficient and unlikely to ever take a sick day.

Against this ideal stand the unwanted lives of people with disabilities and chronic illnesses. Intellectual disability was among eugenics’ biggest bugbears, but a range of other conditions recur as targets to be eradicated. In a way, this is unsurprising. Disability really does mean disadvantage. That is something I know in my bones – and my muscles. Disability, as the scholar Tom Shakespeare has written, is a predicament. It means limitation and restriction; it can mean pain and suffering. There are simple reasons why I longed so deeply for a cure. The reasons why and how that longing began to fade are more complex.

As it turned out, medical genetics really did produce an effective treatment for spinal muscular atrophy. About a decade ago, a drug called nusinersen was being developed. Some studies suggest that if it is administered early enough, it can wholly counteract the symptoms of the condition, while arresting its progression in adults. But medical genetics also proved that I didn’t have SMA after all. The original diagnosis was made on the basis of muscle biopsies and clinical guesswork. When a test for the genetic markers for SMA became available, mine came back negative. Instead, I was shown to have an even rarer condition – rarer, and less likely to attract research funding. I am tempted to quote Franz Kafka, who once remarked that there is infinite hope in the universe, only not for us.

But, in truth, that isn’t quite apt. Losing both the original diagnosis and the possibility of a treatment felt like a wave of sorrow, tinged with relief. Strange as it may seem, it also gave me a greater sense of freedom, that my life was really my own.

Don’t get me wrong. If there was an actual cure for my condition, I would take it. But there won’t be one, at least not for me. Too much time has passed; too much of my life is behind me. It is my life as it unfolded, and I try my best not to compare it to lives I didn’t live.

It is easier to think this way in your forties than in your teens. In the company of my nondisabled friends, I see plenty of injuries, illnesses and vaguely defined aches. We all have the markings of life. It’s not exactly that my disability ceases to matter as I grow older. In one way, it’s quite the opposite, as I feel the physical impact of the world on my muscles and joints. But I do feel a sense of convergence with my kith and my kin about the tenuousness and frailty of it all, about the need to take care of each other, as we hurtle towards what is coming.

Call it a kind of realism. Those of us who have kids know another side of it. If you plan to have a particular kind of child, you are setting yourself up for failure. Every parent I know has had to abandon their notions of what they thought their children would be for the reality of their particular children. I don’t think any one of them subscribed to the idea of an ideal baby. I hope they didn’t. Such an ideal is a terrible thing for parents as well as children to live up to.

This is the most corrosive effect of liberal neo-eugenics: in positing that an individual ideal of embodiment is something that can be specified, quantified and realised, it creates a framework for torturing both our children and ourselves. Why are we not this perfect thing? Why are we not fitter, happier, more productive? I’m not particularly sentimental about the value of disability in any particular case, but I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.

For me, hope comes from working to change the world so that it accommodates imperfection. One of the reasons I dislike liberal eugenics is that its individualist ethos runs counter to political measures that have mattered immensely in my lifetime. I believe we should direct our efforts toward making better societies rather than making better people.

During the postwar era, in parallel with the eugenic shift from the population level to the individual level, disability began to become a socio-political issue rather than a medical one. What the sociologist Mike Oliver once called the “personal tragedy theory” of disability was challenged by a social model that explained how people with a range of different impairments and illnesses were made disabled by societal structures.

Essentially, what constitutes “disability” varies with place and time. Although dyslexia can be hugely disadvantageous in the modern world, in a nonliterate society it amounts only to neurological difference. The kind of mobility impairment that I have – that is, being unable to walk for more than a few steps, or get up from the floor – is restricting under any circumstances. But it is orders of magnitude more disabling in a society without wheelchairs, or wheelchair accessibility. In between these extremes, there are conditions, illnesses and impairments that amount to disability in some contexts but not in others.

The goal is not to abolish cures, but to abolish the idea that only cures, or the prenatal optimisation of an embryo, can make for a life worth living. For the disability movement, the aim has always been to make a better world for everyone: a world where people with all kinds of bodies can thrive and flourish. That includes both people who were born disabled and people who had disability thrust upon them. It is a project that accounts for human variation, and the variability of life.

That is why it stands opposed to the neo-eugenic notion that there is a “best baby”; the best, in the singular, is not something the human species should be striving towards at all. It also bears remembering that the majority of disabilities do not stem from wholly genetic causes, but from an interaction of human genetic variation with the wear and tear of the world. There are good reasons to research cures, treatments and interventions whenever possible; there are equally good reasons to temper our expectations for how the human species may be perfected.

Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, a scholar of disability and bioethics, has put forward the “case for conserving disability”. It is a provocative case, for the obvious reason that disability, and chronic illness, are qualities which entail vulnerability and dependence on others. But, then again, so does the human condition. We are born helpless, and we age into helplessness. Even if we come into the world equipped for perfect health, we are always at risk of illness and injury. Neo-eugenics offers a vision of total independence, of a disconnect from society. Measured against such an ideal, all of us fall short. However strong and self-reliant we may think ourselves to be, we are a social species, with few prospects of surviving, let alone thriving, on our own.

The aim of control, and so of predictability, is intrinsic to eugenics’ notion of the ideal society. But who wants to live in a fully controlled, fully predictable world? A world where an external entity tells you how to live your life down to the last detail, what to eat, when and where to move, what to watch, all in the name of becoming your best possible self? Oh, right.

Against this vision of total algorithmic control, we must appeal to the unpredictability of the human condition. Shortly after the second world war, Hannah Arendt wrote her magnum opus The Origins of Totalitarianism, in which she traced the construction of “superfluous people” – whole swathes of the population made disenfranchised and killable by states that saw them as useless at best and dangerous at worst. Eugenics was central to this idea of superfluousness: of people who were incidental to the future of the species, or the nation, or the race.

Arendt described totalitarianism as, among other things, a vision for the absolute closure of the future, against all alternatives. In a subsequent book, titled The Human Condition, she laid out the alternative principle, by which human societies could grow and develop. That principle was plurality – the encounter with difference. Only this encounter provided the possibility for what Arendt saw as humanity’s highest calling – namely action: something with unforeseeable consequences and unpredictable results.

With her notion of plurality, Arendt was not referring to disability as such. But the concept can be extended to human embodiment. As humans, we are very much alike, but we are not the same. We may share the same bodily needs that must be met if we are to flourish, but our varying capabilities, talents and preferences mean that flourishing may look very different from one case to the next. Against the narrow-minded eugenic idea of “the best baby”, we can perhaps set another concept of Arendt’s: what she called natality. With each birth, with each new person, something wholly unique comes into being. And the world is made anew.

European Leaders Split Over Phone Call to Putin

The New York Times October 27, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The diplomatic outreach was part of an effort to push talks to end the war in Ukraine, though it was not welcome by all European leaders.

By Jeffrey GettlemanPaul Sonne and Jeanna Smialek

The leaders of Finland and Norway made a rare phone call to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Tuesday as part of the ongoing efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

As President Trump has tilted more toward Russia in recent days, casting doubt on Ukraine’s president and agreeing to buy diesel from Russia, European leaders have tried to step into the peace process to assure European interests are taken into account and protect Ukraine from being steamrolled.

According to the Norwegian government, the purpose of the call was “to convey messages directly to President Putin regarding future negotiations to help to end the war.” The call was supposed to last 20 minutes but ran for 90 and was an extension of a high-level meeting last week in Oslo. More meetings on the Ukraine war are scheduled next month in Abu Dhabi.

But not all European leaders were happy about the phone call. It immediately reopened a sore subject: Who should be the one to talk to Mr. Putin?

“I am very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative,” said Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister. “It is not coordinated with the rest of us.”

She said that she couldn’t see “any signs that Russia wants peace” and that “we should keep Europe together instead of going solo.”

Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, piled onto the criticism.

“Holding talks that risk dividing a united European voice is risky,” he said.

He added, “I’m not saying they have done that at all. I don’t yet know what those talks were about.”

Europe has been flailing to find a way into the Ukraine peace process. The war has been grinding on for almost five years, costing hundreds of thousands of lives. And the consensus is growing that Mr. Trump is too pro-Russian and not a reliable mediator to bring it to a just end.

Mr. Trump recently insisted that Ukraine “get a new president” and he continues to shift his position in favor of Russia. Earlier this month, he opened the doors for the United States to buy billions of dollars of Russian diesel, which European countries and Ukraine especially saw as a boost for the Russian war machine. Mr. Trump also recently used a crude word to refer to Norway, one of the most developed nations on the planet.

While Mr. Putin clearly benefits from all this, the Russians are increasingly aware that they need to negotiate with Europe as well. In Moscow’s view, the unwavering support — financial, diplomatic and military — that Europe has given Ukraine has enabled Kyiv to withstand pressure from the United States to make certain compromises in a peace deal.

Kremlin officials recently said that it would be good if Europe could appoint a single negotiator. For months now, European leaders have struggled to do that.

Many of the issues on the table are directly related to the European Union, like the rounds of economic sanctions that Europe has imposed on Russia and the billions of dollars of Russian state assets frozen in Belgium. European Union officials were given a heads up about the phone call on Tuesday before it happened, according to two people with knowledge of the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss an evolving issue.

Last week, Oslo hosted a meeting with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky; Jonas Gahr Store, Norway’s prime minister; Alexander Stubb, Finland’s president; and representatives of the Trump administration. A European Union official also attended.

Paula Pinho, a spokeswoman for the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, said “negotiations are happening in different formats, different places and different levels” and that the phone call between Mr. Store, Mr. Stubb and Mr. Putin was a “follow-up” to the meeting in Oslo. While Finland is part of the European Union, Norway is not.

It’s not clear if the Trump administration had encouraged the call. Mr. Stubb is considered one of the last European leaders to enjoy cordial relations with Mr. Trump — they’ve golfed together and Mr. Trump has said they’ve been friends for a long time.

Analysts believe Mr. Stubb could be an important asset if Europe and the United States ever coordinate their approaches to Ukraine. Top Russian officials have criticized Mr. Stubb, in particular over his support for Ukrainian strikes inside Russia. But a person familiar with Mr. Putin’s thinking said the Russian leader would likely accept the Finnish president as Europe’s designated interlocutor.

Mr. Store, Norway’s prime minister, said that much of what Mr. Putin conveyed on the call was “familiar.”

“He goes through how he sees this conflict as having developed since 2014. And then we state our positions,” he said. “He presents his views, we present ours.”

Henrik Pryser Libell contributed from Oslo and Christina Anderson from Stockholm.

Jeffrey Gettleman is an international correspondent based in London covering global events. He has worked for The Times for more than 20 years.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

Alexander Brothers Sentenced to 30 Years Each in Prison

The New York Times October 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The three siblings were convicted earlier this year of a sex trafficking conspiracy that lasted more than a decade. At least 11 of the victims spoke on Tuesday before the brothers were sentenced.

By Debra Kamin and Kate Christobek

Three brothers who ran a yearslong conspiracy to traffic women and girls for sex were sentenced to decades in prison on Tuesday, capping a dramatic fall from the heights of Manhattan’s wealthiest circles.

Judge Valerie E. Caproni, who presided over the trial of Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander earlier this year, handed down the sentences in a packed courtroom. Each brother received a sentence of 30 years.

All three brothers continue to deny any wrongdoing and are expected to appeal their conviction.

Eleven victims spoke for almost 90 minutes at the sentencing. A 12th woman asked for the government to read her statement on her behalf.

“What happened to me was not a misunderstanding,” said a woman using the pseudonym Maya Miller, who spoke at the sentencing Tuesday. She testified at trial that Tal Alexander assaulted her in a shower while she was visiting him in the Hamptons in 2014. “There was no confusion. Tal Alexander raped me.”

She added, “I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might have become had this never happened to me.”

Many of the women described the men as predators without remorse. Two of them described the brothers’ eyes as “going black” while they attacked them.

“It was like I was being mauled by animals,” said a woman using the pseudonym Isa Brooks, who testified during trial that she was raped at 16 by Tal and Alon Alexander, as well as two other men, at a party in 2009. Ms. Brooks was allowed to testify using a pseudonym. “It radically altered the trajectory of my life.”

Lawyers for the brothers pleaded with the judge for leniency and asked her to limit their time in prison to 15 years each.

Just a few years ago, Oren and Tal Alexander had conquered the Manhattan real estate scene, regularly selling million-dollar homes and frequenting New York and Miami nightlife hot spots with Oren’s twin Alon.

But in June 2024, a real estate trade publication, The Real Deal, reported on two civil lawsuits accusing Oren and Alon of rape. Those lawsuits led to more women coming forward and accusing all three men of sexual assault. The men were arrested in predawn raids in December 2024 in Miami at their homes, each worth millions of dollars.

Prosecutors argued that the Alexander brothers began engaging in acts of sexual violence as high school students in Miami. The brothers then built careers in real estate and security, ascending to some of the most powerful and elite circles in New York and Miami.

They used their wealth and influence, according to prosecutors, to lure women, and in some cases drug and sexually assault and rape them. In federal court, prosecutors have increasingly turned to charging defendants with sex trafficking when there is a pattern of repeated sexual assault, which is often considered a more likely path to conviction.

The New York Times has interviewed multiple women who say they were assaulted by the men, including those who say they were in their teens when the assault occurred. One of those women said she was assaulted by Oren and Alon together when she was a senior in high school.

Another woman told The Times she was raped by Tal when she was 13 and he was 16. The men have denied all allegations, including those in the civil lawsuits they face and reported by news organizations.

In the run-up to the trial, the brothers also conducted an elaborate public relations campaign that included hiring Juda Engelmayer, a public relations consultant whose other clients have included Harvey Weinstein and Sean “Diddy” Combs.

The Times also reported that they had worked with a Hollywood public relations firm that has been linked to several high-profile smear campaigns.

Shortly after they reached out to the firm, a website appeared, purporting to expose a conspiracy meant to take down the brothers. It featured photographs of women who had accused the men of rape, as well as photos of people described as crime bosses and leaders in an extortion ring. The brothers also arranged for payments to influencers and podcasters who made sympathetic social media posts about the case.

Mr. Engelmayer confirmed both payments to The Times.

At the trial, which lasted five weeks, 11 women ultimately testified. At one point, the jury watched a video of one of the Alexander brothers assaulting a 17-year-old girl.

Toward the end of the trial, prosecutors dropped two counts against the brothers, telling Judge Caproni that a victim had refused to testify after a private investigator hired by the defense pretended to be an insurance agent, visited her neighborhood and inquired about her children.

The brothers still face around two dozen civil lawsuits accusing them of sexual assault and rape.

Several of the women who spoke on Tuesday paid tribute to Kate Whiteman, the first woman to file a lawsuit against the brothers. She was found dead in Australia late last year. Many also noted that they chose to speak up to help give others the courage to do the same.

“I was in utter shock to learn how many others there were,” Ms. Brooks said. “It is a miracle we survived.”

Debra Kamin is an investigative reporter for The Times who covers wealth and power in New York.

Kate Christobek is a reporter covering breaking news for The Times.
