Karl Russell and Theodore Schleifer/The New York Times

“The effort to beat it is nothing short of an Avenger-level effort,” said Trevor Traina, a Silicon Valley investor who knows many of the billionaires socially but is not involved with the group. “Like the Avengers, this is not a homogenous group of people, but rather heroes of different stripes who share the same goal of protecting California. I, for one, pray they prevail.”

Many are aware of how it looks. Fighting a billionaire tax as populist outrage grows over inequality requires finesse. In a recent memo circulated among donors and viewed by The New York Times, organizers stressed that other supporters — not the billionaires — must be “the ‘face’ of campaigns.”

This account of Building a Better California’s efforts is based on conversations with about two dozen of the group’s donors, people solicited by it, or others close to it, most of whom spoke on condition of anonymity because the group’s mechanics are secretive. The Times also reviewed California campaign-finance documents and some of the nonprofit’s confidential presentations and internal documents.

“Our supporters have created companies, entirely new industries and hundreds of thousands of jobs here in California, and they want our state to remain the place where the future is built and where people can still afford to live, dream big and succeed,” said Abby Lunardini, a group spokeswoman. She said the wealth tax would “permanently damage the state’s budget, tax base and economy.”

The effort to fight Proposition 40 began with Mr. Brin and has swelled to include a wide cross-section of Silicon Valley power brokers. Donors have pressed business peers to consider giving to the organization and joining the Tuesday calls. Sometimes, the ask is for billionaires to consider donating a percentage of their net worth, a cheap commitment if it helps kill a 5 percent tax.

Mr. Doerr and Mr. Collison, or people who work on their political operations, have made many of the fund-raising calls. They are Building a Better California’s third and fourth largest donors, shelling out $40 million and $33 million, respectively. Each declined to comment.

Mr. Doerr, 75, is famous for having invested in Google and Amazon and leading the venture firm Kleiner Perkins before becoming its chairman in 2016. A longtime Democratic fund-raiser, he has a history of political engagement in California, including squashing propositions he viewed as damaging to Silicon Valley’s ecosystem.

Mr. Collison, by contrast, is still learning the ropes. The 38-year-old Irish citizen prides himself on a bookish disposition, and has invested money and time into arcane policy topics like housing reform and science funding streams.

The wealth-tax fight is Mr. Collison’s most serious campaign engagement to date. The tax could be particularly disruptive to him because most of his net worth consists of stock in Stripe, his privately held payments company valued at $159 billion, which is harder to sell. Mr. Collison has occasionally talked of his frustrations with the tax and tried to game out the politics of the ballot measure in private conversations, people who have spoken to him said.

Those dialing-for-dollars are presenting tech entrepreneurs with the option to donate stock that has appreciated in value, according to a donation form seen by The Times. That is appealing because the stockholder can avoid paying a capital-gains tax on donated shares. The strategy has borne fruit: Over two-thirds of the money received by the group over the last six weeks has been in stock.

Backers have included venture capitalists from top firms like Sequoia Capital, Coatue, General Catalyst and Benchmark, as well as founders of tech companies including Robinhood, Rippling, DoorDash, Reddit, Figma and Coinbase.

A spokeswoman for Kleiner Perkins, which has donated $1 million to the group, said its donation reflected its belief that “California should be the place where the most ambitious people in the world choose to start and grow their companies.”

A half-dozen other donors said they gave out of frustration and believe the proposition is poorly written, is illegal, and will not, despite promises from its architects, be a “one-time” tax. Some donors are not even billionaires who would be affected by the tax, but oppose the measure on principle.

Others, such as the Rippling chief Parker Conrad, argued on social media that the tax would unfairly hurt “unicorn” founders of valuable companies that have not yet sold or gone public, because it applies to illiquid assets like private start-up stock.

Several said they heard about the nonprofit through word of mouth. One said he went looking for an effort to support after California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who opposes Proposition 40 and said he could strike a deal with the labor union behind it to remove it from the ballot, failed to do so in June. The union pushed the tax to fund health care in the state.

Mr. Brin kicked off the Silicon Valley backlash in late 2025 when he moved his residence and businesses to Nevada to avoid the proposed tax. This year, he began working with the head of his family office, George Pavlov, and two political hands, the lawyer Kurt Oneto and the ballot expert Ned Wigglesworth, to beat the measure.

Competing efforts against the wealth tax sprouted, but quickly petered out partly because of Mr. Brin’s credibility. Mr. Brin’s team canvassed policy experts and other wealthy Silicon Valley individuals. Another group, organized by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen, joined forces with Mr. Brin’s.

Over the group’s first six months, Mr. Brin, whose political activity was previously minimal, donated $102 million of his roughly $260 billion net worth. He told The Times in April that he worried about socialism taking root, as it had in his home country of the Soviet Union, which he fled when he was a child.

“I don’t want California to end up in the same place,” Mr. Brin said.

He has written seven checks to Building a Better California, but none since July. His advisers have made clear that Mr. Brin wanted others to shoulder more of the financial burden this fall. And so his allies have aggressively tried to broaden the fund-raising base recently.

“Brin giving $100 million is like a middle-class family splurging on a big night out at Olive Garden. It’s nothing to him,” said Eric Jaye, a San Francisco political consultant close with some tech leaders. “The amount of wealth being created is an order of magnitude above norms. This is what late-stage democracy looks like.”

The group told donors this month that it was about $25 million under its targeted budget, with an unnamed donor willing to give $13 million more if others stepped up with a matching amount.

The group has sought to use its billionaires as validators. Professional fund-raisers for Building a Better California have told potential donors that they “have a number of principal supporters who are seriously engaged in the effort who may also be available for a briefing,” according to pitch seen by The Times.

Not that the group is highlighting these billionaires publicly.

Building a Better California’s polling showed “billionaires are seen as having a net negative impact across issues,” according to a donor presentation obtained by The Times. The tax’s opponents said they have an “understandable deficit on grass roots engagement” compared with its proponents.

The nonprofit has hired a social media agency that specializes in influencer programs to create content that “appears more ‘newsy’ and left-leaning than campaign branding, allowing the content to breakthrough Democratic audiences more easily,” according to the presentation.

Most of its money, though, has gone toward political ads.

This summer, the group bought as much as $97 million of advertising time in California. Over half of that early buy has been transferred to the effort opposing Proposition 40, according to AdImpact, a media-tracking firm.

Another third of the airtime has gone toward an effort supporting Proposition 42, a “countermeasure” on the ballot that the group stood up to effectively ban future wealth taxes. (Another ballot measure allied with the group, Proposition 41, has been de-prioritized.) Even if Proposition 40 passes, the tax can be nullified if Proposition 42 passes with a higher percentage of the vote.

This complicated, multi-measure strategy has not been universally appreciated in the Silicon Valley coalition. Mr. Schmidt told others this summer that he wished the group had stuck more narrowly to trying to defeat the billionaires tax, rather than trying to pass Proposition 42, a person close to him said. He has since donated more, totaling more than $40 million, and is the group’s second-largest backer.

Building a Better California’s leaders are hoping their efforts defeat Proposition 40 so “decisively” that it will “chill wealth-tax efforts nationally,” according to one internal document. If Proposition 42 passes, it “would provide more lasting constitutional protection from wealth taxes,” the document said.

The goal? Win on both, a second internal document said, and send “a dissuasion signal by defeating 40 convincingly.”

Conor Dougherty and Laurel Rosenhall contributed reporting.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

Our favorite restaurants of the moment in the city that never stops eating; updated monthly.

Credit...

Supported by

By Ligaya MishanLuke FortneyMahira Rivers and Ryan Sutton

The New York City dining scene is like no other in the world, changing almost daily. Our critics, reporters and editors are dining out constantly, bringing you more restaurant coverage than ever before, including our weekly starred reviews, our chief critic Ligaya Mishan’s annual ranking of the 100 best restaurants in the city, and the Where to Eat newsletter.

But we also want to tell you where to eat right this second — today, tonight, this weekend. That’s where this guide comes in. Updated monthly, it gathers recommendations from our entire team in one spot. Here’s what you’ll get:

A mix of old and new restaurants, and longtime standouts that we’re loving at the moment.

Restaurants recently reviewed by Ligaya and our contributing critics, Mahira Rivers and Ryan Sutton.

Highlights from the Where to Eat newsletter, written by Luke Fortney and Becky Hughes and edited by Nikita Richardson.

And don’t forget to save your favorites: You’ll always be able to find your saved recommendations under the You tab on The New York Times app, even as this list changes.

Alphabet City | Sandwiches | $

If you missed the Corn Star, a grilled cheese that oozes, photogenically, with sweet corn and scallions, you’ll have to wait until next year to try it. That’s the trouble with, and the beauty of, my new favorite sandwich shop, 20 Blocks. In the summer, this was the place to go for sandwiches built with fried green tomatoes, pickled green beans and other in-season produce. Then, in the fall, 20 Blocks replaced its entire menu with new dishes, like the George Squashington, a vegetarian sandwich with soft squash and pickled raisins. Don’t get too attached to it? Easy for you to say. LUKE FORTNEY

215 East 4th Street (Avenue B), Manhattan; no phone; asandwichshop. com

Save to your restaurant list:

NoMad | Indian, Pakistani | $$$

★★

More — more flavors, more textures, more life — is the theme at this New York outpost of the blockbuster London restaurant. Amber-lit and extravagantly appointed in gold, silver, crystal, lacquer, etched brass and embossed leather, the two-story space pays homage to an actual ambassador, the maternal grandfather of the sibling owners, Jyotin, Karam and Sunaina Sethi. Beneath the gleaming surfaces, the food, too, is the real thing: rich and vivid, drawing on the traditions of undivided, pre-Partition Punjab. Some dishes are so elaborate that a third shift comes in overnight to get all the details right. LIGAYA MISHAN

1245 Broadway (West 30th Street), Manhattan; 607-247-8870; ambassadorsclubhouse. com/newyork

Save to your restaurant list:

Park Slope | Korean | $

★

Meteorologists have predicted that we’re in for a mild winter, but don’t let that stop you from visiting Andamiro in Park Slope for a steaming bowl of gukbap, the Korean comfort dish of soup (guk) with rice (bap). The chef, Suho Lee, prepares an exceptional trio of long-simmered soups to customize with your choice of rice or noodles and condiments. My favorite is the milky beef-bone soup with rice and salty, peanut butter-thick doenjang. A tip: go for lunch, when Mr. Lee serves the beef gukbap with tender brisket. MAHIRA RIVERS

276 Fifth Avenue (Garfield Place), Brooklyn; no phone; andamirobk. com

Save to your restaurant list:

East Village | Vietnamese | $

★★

Few restaurants take baking as seriously as this Vietnamese spot. The chef Nhu Ton, an owner of Bánh on the Upper West Side, spent years refining her bánh mì after repeated trips to Vietnam. The result is crisp-crusted baguette that’s baked throughout the day to house pork liver pâté, wobbly slices of head cheese, barely set eggs and battered tofu slathered, radically, with peanut pesto. On bread this good, anything and everything belongs. LUKE FORTNEY

99 Third Avenue (East 13th Street), Manhattan; 833-674-5878; banhanhem. com

Save to your restaurant list:

Williamsburg | Seafood | $$$

★

Daylight saving time hasn’t set us back to 5 p. m. sunsets just yet, which means there’s still time to pop into Bar Susanne along the Williamsburg waterfront, order a heaping pile of the restaurant’s excellent pencil-thin fries and admire the grand East River views. But don’t stop there. The rest of the menu shows off the unique and unpredictable cooking style of the chef Jackie Carnesi while celebrating the East Coast catch: Think littleneck clam aguachile or scallops dressed in sweet corn purée. Order the ice cream sundae for dessert. MAHIRA RIVERS

6 River Street (South Fourth Street), Brooklyn; 718-938-3765; barsusanne. com

Save to your restaurant list:

Lower East Side | Vietnamese, Southeast Asian, French | $$$

★★

Bistrot Ha is every inch a bistro, clattery and electric. The young chef-owners, Sadie Mae Burns and Anthony Ha, started out cooking from a retrofitted Mexican paletas cart, as a side gig to their official restaurant jobs, before opening the wildly popular and claustrophobically tiny Ha’s Snack Bar around the corner in late 2024. Now they have a little more room to stretch out. (But only just: Tables are tight.) The cooking, drawing from French tradition and Mr. Ha’s Vietnamese heritage — fish sauce is a steady pulse through the meal — is often brilliant, sometimes erratic, and never less than original. LIGAYA MISHAN

137 Eldridge Street (Broome Street), Manhattan; no phone; instagram. com/has_dac_biet

Save to your restaurant list:

Astoria | Asian, Southeast Asian | $

★★

I first encountered the Burmese Bites tent in 2016 at the Queens Night Market, where Myo Lin Thway was serving dusky red chicken curry with rich, diaphanously flaky palata (flatbread) for just $5. He started cooking as a teenager in military-ruled Myanmar and sold his first palata more than three decades ago, at the Myanmar Baptist Church Fun Fair in Queens, his future wife, Rebecca Nant, already at his side. (Today she is the restaurant’s official chef, though her husband is still in charge of the palata.) The journey was long, but here they are at last, in a humble corner storefront in Astoria, ready to share the thrilling contrasts of Burmese food: fresh and aged, cool and hot, brine and turf, crunchy and chewy. LIGAYA MISHAN

38-01 31st Avenue (Steinway Street), Queens; 917-560-2480; instagram. com/burmesebites

Save to your restaurant list:

Williamsburg | Latin American | $$$

★★

The chic, loftlike dining room at Cafe Bar J. F. looks great in the daylight thanks to some enviously large windows, but the real charm here is a post-sunset dinner in the dim, cinematically lit space. It’s equal parts special and cozy, with elegant cloth-covered tables and the chef Francisco Castillo’s creative, South American-inspired cuisine. Dishes are labeled simply, like “rib eye with tonnato sauce,” but are surprisingly original; said rib-eye is pounded flat, seared on one side and dressed with the briny sauce, peppery greens, fried capers and grated horseradish. MAHIRA RIVERS

50 Withers Street (Meeker Avenue), Brooklyn; 718-387-3434; cafebarjf. com

Save to your restaurant list:

West Village | European, Mediterranean | $$

★

New York already had such an amazing supply of affordable pollo a la brasa spots, but in 2026 we saw the rise of pricey neighborhood rotisseries. Namely, Gigi’s (see below) in Greenpoint ruffled some feathers with its $40 half chickens. And soon after, Cleo opened in Manhattan with a rare specialty: tender birds seasoned with a warming seven-spice blend and finished in citrus butter. The chef Juliana Latif nods to her Levantine heritage at this cute bistro, serving za’atar corn ribs and haricot verts with minty chermoula. But hey, if you’re feeling extra fancy, maybe splurge on the crisp chicken skin with caviar? RYAN SUTTON

621 Hudson Street (Jane Street); no phone; cleodowntown. com

Save to your restaurant list:

Chinatown | Mexican | $$$, $

★★ | ★

A former Chinatown bus depot is a fitting address for this experimental restaurant, which takes northern Mexico as a point of departure for exploring the world. The chef Fidel Caballero grew up shifting between El Paso and Ciudad Juárez in the bordering Mexican state of Chihuahua, and he brings that liminal sensibility to the kitchen, stuffing enmoladas with Peking duck, turning esquites into a near risotto and dusting dishes with pulverized chapulines. The tasting menu is a bit too rigid to convey the zanier side of the restaurant’s charms; better to go à la carte, and to double up on the gorgeously blistered and chewy tortillas, fried to order on an upside-down wok. (For a chill neighborhood vibe — and a killer brisket burger — check out the restaurant’s nearby drinking hole, Bar Chucho.) LIGAYA MISHAN

3 Allen Street (Canal Street), Manhattan; 646-964-4836; corimanyc. com

37 Market Street (Madison Street), Manhattan; no phone; instagram. com/barchucho. nyc

Save to your restaurant list:

Save to your restaurant list:

West Village | English | $$

★★

At this loud, chummy pub, the chef Jess Shadbolt (of the acclaimed Mediterranean-leaning restaurant King, next door) honors her upbringing in Essex and Suffolk, England. The classics appear — brined unripe walnuts alongside cold roast beef, faultless fish and chips, the greenest mushy peas — with a few sly modulations, like bubble and squeak hidden inside a perfectly crimped pasty and butter marbled with Marmite. Rack up enough pints of Guinness, pulled in proper two-part, two-minute pours, and you might get your name engraved on a pewter tankard. LIGAYA MISHAN

213 Avenue of the Americas (King Street), Manhattan; no phone; deans. nyc

Save to your restaurant list:

West Village | wine bar | $$$

★★

The reservation game in New York City is not much of a game at all — it’s not very fun and you hardly ever win. Thankfully, Demo in the West Village always seems to have availability while still guaranteeing a bustling dining room of stylishly cool people, a well-priced natural wine list and, best of all, precise, imaginative cooking. The chef Quang Nguyen and his business partners, Jacob Nass and Ian Henderson-Charnow, along with the chef Dina Fan, have successfully channeled the gutsy, chef-driven wine bars of the 2010s. Dishes like lengua tonnata or lobster au poivre give substance to a talented kitchen’s ambition. MAHIRA RIVERS

34 Carmine Street (Bleecker Street); no phone; demowestvillage. com

Save to your restaurant list:

Greenpoint | French | $$

★

Gigi’s rotisserie chicken may be the talk of the town, but in many ways, chicken isn’t even the most interesting thing about this Greenpoint newcomer. Sure, the chefs have solved the age-old problem of dry, bland meat, but you’d do just as well with the umami-packed roasted maitake mushroom with buttery pomme purée. Or a well-curated cheese plate paired with a racy 2024 Mosel Kabinett from the bookishly long wine list. To top it all off, the atmosphere is cool, drop-in casual and genuinely unpretentious. MAHIRA RIVERS

★★

The great borough of Queens was once New York’s primary destination for Thai food that could transport you to a street food stall in Sukhumvit. But thanks to a slew of recent openings, like Hungry Spicy in Chelsea, Manhattan has entered the “Thai spicy” chat. The food here is hot, yes, but the menu has many perfectly palatable gems that showcase this kitchen’s balanced, flavor-forward cuisine. Fresh spice pastes, good ingredients and generous portions — who knows, maybe Queens residents will make the trek into Manhattan for Thai food now! MAHIRA RIVERS

★★★ | ★★

All the rigor of fine dining, without the fuss: The mood at this forward-thinking Caribbean restaurant is breezy and exuberant. To the right is the main dining room, where a prix fixe menu juxtaposes tradition and innovation — say, pepper shrimp reimagined as crudo, anointed with explosive drops of fermented Scotch bonnet, or goat shoulder dismantling itself in a sauce of dried scallops revived by rum. This is nominally three courses, but somehow expands. (“Fill yuh belly,” the menu exhorts.) To the left is the smaller, more freewheeling bar, for excellent daiquiris poured over feathery shaved ice, and butter-glossed patties that leave a trail of shards. The chef Paul Carmichael’s cooking is personal, distinct, precise and refined, but never overly convoluted. The work is invisible to the diner, who gets to just sit back and love life. LIGAYA MISHAN

That hasn’t stopped Chuck Charnichart of Barbs B Q in Lockhart, Texas, or her mentor Jonny White, formerly of Goldee’s in Fort Worth from trying. In August, the two pitmasters turned a slim building in Greenpoint into a barbecue shack you can smell up and down McGuinness Boulevard. Texas, this is not: The meats — turkey, pork ribs et al — are cooked in an electric smoker. And everything is sold in $45 set meals, no substitutions! Blasphemy? Not after the brisket arrives with a girdle of rendered fat. LUKE FORTNEY

★

The motto at Lonnies should be come for the burger, stay for the steak. The roughly 16-ounce prime rib on the dinner menu at this buzzy neighborhood restaurant, from the couple behind Inga’s Bar, is priced at a competitive $48. If that’s not your thing, know that some of this kitchen’s best work is produce-driven and fleetingly seasonal, like sweet watermelon paired with briny black olives. Grab a stool at the bar (there’s two) amid regulars sipping on smooth gin martinis and settle in for a cozy dinner, or weekend brunch. MAHIRA RIVERS

★★

Lungi is part of a vanguard of Indian restaurants to open in the past decade that are devoted to the cuisines of the south. But its sweep is broader, reaching across the Gulf of Mannar to Sri Lanka, a nation whose food is still rare in this city, outside an immigrant enclave on Staten Island. Rarer yet, perhaps, is finding a restaurant on the generally sedate Upper East Side that is so uncompromising in its deployment of chiles. The chef Albin Vincent is exacting in his calibrations of spice and attuned to texture, whether slow-cooking lamb, beef and goat into luxuriant shambles or teasing a batter of fermented rice and coconut milk into the lacy-edged, blooming pancakes known as hoppers. Much like “Paddington 2” or “Top Gun: Maverick,” you can love Mary’s Fish Camp without ever having seen the original. After a heartbreaking closing in 2024, this West Village restaurant returned this summer under the same Mary Redding. Look out for new dishes and old favorites like her superbly salty smoked trout dip, clam rolls spilling over with fried bellies and Canadian steamers poking out of their shells like wagging tongues. Consider the lobster roll? Hard to when there are cod sandwiches stacked on warm ciabatta and shrimp burgers zapped with sambal aioli. We are so back. LUKE FORTNEY

626 Hudson Street (Jane Street), Manhattan; 212-933-4414; marysfishcamp. com

At this serious-minded Italian spot — which was shuttered by a fire last year and reopened in July — the chef Stefano Secchi, of the acclaimed Italian restaurant Rezdôra, turns his gaze from north to south, Emilia-Romagna to Campania, with its surfeit of sun and mineral-rich volcanic soil. These are not the heaping plates of red-sauce joints, but each bite is so rich, you won’t go hungry: baby gem lettuces under a flurry of Parmigiano and charred onion powder; ragù Genovese, deep and hearty, each batch representing three days’ labor; a tart of ultrabright Sorrento lemons, the tang softened by olive oil crémeux and torched meringue. The dining rooms don’t have quite as much character as the sibling restaurant’s, but no matter: The food tells you exactly where you are. LIGAYA MISHAN

Nothing quite prepares you for the meal that unfolds at this darkly elegant tasting counter, entered via a half-invisible door. Fermentation is the mission and passion of the chef, Hooni Kim, and boosting health is his primary goal, not deliciousness, he will tell you, with a bit of a wink — because everything, it turns out, is delicious, and marvelously so. There are no experiments here, no modern adornments. The menu hews to tradition, with dishes that are rustic and rigorous at once, like a small yet bountiful bowl of stewed beef and doenjang simmered with vegetables, a doppelgänger for an Italian ragù, spooned over tofu made just an hour before. The reason Nishaan gets a pass: This is the only place in town — and likely, the world — to find a Pakistani chopped cheese with kebab spices. Or a halal cheese steak with tamarind chutney. Anthropic Says It Will Revolutionize Biology—Some Day

Wired October 27, 2026

AI giant Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have repeatedly claimed that the company’s models will revolutionize biology and drug discovery. But in its IPO filing Monday, Anthropic struck a humbler note, acknowledging its lack of experience in physical experimentation and the potential pitfalls of drug development. Wherever it’s going, it seems, it will take some time to get there.

Two years ago, Amodei wrote that he was “open” to the idea that AI systems could produce a thousand years of progress in biology in just five to 10 years. In August, he said on X that “Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine.” In the same post, he predicted that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in the next five to 10 years and promised a “deluge of AI-accelerated drugs.” The company also promoted the discovery of a “Crispr-like” enzyme by Claude in September.

While the new IPO filing still touts AI’s ability to “profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine” and compress “decades of scientific progress into years,” it’s reserved about how it will turn the potential into the actual.

The company says that its teams “need first-hand experience doing scientific research and drug discovery” and that its life sciences activities will require it “to engage in activities outside our historical experience as a software and research organization.” That includes handling potentially hazardous materials, operating laboratory equipment, and complying with a bevy of regulations.

Anthropic also toned down its language about its enzyme discovery, saying it “might have the potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool, perhaps for gene editing.” (Italics added for emphasis.) Researchers previously told WIRED they were skeptical of the enzyme discovery’s value and utility, and one scientist who had been studying these exact enzymes became suspicious that Claude used his research. (The company said neither its model nor its molecular biology team would have had access to this material.)

The IPO filing indicates that Anthropic no longer sees itself solely as an outside provider of AI tools to the biotech industry; it sees biotech discovery as a core part of its business model. And like all biotech companies, it faces the long timeline of drug development. Any AI-assisted discoveries still have to be researched in a test tube, then in animals, and eventually in people. Even if AI could help sort out which new drugs or targets will work in humans versus those likely to be duds, it will still take years of testing to prove their safety and efficacy.

Anthropic recognizes these challenges in its filing. “Any drug candidates or other discoveries resulting from these efforts would face the lengthy, costly, and uncertain development and regulatory pathways characteristic of the life sciences industry, and may never generate revenue,” the filing says. (For his part, Amodei made the case in his August X post for streamlining regulations for the coming wave of AI-generated drugs.)

US Security and Exchange Commission filings are generally more cautious than statements made by companies or their executives given the legal risks of overstating claims to would-be investors. And the IPO makes clear that the company believes its technology will drive revolutionary advancements.

But as Anthropic pushes further into biological discovery, it will face the same conundrum as other biotech companies: proving their worth in trials that can’t be hastened simply by adding computers.

I test gadgets for a living, but my favorite gadget this year has easily been a digital calendar. I've tried everything from the popular Skylight Calendar to other brands you might not have heard of if you haven't hunted the internet like I have. These handy tools take the contents of many popular calendar apps—Google Calendar, iCal, Outlook, etc.—and put them into a physical device, so you can see what's on your digital calendars without needing to pull out a phone. You can add multiple calendars, too, so I see both my personal and work calendars, my husband's calendar, my son's school calendar, and even the calendar I made to track my pregnancy, all in one device.

Digital calendars don't stop at just showing you your Google Calendar on a bigger screen. Many also double as chore trackers for your family (and one calendar will even give your kids their allowance based on chore completion), digital photo frames, and meal planners. It's a device that's felt more useful than the smart displays I've used for years.

I've tried five digital calendars just this year and have a few easy favorites. While Skylight has been an enduring favorite for the overall experience, you will hit a paywall to use two of my favorite features, the photo screensaver and meal planning. If you're looking to pick a digital calendar that's subscription-free, my favorite of these is on sale right now.

Everblog

Amazon

Everblog

Everblog's HomeCal packs an incredibly similar user experience to Skylight, but unlike the latter, it doesn't require a subscription to access all its features. You'll get tabs to track chores, to-dos, rewards (for completing those chores and tasks), and meal planning. Use the accompanying app to set up the calendars and organize profiles for your family members, then you're ready to go. The photo uploader tool in Everblog's app is slower than Skylight's since you can upload only one image at a time, but I'd take that over needing to pay a recurring fee. Everblog's 21.5-inch screen is large, but not so large that I didn't feel like I couldn't find a place for it. Neither of those accessories is on sale right now, but buying the calendar on sale (currently $300 at Amazon—or $100 off—and $50 off directly from Everblog) will give you some room in the budget to consider these handy add-ons. Enjoy your most organized holiday season yet.

Anthropic Flags Gas Supply as One of Its Biggest Near-Term Risks

Wired October 27, 2026

Data centers’ reliance on private natural gas plants is a key near-term risk to Anthropic. In the company’s IPO filing on Monday, it warned that the data center gas buildout could drive prices higher in some regions, affecting its AI ambitions and other data center operators around the country.

As America’s data center boom keeps growing, the facilities are set to consume a staggering amount of natural gas, with many companies opting to build their own plants rather than wait years for grid connection. Energy analyst company Cleanview estimates that behind-the-meter gas projects in development as of October 2026 at 110 gigawatts, up from just 20 gigawatts in July of 2025.

Competition from other natural gas-fired data centers could leave Anthropic exposed to “fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control,” the company wrote in its IPO filing, and “could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

The surge in demand for gas comes on top of an already tight market for natural gas. US export terminals are sending more gas abroad for a variety of reasons, including geopolitical conflicts and federal support for exports. Export demand is expected to double over the next decade.

Still, data centers could add a hefty chunk of demand, even if just some of what’s in the pipeline is built. BloombergNEF estimates that grid-connected data centers alone could add an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas demand by 2035, a 15 percent increase in overall demand. Adding on a conservative estimate of onsite gas capacity in the pipeline would add another 3 billion cubic feet per day by the next decade.

Anthropic has traditionally relied on renting compute from major cloud service providers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX are specifically named in the IPO. (Anthropic is renting server space from the latter’s Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee, which is facing a lawsuit for relying on unpermitted gas turbines.)

But the company has moved in recent months to directly lease and develop data centers, in a bid to lessen its reliance on other tech giants and more directly control its own data centers. In the IPO, it singles out its $50 billion partnership with Fluidstack, announced last year, which “provides data center development and operations services” for the company. It has announced data center sites in Texas and New York.

Doing so, though, exposes it to more risks, including the rises in natural gas prices. The company has also been tied to developing data centers with major on-site gas projects in states as spread out as Louisiana, Texas, and West Virginia. The latter could eventually be among the largest gas plants in the US, according to developer Nscale’s own IPO filing.

The geographical dispersion of its data centers opens Anthropic up to regional gas supply shocks and markets. That’s particularly true in the Southeast, where projects will have to compete with LNG exports.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if you start to see gas start to get more expensive in Louisiana and Texas, where all the LNG projects are concentrated,” says Enrique Gonzalez, BNEF’s head of gas research for the Americas.

Texas is also the national hotspot for behind-the-meter data center development, putting multiple developers in competition for the same, potentially limited gas supply. Anthropic acknowledges this risk in its IPO filing, writing that “we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply.”

Any strain on gas supply could have knock-on prices for home energy bills. Gonzalez thinks that natural gas producers learned their lesson from the energy crisis of 2022, when high gas prices caused production to increase, in turn knocking down prices. While markets are unlikely to be that extreme in the coming years, “if hub prices rise, there’s a chance—unless you have legislation—that it goes to consumers,” he says.

One solution for this is, of course, to look at renewables, which also have the added climate benefit of being carbon-free. But Anthropic mentions them once in its IPO filing, and only to dismiss them. “Newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost,” the prospectus states.

While the Friday after Thanksgiving has traditionally been the busiest shopping day of the year, Black Friday deals have gradually spread well beyond the day. The tricky part for early birds is knowing what’s a genuine deal and what’s likely to go even lower when Black Friday arrives.

The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we only highlight deals on devices we have tested that we’d be comfortable recommending to friends and family. Some of these picks may be cheaper for Black Friday, but these are the discounts that have caught our eye so far.

Apple

Amazon

Amazon (4-Pack)

This is the lowest price we have seen on the single tag, but it drops this low pretty frequently.

Apple

Best Buy

Amazon

Best Buy

This Merino Wool T-Shirt Doesn’t Cost a Fortune

Wired October 27, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I've been singing the praises of merino wool in these pages for over five years. Most people have come around to the fact that merino wool is a super fiber; it's both sustainable and quite remarkable in its capabilities. Merino wool somehow manages to be comfortable in 95-degree heat, and it'll insulate you against below-freezing temperatures. Unlike synthetic fibers derived from petroleum, merino wool resists odors and is naturally breathable. What's not to love? The price.

Merino wool isn't cheap. That's why I love these merino T-shirts from Quince: They're just $42.

Quince

Quince (Men's)

Quince (Women's)

The Quince All-Season T-shirt is 100 percent extra-fine merino wool with a 165-gsm weave, which is perfect even on the warmest summer days where I live. (Admittedly, I think the hottest it got this summer was 92 Fahrenheit). I like the relaxed fit here as well. It's neither skintight technical nor overly loose and baggy. It fits like a T-shirt is supposed to. That's what Quince does well in a number of categories: offer a solid, no-nonsense, competitively priced merino wool T-shirt that fits well and feels great. As an added bonus, Quince offers free shipping and free returns for 365 days. I haven't actually tested either—I haven't needed to, my Quince T-shirt is still going strong after two years of use. But there are plenty of customer reviews on Reddit suggesting the company does honor that offer.

Not sold on the idea of a wool T-shirt? I understand. When I started testing merino, I too had visions of lumberjacks in plaid and itchy sweaters someone's grandma had knitted. None of that is merino wool. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool, which has evolved to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures and is comfortable to wear next to your skin.

One wool myth that's not just a myth is care. Merino isn't cotton. Quince's care instructions for the All Season T-shirt say to wash it in cold water and lay flat to dry. The latter is important, as hanging merino wool to dry will stretch it out (because of the water weight). Can you throw it in the dryer? Yes. I have, for testing purposes only. It will shrink, and it will wear it out much, much faster, but you can do it.

A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There

Wired October 27, 2026

On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.

For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.

Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.

Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”

Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.

Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U. S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”

According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.

By March 26, the emails show, Lewin still hadn’t accepted the job offer, and had not filed his OF-306, the federal government's standard pre-employment background screening form; without this document, a federal agency cannot lawfully issue a final job offer or consummate an appointment. An HR executive noted in an email dated March 31 that Lewin had not completed the onboarding tasks required to initiate “the security reciprocity process,” which recognizes the transfer of an employees’ security clearance from one agency to another. (A detailing agreement between the GSA and USAID dated February 14—two weeks after Lewin says he began at USAID—specifes that “commencement of the detail is contingent upon the Detailee’s successful adjudication and receipt of any necessary security clearances and other pre-employment screening required by USAID.”)

On March 28, Lewin signed a letter terminating all remaining USAID staff. And as he executed sweeping powers to liquidate all 60 of USAID’s overseas missions and cancel thousands of lifesaving projects worldwide, HR repeatedly followed up with Korzeniewski.

More than a week after Lewin’s appointment, the emails show, a USAID official told Korzeniewski that the agency’s office of security was “unable to issue a USAID ID card to Jeremy Lewin as SEC [the agency’s secure database] did not have a record of Jeremy as an employee.”

“Until you’re onboarded at USAID, you aren’t even in the system,” says Natalia Machuca, a 15-year agency veteran who hired many staff. “You can’t get a badge, get into your computer, or even walk around the building.”

Lewin tells WIRED, “I was a regular government employee with a valid security clearance held by the State Department during this entire period. USAID HR was confused about this paperwork for a period of days, but this issue was cleared up once they were made aware of the dual appointment and my State Department position.”

But according to a top executive in HR, no one from their office saw any delegation documents until late April 2025. As one longtime HR executive at the agency, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of Lewin: “He was the equivalent of an administrative ghost.”

“I think this creates a huge accountability problem if you have these actors who are making really consequential life-or-death decisions who didn't go through any standard confirmation process,” says Don Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, “or in this case didn't even complete their paperwork to become a formal employee.”

Lewin—who a White House official says submitted all the paperwork required for employment and clearance—provided WIRED with two documents, both dated March 18, 2025. One is an appointment and compensation waiver, signed by Rubio, naming Lewin director of strategy and planning, and stating that he would not be paid “pursuant to, among other provisions of law, 22 U. S. C. § 2385(b).” The other is a standard appointment affidavit naming Lewin USAID’s director of strategy and programs. A signature on the form appears to be Rubio’s, with the title given as “HRO”—usually an abbreviation for human resources officer. The State Department did not answer questions about this document.

To one former senior USAID official, Rubio’s use of 22 U. S. C. § 2385(b)—an obscure provision traditionally reserved for rapidly deploying emergency-response staff to disaster zones abroad—to appoint Lewin looks like a legal contortion.

“It is so unconventional that I’d never seen it used before I got to USAID,” the official said. “It was created for the purposes of scaling up really quickly if there was some outbreak of a virus somewhere and they needed to bring people on, then let them go.”

Brian Feinstein, a law professor at the Wharton School of Business, acknowledged that while using 22 U. S. C. § 2385(b) to appoint Lewin is complex, it appears to him to be legal. “Because Lewin's appointment is consistent with this law regarding USAID personnel,” he says, “his unusual status should not be a factor.”

Outside of this point, legal questions also remain about Lewin’s actions at the agency before he was appointed by Rubio, and his failure to complete the onboarding required to begin his initial detail period at USAID. During this time he was part of a team that issued sweeping orders, including one to then acting administrator Jason Gray to lock all USAID staff worldwide out of email and all communication systems, which could have put many staff’s lives at risk, and to terminate 57 of the agency’s top officials.

David A. Super, professor of law and economics at Georgetown University, describes Lewin’s failure to complete his onboarding as much more than an administrative slip-up. “You can’t just walk in the door of a federal agency and become an employee,” he says. Under federal law, a cabinet secretary can only assign the authority of a Senate-confirmed position such as USAID administrator to a subordinate official—an agency employee or officer who works under the supervision of a higher-ranking officer. These regulations, Super says, are a way for Congress to guarantee that “someone walking off the street should not be given these enormous powers.”

Nina Mendelson, who teaches law at the University of Michigan, agrees. She says the administration appeared to be trying to bypass the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, a federal statute that dictates how temporary vacancies in Senate-confirmed executive branch positions are filled. “The FVRA specifies who may fill in, for a limited time, when a Senate-confirmed post is vacant,” she says. “The possibilities are a first assistant, someone holding another Senate-confirmed post, or a longtime civil servant in the particular agency. Lewin doesn’t seem to have been any one of those.”

Lewin being placed atop USAID came in a specific context. In February 2025, shortly after the arrival of Lewin and other DOGE affiliates at the agency, two dozen current and former USAID employees and contractors sued Musk and DOGE in Maryland District Court. They successfully secured a preliminary injunction on March 18, on the grounds that special government employees—temporary hires from outside USAID and the government—lacked the authority to execute sweeping federal actions. That same day, Rubio delegated powers of the agency’s top job to Lewin.

On March 28, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Justice Department an emergency stay, pausing the injunction based on the administration’s argument that the actions were taken by Lewin in his role as a federally appointed official. In his declaration, Lewin wrote: “I am not, and have never been, an employee of Elon Musk or USDS,” adding, “I report directly and only to Acting Administrator Rubio” in his role at USAID.

The ruling gave Lewin the green light to fire thousands of career civil service and Foreign Service staff that very day, but the legal battle didn’t end there. The district judge has since allowed thousands of affected employees to sue DOGE and the administration as a group and ordered the government to hand over a trove of internal documents.

Kevin Byrnes, a veteran federal employment law attorney representing more than 170 former and current career USAID staff in a separate suit challenging DOGE’s role in the mass firings, says the fact that Lewin had not completed mandatory onboarding paperwork raises even more questions about the authority of nonconfirmed agency leadership, and potentially exposes Lewin personally.

“If Lewin didn’t even fill out the papers and was not authorized to take these actions, then he could be exposed to personal liability,” says Byrnes, who is asking the court to reinstate all the plaintiffs to their USAID jobs, with back pay.

UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech

Wired October 27, 2026

A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.

The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.

The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.

Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.

Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.

“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”

A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”

Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.

In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.

Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.

Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.

Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.

“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”
